  • 2.3 Homeowners
  • 2.4 Dwelling Fire & Other Personal Property
  • 2.5 Personal Umbrella
  • 1.4 The Insurance Market

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Personal auto insurance covers private passenger vehicles owned or used by individuals and families. It protects against:

  • Third-party liability — bodily injury (BI) and property damage (PD) to others for which the insured is legally liable.
  • First-party losses — damage to the insured's own vehicle (collision, comprehensive), medical costs, and loss of use.
  • UM/UIM — claims by the insured against uninsured or underinsured motorists.

Auto insurance is required in almost all US states (with varying minimum limits and fault systems) and is mandatory in the UK for injury to third parties. It is the largest single personal lines product by premium.

docs.title: The Personal Auto Policy (PAP)
docs.text: The standard US Personal Auto Policy (ISO PP 00 01) is the reference form. It has six parts:

docs.title: Part A — Liability Coverage
docs.text:
• Insures bodily injury and property damage liability of the named insured and family members arising from the ownership, maintenance, or use of a covered auto.
  • Covers claims and defense costs (defense is generally in addition to the limit in many states).
  • Provides coverage for covered persons using a non-owned auto (e.g., a rental or borrowed car) within limits.
  • Exclusions: intentional acts, using a vehicle without a reasonable belief of right, bodily injury to employees (covered by workers compensation), commercial use, racing, and vehicles furnished for regular use without coverage.

docs.title: Part B — Medical Payments (MedPay)
docs.text:
• Pays reasonable medical and funeral expenses for the insured and passengers injured in an auto accident, regardless of fault.
  • Limited to a stated per-person amount.
  • Does not duplicate health insurance benefits in all states; coordinates with those policies.

docs.title: Part C — Uninsured/Underinsured Motorist (UM/UIM)
docs.text:
• UM — pays for the insured's bodily injury caused by an uninsured motorist or a hit-and-run driver.
  • UIM — pays when the at-fault driver's limits are insufficient to cover the insured's damages.
  • Offered or required in most states; coverage triggers and stacking rules vary by state.

docs.title: Part D — Coverage for Damage to Your Auto
docs.text:
• Collision — damage to the insured's vehicle from collision with another object or overturn.
  • Other than collision (Comprehensive) — damage from fire, theft, vandalism, wind, hail, flood, falling objects, or animal collision.
  • Each is subject to a deductible chosen by the insured.
  • Replacement cost / stated amount / actual cash value options exist for newer, classic, or modified vehicles.
  • Transportation expenses and loss of use may be added by endorsement.

docs.title: Part E — Duties After an Accident
docs.text:
• Prompt notice to the insurer.
  • Cooperation with investigation and defense.
  • Submitting to examinations under oath when required.
  • Authorizing the insurer to obtain records.

docs.title: Part F — General Provisions
docs.text:
• Bankruptcy of the insured does not relieve the insurer.
  • Cancellation and non-renewal provisions.
  • Fraud, concealment, misrepresentation can void coverage.
  • The policy is not automatically assignable.

docs.title: Rating Personal Auto
docs.text:
Auto insurance is class-rated using a large set of rating factors. Key factors:

Factor Explanation Territory Where the vehicle is principally garaged; reflects traffic density, theft rates, litigation climate Operator age and gender Younger and less experienced drivers have higher frequency and severity (age restrictions on gender apply in some jurisdictions due to equality law) Driving record (MVR) Accidents, violations, points, and suspensions Vehicle use Pleasure vs. business vs. farm; annual mileage Vehicle characteristics Make, model, model year, body type, value, safety and anti-theft features Prior insurance / continuity Gaps in coverage correlate with higher risk (this is a pricing and underwriting factor) Credit-based insurance score Used in many states; legally restricted in others Claims history At-fault accidents and claim frequency; first-party claim surcharges Discounts Multi-policy, multi-vehicle, safe driver, defensive driving course, telematics, good student, anti-theft, paperless

docs.title: Rating Example (Illustrative)
docs.text:
Factor Relativities Base premium \$800 Territory × 1.10 Young driver × 1.85 Clean MVR × 0.90 Annual miles < 8,000 × 0.90 Anti-theft device × 0.95 Indicated premium \$800 × 1.10 × 1.85 × 0.90 × 0.90 × 0.95 ≈ \$1,256

(Illustrative only — actual rates vary by insurer, state, and filing.)

docs.title: Eligibility Rules
docs.text:
• Vehicle type — private passenger autos; some insurers accept light pickups/SUVs.
  • Number of vehicles and drivers.
  • Territory — some insurers do not write in high-risk territories.
  • Business use — must be classified or declined.

docs.title: Underwriting Data Sources
docs.text: Source Use Application Vehicle, driver, use, prior insurance, garage address MVR License status, violations, accidents CLUE / A-Plus Personal auto loss history (5 years) ISO / claim databases Loss runs across carriers Credit-based score Insurance score (subject to state law) Telematics Actual driving behavior when installed Prior insurer verification Continuous coverage

docs.title: Driver Classification
docs.text:
Every licensed household member who drives is classified. Household drivers include:

  • Named insured and spouse.
  • Other relatives living in the household (licensed).
  • Drivers with regular use of a vehicle.

Sometimes a driver must be excluded (signed driver exclusion) to obtain coverage — e.g., a high-risk teenager or an unlicensed individual. Exclusions are strictly interpreted; a claims denial can result if an excluded driver uses the vehicle without permission being established.

docs.title: Underwriting Declines
docs.text:
Common declines in personal auto:

  • Major violations: DUI/DWI (within a defined period), reckless driving, license suspension.
  • Multiple at-fault accidents in a stated period.
  • Fraud or material misrepresentation.
  • Non-payment of premium history.
  • Use of vehicle in a business not rated (e.g., delivery).
  • High-performance or modified vehicles outside appetite.

docs.title: Telematics and Usage-Based Insurance (UBI)
docs.text:
• Pay-as-you-drive (PAYD) — premium based on miles driven.
  • Pay-how-you-drive (PHYD) — premium based on driving behavior: speed, hard braking, cornering, time of day, phone use.
  • Telematics improves risk selection, gives safe drivers discounts, and provides claim data (e.g., crash reconstruction).

docs.title: No-Fault and Fault Systems
docs.text:
System Description Tort (fault) The at-fault driver's insurer pays third-party BI/PD claims; the injured party may sue for damages No-fault Each driver's own insurer pays their medical and economic losses up to a threshold; tort rights limited (e.g., NY, FL, MA, MI historically) Choice ("add-on") Tort system with optional first-party benefits (e.g., "no-fault add-on" states)

State no-fault laws affect:

  • PIP coverages and limits — required first-party benefits.
  • Thresholds — verbal vs. monetary thresholds for suing.
  • Claim severities — litigation rates and BI costs.

Underwriters must know the state system where the vehicle is garaged.

docs.title: UK Personal Auto (Motor) Insurance
docs.text:
UK private car insurance operates under:

  • Road Traffic Act 1988 — third-party bodily injury compulsory cover.
  • FCA regulation — fair value, pricing rules (including the "price walking" ban for renewals), and disclosure.
  • Cover levels: Third Party Only, Third Party Fire & Theft, and Comprehensive.
  • Rating factors similar to the US: age, driving experience, no-claims discount (NCD), vehicle group, territory (postcode), and occupation.
  • No claims discount (NCD) — up to a maximum (e.g., 9+ years) reduces premium; protected NCD available.
  • Telematics ("black box") policies are common for young drivers.

docs.title: Claims Considerations
docs.text:
• FNOL — capture accident details, injuries, witnesses.
  • Coverage determination — verify covered auto, driver, use.
  • Liability investigation — police reports, statements, scene evidence.
  • Physical damage appraisal — repair vs. total loss; ACV vs. replacement cost.
  • Total loss — vehicle value using market comparisons; salvage handling.
  • Subrogation — pursue at-fault third parties (in tort states).
  • Fraud — staged accidents, inflated claims, "slip-and-fall" style auto injury fraud, SIU referral.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Personal auto provides liability, medical, UM/UIM, and physical damage coverages.
  • Rating is class-based on territory, driver, use, vehicle, and experience factors.
  • Underwriting relies on MVR, claim history, credit (where allowed), and telematics.
  • State/legal systems (tort vs. no-fault) and UK motor rules shape both coverage and pricing.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 2.1 Personal Lines Overview
  • 2.3 Homeowners
  • 4.6 Underwriting by Line
  • 5.6 Rating by Line
  • 7.2 Claims Process

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Homeowners insurance combines property and liability coverages for owner-occupied dwellings. It protects:

  • The dwelling, other structures, personal property, and loss of use.
  • The owner's personal liability for bodily injury or property damage to others.
  • Medical payments for minor injuries to others.

Homeowners is typically required by mortgage lenders for financed homes. It is one of the most rate-regulated personal lines products.

docs.title: The Homeowners (HO) Forms
docs.text:
The standard US ISO homeowners forms are:

Form Dwelling Occupancy Property Perils HO-2 (Broad) Owner-occupied 1–4 family Named perils (16) HO-3 (Special) Owner-occupied 1–4 family Open perils for dwelling; named perils for personal property HO-5 (Comprehensive) Owner-occupied Open perils for dwelling and personal property HO-6 (Condo) Condominium unit owner Personal property (open or named perils) + unit owner additions HO-7 (Mobile Home) Mobile/manufactured home Perils as HO-3 HO-8 (Modified/Older Home) Owner-occupied older home Named perils; repair cost basis

Many insurers use their own "homeowners package" forms modeled on these, or choose "modified" forms (HO-3 with HO-5-style coverage for contents).

docs.title: Section I — Property
docs.text:
Coverage Protection A — Dwelling Structure and attached structures (garage, deck, built-in appliances) B — Other Structures Detached structures (shed, fence, detached garage) — typically 10% of Coverage A C — Personal Property Contents and personal belongings — typically 50–70% of Coverage A D — Loss of Use Additional living expenses and fair rental value when the dwelling is uninhabitable — typically 20–30% of Coverage A

Named perils for contents in HO-3 include: fire, lightning, windstorm, hail, explosion, riot/civil commotion, aircraft, vehicles, smoke, vandalism, theft, and others.

Open perils for the dwelling cover all risks of physical loss unless specifically excluded.

docs.title: Common Exclusions
docs.text:
• Flood (surface water, overflow, tidal water, etc.) — separate flood policy (NFIP/private).
  • Earthquake — separate earthquake endorsement/policy.
  • Wear and tear, deterioration, latent defect — excluded as "not a risk of physical loss" or expressly excluded.
  • Mold — limited or excluded beyond specified amounts.
  • Ordinance or law — cost to rebuild to current code (limited; increase cover).
  • Intentional loss, neglect, and power failure.
  • Business property and business use (limited).
  • Animal liability — dog bites covered but certain breeds may be excluded.

docs.title: Valuation
docs.text:
• Dwelling — replacement cost (up to the limit) with extended replacement cost endorsements (e.g., 125% or 150%).
  • Personal property — replacement cost or actual cash value (ACV) option.
  • HO-8 — repair cost basis.
  • Inflation guard — automatic annual adjustment.

docs.title: Coinsurance / Adequate Insurance
docs.text: Most homeowners forms do not apply a coinsurance penalty as such, but payment is limited to the limit plus the extended replacement cost percentage. Underinsuring leaves the insured personally exposed. Underwriters estimate the replacement cost using a replacement-cost estimator (square footage, construction quality, features, local building costs).

docs.title: Section II — Liability
docs.text: Coverage Protection E — Personal Liability Bodily injury or property damage to others caused by an occurrence on or off the insured premises; includes defense costs F — Medical Payments to Others Minor injuries to guests, typically \$1,000–\$5,000 per person

docs.title: Exclusions to Liability
docs.text:
• Intentional acts.
  • Business activities (some may be covered by endorsement or separate policy).
  • Motor vehicles (covered by auto policy).
  • Watercraft above stated size/power (may be added by endorsement).
  • Aircraft.
  • Workers compensation / employment liability.
  • Professional services.

docs.title: Endorsements
docs.text:
Common endorsements include:

  • Scheduled personal property (jewelry, fine arts, firearms, collectibles).
  • Water backup and sump overflow.
  • Service line coverage.
  • Equipment breakdown.
  • Identity theft.
  • Home business extensions.
  • Increased replacement cost and ordinance/law coverage.
  • Dog liability (underwritten by breed).
  • Additional insureds (e.g., landlord, mortgagee).

docs.title: Rating Homeowners
docs.text:
The premium is computed from:

Factor Explanation Replacement cost (Coverage A) The dominant rating factor; estimated by RCE tools Territory (protection class/ISO) Fire protection district, claim frequency, litigation Construction Frame vs. masonry vs. manufactured Age and condition Roof age, HVAC/electrical/plumbing updates Claims history CLUE and internal loss history Credit-based score In many states (legally restricted in others) Deductible % based deductibles (e.g., 1%, 2%, 5% of Coverage A) common in catastrophe states Discounts Multi-policy, alarm, sprinkler, impact-resistant roof, no-claims, new home, retirement community Catastrophe surcharges Wind/hail, hurricane, wildfire risk areas

docs.title: Key Underwriting Checks
docs.text:
1. Replacement cost adequacy — ensure Coverage A is sufficient; recommend extended replacement cost.
  2. Condition of the home — age, roof, electrical, plumbing, heating, and apparent maintenance.
  3. Claims history — prior losses (CLUE) for frequency and severity.
  4. Dogs and exotic pets — breed and bite history.
  5. Trampolines, pools, and playgrounds — attractive nuisance and liability exposure.
  6. Business use — home offices, inventory, daycare, rental of rooms/units.
  7. Location hazards — flood zone, wildfire zone, earthquake zone, wind/hail territory; require appropriate coverage or endorsements.
  8. Vacancy — a vacant home is a higher risk; long vacancy may require special coverage or be declined.
  9. Short-term rentals — Airbnb/VRBO require special endorsement or separate policy.
  10. High-value homes — require appraisal/inspection-based replacement cost, and may fall outside standard guidelines.

docs.title: Inspection Triggers
docs.text:
Inspections (virtual or physical) are typically required when:

  • Coverage A exceeds a threshold (e.g., \$750k–\$1M).
  • Older construction (e.g., 40+ years) without updates.
  • High-value or specialty risks.
  • The application raises questions (unknown square footage, recent purchase, etc.).
  • Claims history suggests condition issues.

docs.title: Underwriting Declines
docs.text:
• Commercial or excessive business exposure.
  • Uninsurable condition (severe deferred maintenance, active leaks, unsafe structures).
  • Certain dog breeds / bite history (by insurer rules).
  • Illegal activity or occupation hazards.
  • Failure to maintain required minimum deductibles in catastrophe areas.
  • Non-payment or fraud history.

docs.title: Flood
docs.text:
• NFIP (National Flood Insurance Program) — federal program; separate policy; 30-day waiting period; limit of \$250k building / \$100k contents (single-family).
  • Private flood insurance — growing market; higher limits and broader terms.
  • Determining flood risk: FEMA flood zone maps (A, V, X, etc.), elevation, history.
  • Underwriters require flood coverage for homes in Special Flood Hazard Areas (A/V zones) when financing.

docs.title: Earthquake
docs.text:
• Typically an endorsement or separate policy with a percentage deductible (e.g., 10–15% of Coverage A).
  • Offered by insurers or state pools (e.g., California Earthquake Authority, CEA).
  • Not required by lenders but recommended in seismic zones.

docs.title: UK Home Insurance
docs.text:
UK home insurance has two main components, typically sold as one policy:

Component Covers Buildings Structure, permanent fixtures, and fittings; sum insured based on rebuild cost (not market value) Contents Personal belongings; sum insured or "unlimited" with limits on valuables

Key UK special features:

  • Sum insured — rebuild cost for buildings; contents value for contents. Flood risk is included in standard buildings cover.
  • Excess — compulsory and voluntary excesses.
  • New-for-old — most contents policies pay replacement value.
  • Accidental damage — optional extension to buildings and contents.
  • Home emergency and legal expenses are common add-ons.
  • FCA pricing rules — renewal pricing cannot be higher than new business (price walking ban).
  • Flood Re — the UK government-backed scheme that makes flood cover available through participating insurers for eligible homes.

docs.title: Claims Considerations
docs.text:
• Property claims — fire, water damage, theft, wind/hail; adjusters verify coverage, cause, and quantum (ACV vs. RCV; depreciation recovery upon repair).
  • Liability claims — third-party injury on premises, dog bites; liability investigation and defense.
  • Catastrophe claims — hurricanes, tornadoes, wildfires, floods mobilize surge adjusters and special handling.
  • Fraud — content inflation, arson-for-profit, staged "slip and fall", contractor fraud.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Homeowners binds property and liability cover in one product.
  • Forms differ by occupancy and peril basis (HO-2, HO-3, HO-5, HO-6, HO-7, HO-8).
  • Replacement cost adequacy is the central underwriting concern.
  • Catastrophe exposure (flood, wind, earthquake, wildfire) requires special handling and endorsements.
  • UK home insurance operates with different terminology and flood scheme (Flood Re).

docs.title: Related Chapters

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Not all residential property is owner-occupied under a homeowners policy. Dwelling fire and related coverages serve:

  • Non-owner-occupied dwellings — rental properties, vacant dwellings, seasonal homes.
  • Owner-occupied dwellings that do not qualify for HO — older homes, unique construction, high-value, or where the owner prefers a simpler form.
  • Tenants — renters contents and liability.
  • Condominium unit owners — unit contents and improvements.
  • Mobile/manufactured homes — where HO-7 or a specialist policy applies.
  • Unique personal property — scheduled jewelry, fine arts, collectibles, watercraft.

docs.title: The Dwelling Fire (DF) Policy
docs.text:
The Dwelling Fire (DP) program (ISO DP-1, DP-2, DP-3) is the standard US form:

Form Peril Basis Typical Use DP-1 (Basic) Named perils (fire, lightning, internal explosion) Low-cost; vacant or seasonal dwellings DP-2 (Broad) 16 named perils Rental or qualifying owner-occupied DP-3 (Special) Open perils for dwelling; named perils for contents Owner-occupied or where broader cover needed

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Coverage A (Dwelling), B (Other Structures), C (Contents), D (Fair Rental Value / Loss of Use).
  • Valuation: replacement cost or actual cash value options; DP-1 is often ACV.
  • Deductibles: flat or percentage-based.
  • Rental coverage: fair rental value for landlord-owned homes; contents are normally not covered for tenant property (tenant needs own policy).
  • Vacancy: often limited or suspended after 30–60 days vacant (vandalism, water damage exclusions apply while vacant).

docs.title: Underwriting Considerations for Dwelling Fire
docs.text: Factor Underwriting Concern Occupancy Owner-occupied, tenant-occupied, seasonal, vacant Tenant type Single family, multi-family, short-term rental, rooming house Condition Age, roof, systems, deferred maintenance (higher for rentals) Property management Managed vs. self-managed; screening of tenants Protection Fire district, hydrants, alarms, sprinklers Catastrophe exposure Flood, wind, wildfire zones Replacement cost adequacy Accurate RCE needed; underinsurance penalizes at claim time

docs.title: Rental Property Underwriting
docs.text:
• Screening — some insurers require the landlord to use tenant screening (credit, eviction history).
  • Limits — contents coverage for the landlord's fixtures and personal property only.
  • Loss of rent — verify actual rental income/agreement.
  • Short-term rentals — normally excluded or specially rated; require endorsement.
  • Multi-unit dwellings — higher frequency; check fire separation, egress, smoke detectors.

docs.title: Tenants (Renters) Insurance
docs.text:
HO-4 (Contents) covers:

  • Personal property (contents) against named or open perils.
  • Loss of use (additional living expense).
  • Personal liability and medical payments for the tenant.

Underwriting focuses on:

  • Building safety — the landlord's building systems affect loss potential (fire, water).
  • Claims history — tenant contents losses.
  • Pets and liability exposures.
  • High-risk contents — cash, jewelry, guns, watercraft (limit or schedule).

docs.title: Condominium (HO-6)
docs.text:
HO-6 covers:

  • Personal property, unit owner's additions/improvements.
  • Loss of use, personal liability, medical payments.

The condominium association's master policy covers the building and common areas. The unit owner needs walls-in coverage for their improvements and betterments. Underwriting checks the master policy adequacy and the association's financial health (special assessments, litigation, reserve adequacy).

docs.title: Mobile and Manufactured Homes
docs.text:
HO-7 / specialist mobile home policies cover:

  • The mobile home unit (including attached additions).
  • Contents, liability, and loss of use (as applicable).

Underwriting considerations:

  • Age and condition of the unit; HUD certification.
  • Tie-downs, foundation, and anchoring — wind risk.
  • Location — parks vs. private land; flood/wind zones.
  • Use — permanent residence vs. seasonal.

docs.title: Other Residential Structures
docs.text: Exposure Coverage Seasonal/second homes Dwelling fire or HO with higher rates, vacancy limitations Row/townhouses HO or dwelling fire; fire separation and association arrangements Farm/ranch dwellings Farmowners package or HO with farm endorsements Student housing / dorm contents Renter contents forms Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) Often covered under the main home policy, subject to limits and conditions

docs.title: Personal Property Floaters and Scheduled Articles
docs.text:
The homeowners policy provides limited amounts for certain categories:

  • Jewelry, furs: typically \$1,500–\$2,500 limit.
  • Money, securities: limited (e.g., \$200–\$500).
  • Watercraft: limited liability and property.

Scheduled personal property (floater) endorsements provide:

  • All-risk-type coverage (open perils) for the scheduled items.
  • Agreed value or stated amount.
  • Worldwide coverage.
  • No deductible options.

Articles commonly scheduled: jewelry, watches, fine arts, cameras, musical instruments, firearms, collectibles, golf equipment.

Underwriting the floater:

  • Appraisal or proof of value.
  • Security measures (safe, alarm).
  • Risk location and travel patterns.
  • Loss history (theft/fire frequency).

docs.title: Watercraft
docs.text:
Personal watercraft (boats, PWCs) may be covered under:

  • Homeowners (small boats, limited liability and property).
  • Separate boat/yacht policy — for larger or higher-value craft:
  • Hull coverage (agreed value or ACV).
  • Liability (P&I or broad form).
  • Medical payments.
  • Uninsured boater.

Underwriting factors: boat type, size, horsepower, age, storage (dry vs. wet), operator experience, navigable waters, and loss history.

docs.title: UK Perspective
docs.text:
• Buildings & contents as covered in 2.3 apply to owner-occupied and rented homes.
  • Landlord insurance — buildings cover for rental property; contents may include landlord's fixtures; loss of rent/rent guarantee covers; liability for the landlord's interest.
  • Tenant's insurance — contents only; buildings are the landlord's.
  • Scheduled valuables — "specified items" added to contents policies; high-value items require individual sums insured.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Dwelling fire forms serve non-owner-occupied and non-qualifying dwellings.
  • Renters (HO-4), condos (HO-6), and mobile homes (HO-7) address specific occupancies.
  • Scheduled floaters cover high-value personal property with broader terms.
  • Underwriting emphasizes occupancy, condition, protection, catastrophe exposure, and coverage adequacy.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A personal umbrella policy (PUP) provides excess liability protection above the limits of the insured's underlying policies (home, auto, watercraft) and extends coverage to some gaps not covered by the underlying policies. It is designed for individuals with assets to protect or a high risk of liability judgment.

  • Excess coverage — pays when the underlying policy limits are exhausted.
  • Drop-down coverage — extends coverage to claims not covered by an underlying policy (subject to a self-insured retention, SIR).
  • Broad coverage — may include libel, slander, defamation, false arrest, and other personal injury offenses.

Umbrella liability is typically written in increments:

  • \$1,000,000
  • \$2,000,000
  • \$5,000,000
  • \$10,000,000 (higher limits written on a case-by-case basis)

docs.title: Excess Over Underlying
docs.text:
The umbrella sits above:

Underlying Policy Typical Required Minimum Limit Auto liability \$250,000–\$500,000 per person / \$500,000–\$1,000,000 per occurrence (state-dependent) Homeowners liability \$300,000–\$500,000 Watercraft liability \$300,000–\$1,000,000 (if owned) Other liability As required (e.g., recreational vehicles, rental properties)

The umbrella responds when the underlying limit is exhausted, subject to the terms of the umbrella.

docs.title: Drop-Down / SIR
docs.text:
• For claims not covered by an underlying policy, the umbrella may provide coverage subject to a self-insured retention (typically \$250–\$2,500).
  • The insured is responsible for the SIR before the umbrella responds.
  • Not all umbrella policies provide drop-down; read the form carefully.

docs.title: Common Exclusions
docs.text:
• Intentional acts.
  • Business and professional activities (unless endorsed).
  • Aircraft.
  • Workers compensation / employers liability.
  • Punitive damages (many states).
  • Certain watercraft unless scheduled.
  • Damage to the insured's own property.
  • Contractual liability assumed by the insured (subject to terms).

docs.title: Underwriting Personal Umbrella
docs.text: The primary underwriting question: is the risk acceptable and is the underlying coverage verified?

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Underlying policies must be in force at the required limits.
  2. Underlying insurers must be acceptable (financially sound; admitted).
  3. All household drivers and vehicles must be listed and rated.
  4. Watercraft and recreational vehicles must be declared and underwritten separately if above a size threshold.
  5. The insured's assets and exposures must be consistent with the limit requested.

docs.title: Underwriting Data Sources
docs.text:
• Application (assets, vehicles, watercraft, rental properties, pets).
  • Underlying policy declarations pages.
  • MVR / CLUE for the household.
  • Inspection if complex exposures (high-value home, large watercraft).

docs.title: Decline Triggers
docs.text:
• Unacceptable underlying carriers or lapsed coverages.
  • High-risk drivers (DUI, multiple violations/accidents) not acceptable.
  • Unscheduled watercraft or RVs.
  • Business exposures not covered.
  • Intentional or criminal activity exposures.
  • Uninsurable pets (certain breeds) if liability history exists.

docs.title: Rating Personal Umbrella
docs.text:
Umbrella premiums are relatively low relative to limit because severity is low-frequency. Pricing factors:

  • Number of cars and drivers.
  • Number of homes and other real estate.
  • Watercraft.
  • Underlying limits carried.
  • Territory.
  • Loss history of the household.
  • Limit selected.

Example (illustrative): base \$250 for \$1M; add \$50 per additional vehicle; add \$100 for second home; add \$150–\$300 for a watercraft; credits for higher underlying limits.

docs.title: UK Perspective
docs.text:
• Personal liability / "umbrella" products are less standardized in the UK; excess layer products exist but are less common.
  • UK personal liability is usually embedded in home contents policies (liability section) with modest limits (e.g., £2M–£5M legal liability is common under home emergency / legal protection or as "personal liability" cover).
  • Individual "legal liability" policies and personal injury cover may supplement.
  • Where high limits are required (e.g., public figures), bespoke products or excess liability through brokers are arranged.

docs.title: Claims Considerations
docs.text:
• Trigger — underlying limit exhaustion or covered drop-down claim.
  • Notice — prompt notice to the umbrella carrier of any claim that may involve the umbrella.
  • Defense — the umbrella may provide defense when underlying is exhausted or the claim is outside underlying.
  • Allocation — defense costs and indemnity may be allocated between underlying layers.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The personal umbrella gives excess limits and broadened drop-down cover for a relatively low premium.
  • Underwriting centers on verifying underlying coverages, household exposures, and risk acceptability.
  • Careful declaration of vehicles, homes, watercraft, and business use is essential.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Life insurance pays a defined sum of money (the sum assured) to a named beneficiary upon the death of the life assured, in exchange for premiums. Unlike property and casualty insurance, life insurance is:

  • Not a contract of indemnity — a human life cannot be valued; the sum assured is fixed in the policy.
  • A long-term contract — usually written for the whole of life or a term of years.
  • Valuation-dependent — underwriting mortality risk (and morbidity for related products).

Life insurance serves:

  • Income replacement — protecting dependents against loss of the breadwinner's income.
  • Debt protection — covering mortgages, loans, and business debts.
  • Estate planning — liquidity for inheritance tax, wealth transfer.
  • Business protection — key person, shareholder buy-sell funding.
  • Savings and investment — whole life and endowment products build cash value.

docs.title: Types of Life Insurance
docs.text: Type Description Term insurance Provides cover for a fixed term (e.g., 10, 20, 30 years). Pays only if death occurs within the term. No cash value. Whole life Permanent cover for the whole of life; builds cash value; premium level. Endowment Pays the sum assured at the end of the term or on earlier death. Combines protection with savings. Universal life Flexible premium permanent cover; cash value earns interest; adjustable death benefit. Variable/unit-linked Premiums invested in funds; cash value and death benefit may vary with investment performance. Indexed universal life Cash value linked to a market index. Joint life Covers two lives (often spouses) — pays on first or second death depending on form. Credit life Covers a debt (mortgage, loan) — pays the balance on death. Group life Employer-sponsored cover for employees, usually term-based.

docs.title: Underwriting Questions
docs.text:
1. Mortality risk — will the life assured die during the policy term?
  2. Morbidity risk (for riders) — will the life assure become disabled or critically ill?
  3. Financial need — the sum assured must be justifiable (insurable interest + needs).
  4. Moral hazard — could the policyholder benefit from the death (suicide, homicide)?

docs.title: Key Underwriting Factors
docs.text: Factor Impact Age Higher mortality with age Gender Female mortality generally lower than male at most ages Smoking/tobacco use Significant mortality factor; smokers priced higher Health history Conditions (heart, cancer, diabetes, respiratory) drive underwriting and rate class Family history Hereditary conditions (heart disease, cancer) Occupation Hazardous occupations (aviation, mining, deep-sea) Lifestyle/avocation Extreme sports, sky-diving, scuba diving Foreign travel/residence High-risk travel or residency Financial exposure Sum assured vs. income and assets; insurable interest Driving record MVR for high sums assured

docs.title: Rate Classes (Table Rating)
docs.text:
Insurers classify lives into rate classes:

Class Description Preferred best / super preferred Very low risk; excellent health, lifestyle Preferred Low risk; good health Standard Average risk Substandard (table rated) Elevated risk; additional premium (e.g., Table A–D, or rated +25%, +50%, +100%) Declined Risk too high to underwrite

docs.title: Medical Underwriting
docs.text:
• Application questionnaire — health, family history, lifestyle, occupation.
  • Attending Physician Statement (APS) — for significant conditions.
  • Medical exams and lab tests — blood, urine, for higher sums assured or certain ages.
  • Tele-underwriting / paramedical exams — improve speed and accuracy.
  • Simplified issue — no medical exam; higher premium.
  • Guaranteed issue — no medical questions; for small amounts or group schemes; limited benefits in early years.

docs.title: Non-Medical (Financial) Underwriting
docs.text:
• Verify insurable interest (beneficiary relationship).
  • Verify sum assured vs. income/assets (maximum multiple of income, e.g., 10–20×).
  • Check toxic/debt cover appropriateness.
  • For high sums assured: financial justification documents (income tax returns, net worth, business valuation).

docs.title: Rating and Premium
docs.text:
• Premium = mortality cost + expenses + risk margin, with investment return credited.
  • Level term — premiums level over the term.
  • Annual renewable term — premium increases by age.
  • Whole life — level premium with cash value accumulation.

Key actuarial inputs:

  • Mortality table (e.g., 2015 VBT, select and ultimate tables).
  • Interest rate assumption.
  • Expense load.
  • Lapse assumptions.

docs.title: Policy Provisions
docs.text: Provision Purpose Grace period 30–31 days to pay premium after due date Reinstatement Relapse after lapse within limits (health evidence) Incontestability Insurer cannot contest after 2 years (except fraud in some jurisdictions) Suicide clause 2 years: death by suicide pays premiums returned only Beneficiary designation Revocable/irrevocable; per stirpes vs. per capita Cash value loan Borrow against cash value Non-forfeiture options Cash surrender, reduced paid-up, extended term Waiver of premium Premium waived on disability Accelerated benefits Early payment for terminal illness Riders Term additions, disability income, critical illness, accidental death

docs.title: Life Insurance in the UK
docs.text:
• Term assurance (level, decreasing, increasing) is the most common protection product.
  • Whole of life — often for inheritance tax planning, sometimes written in trust.
  • Endowments — historic "with-profits" products.
  • Critical illness cover — lump sum on diagnosis of listed conditions.
  • Income protection — long-term disability income (replaces a portion of earnings).
  • FCA conduct rules — advised sales through FCA-regulated advisers; consumer duty and fair value apply.
  • Protection distribution — through advisers, banks, and increasingly direct/insurtech digital channels.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Life insurance provides fixed sums on death (and sometimes on survival or disability).
  • Underwriting blends medical, non-medical, and financial risk assessment.
  • Products range from term to whole life, and from guaranteed issue to fully underwritten.
  • Age, health, smoking, occupation, lifestyle, and sum assured drive rating.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Health and accident insurance protects individuals against the financial consequences of illness, injury, and disability. This chapter covers the personal health and accident products an underwriter encounters:

  • Medical expense insurance — hospital, surgical, and physician coverage.
  • Disability income insurance — replaces lost income during disability.
  • Critical illness insurance — lump-sum payment on diagnosis of specified conditions.
  • Accident insurance — pays benefits for accidental injury (medical, lump-sum, AD&D).
  • Long-term care insurance — covers custodial and nursing care needs.

Health insurance is heavily regulated and differs fundamentally between the US and UK markets.

docs.title: US Market
docs.text:
• Private health insurance — employer-sponsored group plans and individual/family plans.
  • ACA (Affordable Care Act) marketplaces — guaranteed issue (no medical underwriting for most plans), essential health benefits, premium subsidies.
  • Medicare — federal coverage for those 65+ and certain disabilities; Medigap supplemental; Medicare Advantage (private plans).
  • Medicaid — state/federal program for low-income individuals.
  • Catastrophic plans — young adults, high deductible.
  • HSAs (Health Savings Accounts) — tax-advantaged accounts paired with high-deductible plans.

docs.title: UK Market
docs.text:
• Private medical insurance (PMI) — covers private hospital treatment for acute conditions; not emergencies or chronic conditions usually.
  • Underwritten individually or by employer groups; medical underwriting (full, moratorium, or moratorium with exclusions) applies.
  • NHS is the primary public system; PMI supplements access.

docs.title: Medical Underwriting
docs.text:
• Individual medical — questionnaires, medical records, lab tests for higher sums.
  • Guaranteed issue (group) — no individual underwriting; group risk rated.
  • Moratorium underwriting (individual PMI) — pre-existing conditions excluded for a period (e.g., 5 years) if symptom-free and untreated.
  • Underwriting factors: age, health history, family history, smoking, occupation, lifestyle, existing conditions.

docs.title: Short-Term vs. Long-Term
docs.text: Feature Short-Term Disability (STD) Long-Term Disability (LTD) Elimination period 0–14 days 90–180 days (or longer) Benefit period Up to 6 months–2 years To age 65 or retirement Benefit amount 60–70% of income 50–65% of income Common in Employer group plans Employer and individual plans

docs.title: Individual Disability (IDI)
docs.text:
• Own occupation — disability defined against own occupation (stronger) vs. any occupation (weaker).
  • Residual/partial disability — benefits for reduced income.
  • Cost of living adjustment (COLA) — inflation protection.
  • Non-cancellable — insurer cannot cancel or raise rates; valuable and more expensive.
  • Guaranteed renewable — insurer cannot cancel but may adjust rates by class.

docs.title: Underwriting Factors
docs.text:
• Age and gender — morbidity curves.
  • Occupation and duty class — sedentary vs. manual; risk of injury.
  • Income — benefit limit relative to earned income (replacement ratio cap).
  • Health history — musculoskeletal, mental health, cardiovascular claims.
  • Lifestyle — smoking, alcohol, extreme sports.
  • Financial motivation — benefit must not exceed income (moral hazard control).

docs.title: Critical Illness Insurance
docs.text:
• Pays a lump sum on diagnosis of a defined list of conditions (cancer, heart attack, stroke, etc.).
  • Underwriting similar to life insurance (medical questionnaire, exam for higher sums).
  • Age limits (e.g., up to 70), benefit periods, and definitions vary by product.
  • Value — covers recovery costs, income loss, or debt.
  • Add-on — often attached to life or mortgage products.

docs.title: Accident Insurance
docs.text:
• Accidental Death & Dismemberment (AD&D) — pays on accidental death or specified injuries (loss of limb, sight).
  • Accident medical — pays medical expenses from an accident.
  • Accident income — short-term weekly benefits during accident recovery.
  • Underwriting — light; occupation and hazardous avocations are the main factors.
  • Often guaranteed issue or simplified issue; excludes illness conditions.

docs.title: Long-Term Care (LTC) Insurance
docs.text:
• Covers nursing home, assisted living, and home care costs.
  • Triggers — inability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs: bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, transferring, continence) or cognitive impairment.
  • Underwriting — extensive medical underwriting; cognitive and functional screening; age at issue.
  • Hybrid products — LTC riders on life insurance or annuities (asset-based LTC).
  • US — private LTC market, state partnership programs; UK — care needs often met by social care funding; private "care insurance" less common (policies like annuities covering care costs in some forms).

docs.title: Regulation and Considerations
docs.text:
Market Key Regulations US ACA (guaranteed issue, essential benefits), HIPAA (portability, privacy), ERISA (employer plans), state insurance regulation UK FCA consumer duty, fair value, advised sales for protection; medical insurance conduct rules

Key considerations for underwriters:

  • Moral hazard — keep replacement ratios low for disability; verify income.
  • Anti-selection — guaranteed issue products require strong group governance.
  • Definitions drive claims — "own occupation" vs. "any occupation" changes claims experience significantly.
  • Chronic vs. acute — PMI excludes chronic conditions; LTC covers chronic needs.
  • Data — morbidity tables, claims studies, and reinsurer guidance underpin pricing.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Health and accident products include medical, disability, critical illness, accident, and long-term care.
  • Medical underwriting ranges from guaranteed issue to full individual underwriting.
  • Disability underwriting focuses on occupation, income, and health.
  • Definitions, benefit periods, and triggers are the principal claims drivers.
  • Regulation (ACA, FCA) constrains underwriting and pricing.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Personal lines are increasingly sold and managed as accounts or packages rather than as standalone policies. A personal package typically combines:

  • Auto (liability, physical damage, UM/UIM)
  • Home (homeowners or dwelling fire)
  • Umbrella / excess liability
  • Watercraft, RV, and other recreational vehicles
  • Life, health, and accident products
  • Identity theft and other personal risk products

The economics of the package are favorable to the insurer:

  • Multi-policy discounts increase retention.
  • Account bundling reduces acquisition and servicing cost per policy.
  • Cross-selling deepens customer relationships and lifetime value.
  • Data sharing across the account improves underwriting and pricing.

docs.title: Why Package Underwriting Matters
docs.text:
Benefit Explanation Retention Households with multiple products are far less likely to lapse Risk selection Viewing the whole household exposes risks hidden by single lines (e.g., a boat, a teenage driver, a rental property) Pricing synergies Multi-policy discounts are earned by account profitability Service efficiency One point of contact, one bill, one renewal Claims experience Claims across lines feed a household-level view

The underwriter must therefore evaluate the whole account, not just the individual policy.

docs.title: Step 1 — Identify All Exposures
docs.text:
Collect the complete household picture:

  • All vehicles, drivers, and auto use.
  • All owned/rented dwellings (primary, second home, rental).
  • Watercraft, RVs, ATVs, trailers.
  • Pets; pools; trampolines.
  • Business activities conducted at home.
  • High-value personal property.
  • Life, health, disability needs.

docs.title: Step 2 — Assess Household Risk Profile
docs.text: Dimension Inputs Driving risk MVR for all drivers, claim history, telematics if available Property risk CLUE, condition, location hazards (flood, wind, wildfire), replacement cost Liability risk Pets, pools, watercraft, rental properties, umbrella needs Financial risk Credit (where legal), assets, continuity Behavioral risk Claims frequency, retention trend, complaint history

docs.title: Step 3 — Package Pricing
docs.text:
• Apply multi-policy and account discounts.
  • Identify surcharges for specific exposures (e.g., watercraft, second homes).
  • Determine whether the account falls within appetite or needs referral.

docs.title: Step 4 — Retention and Growth Strategy
docs.text:
• At renewal, review the account for coverage gaps and cross-sell opportunities.
  • Monitor household tenure and address complaints promptly.
  • Use loss information to re-price rather than simply non-renew.

docs.title: Multi-Policy Discounts
docs.text:
Discounts vary by insurer and product but commonly include:

  • Auto + home (or auto + renters) — the primary package discount.
  • Multi-vehicle — additional vehicles.
  • Multi-line life/health — bundling protection products.
  • Umbrella — adding excess liability on top of the package.

Discounts are regulated: - They must be filed and approved (US) as part of rate filings. - They must not be unfairly discriminatory. - They should be actuarially justified (loss cost savings, expense savings, retention value).

docs.title: Underwriting the Package: Red Flags
docs.text: Red Flag Response Multiple recent at-fault accidents across lines Decline or surcharge; require loss-control actions Significant claims frequency (e.g., 2+ claims in 3 years) Tighten terms; increase deductibles; possibly non-renew High-value unscheduled items Require scheduling or limits reduction Dog bite history Exclude breed or decline; require umbrella Unmanaged short-term rentals Endorse or decline; require landlord product Financial distress signals Review payment performance; manage credit risk Newly acquired high-risk exposures Re-underwrite mid-term; quote or endorse

docs.title: Consumer Risk Management
docs.text:
Beyond product bundling, personal lines serve risk management for the household:

  • Prevention — loss-control advice (fire safety, water leak sensors, safe driving programs).
  • Transfer — insurance and umbrella products.
  • Retention — deductibles, self-insured options.
  • Financial planning — life, disability, and long-term care to protect income and assets.

The modern personal lines insurer increasingly functions as a household risk partner, leveraging data (telematics, IoT, claims analytics) to reduce risk before it becomes a claim.

docs.title: Data and Technology in Personal Lines
docs.text:
Technology Use Telematics Driving behavior pricing and feedback Smart home sensors Leak/fire detection, discount qualification Credit/insurance scores Loss-propensity prediction (where lawful) Claim databases Household loss history (CLUE, A-Plus) Predictive models Conversion, retention, pricing, fraud Customer portals Self-service, document access, policy changes

Underwriters must ensure models and data use comply with fair discrimination and privacy rules.

docs.title: Renewal Underwriting
docs.text:
Renewal is the most important retention event:

  • Evidence of change — new drivers, new vehicles, home improvements, new claims.
  • Re-rate — apply current rates to the account.
  • Check coverage adequacy — inflation-adjusted replacement cost; updated liability needs.
  • Consider the account — do not lose a good account over a single price point; balance profitability with retention.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Personal lines are best underwritten as household accounts, not single policies.
  • Package discounts and cross-sell drive retention and profitability.
  • Account underwriting identifies hidden exposures and manages the whole household risk profile.
  • Data and technology enable more precise underwriting and pricing.
  • Renewal is where the value of the account is realized — or lost.

docs.title: Volume 3 — Commercial Insurance
docs.text: Volume 3 covers insurance for businesses and organizations. It explains commercial property, general liability, commercial auto, workers compensation, and the other commercial products that underwriters encounter, from the perspective of the underwriting function: what is covered, what drives risk, and what underwriting and rating considerations apply.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Chapter Title Contents 3.1 Commercial Lines Overview Market segments, distribution, submission process, package vs. mono-line, regulation 3.2 Commercial Property Building/contents coverages, business income, perils, valuation, coinsurance, COPE, underwriting 3.3 Commercial General Liability CGL structure, coverage triggers, products/completed ops, exposures, underwriting 3.4 Commercial Auto Business auto policy, symbols, hired/non-owned, trucking, underwriting factors 3.5 Workers Compensation Statutory framework, benefits, class codes, experience rating, underwriting, fraud 3.6 Commercial Package & BOP Package structure, BOP eligibility, interline underwriting 3.7 Businessowners Policy (BOP) BOP coverages, eligibility, rating, underwriting (US focus) 3.8 Life, Accident & Health (Commercial) Group life, group health, disability, key person, buy-sell, business travel 3.9 Specialty Lines Inland marine, ocean marine, aviation, surety, professional liability, cyber, D&O, E&O, environmental 3.10 Commercial Risk Management Risk manager's role, program design, captives, retention, claims management

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this volume you should be able to:

  1. Describe the commercial lines marketplace and the submission process.
  2. Explain commercial property coverages, valuation, and coinsurance.
  3. Explain the CGL structure and its coverage triggers.
  4. Identify commercial auto symbols and trucking underwriting considerations.
  5. Explain the workers compensation system, class codes, and experience rating.
  6. Distinguish the BOP from a full commercial package.
  7. Describe life, health, and disability products for businesses.
  8. Recognize specialty lines and their unique underwriting requirements.
  9. Describe how risk managers structure commercial insurance programs.

docs.title: Suggested Reading
docs.text:
• Start with 3.1 Commercial Lines Overview.
  • For the most fundamental commercial coverages see 3.2 Commercial Property, 3.3 CGL, and 3.5 Workers Compensation.
  • For underwriting detail cross-reference 4.6 Underwriting by Line and 5.6 Rating by Line.

docs.title: What Are Commercial Lines?
docs.text:
Commercial lines insure the exposures of businesses, organizations, and professionals. They encompass:

  • Commercial property — buildings, contents, business income.
  • Commercial general liability (CGL) — third-party bodily injury and property damage.
  • Commercial auto — owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles.
  • Workers compensation — statutory employee injury benefits.
  • Package policies — combined property and liability (BOP, commercial package).
  • Specialty lines — marine, aviation, surety, professional, cyber, D&O, E&O, environmental, and more.
  • Life, accident, and health — group benefits and business protection.

docs.title: Commercial Market Segments
docs.text: Segment Characteristics Typical Need Small business Revenues under ~\$5M; few employees; simple exposures BOP, small commercial package Middle market Revenues \$5M–\$500M; complex operations; risk manager or broker-managed Customized package, layered limits Large / national accounts Revenues over \$500M; multi-location; captives and complex programs Program business, self-insurance, bespoke structures Specialty High-risk, unusual, or hard-to-place Non-admitted/surplus lines, London market, specific expertise

docs.title: Distribution in Commercial Lines
docs.text:
• Agents — typically for small business and middle market.
  • Brokers — dominant for middle market and larger; negotiate programs, market submissions.
  • MGAs and coverholders — delegated underwriting authority for niche programs (e.g., trucking, restaurants, high-value property).
  • Direct — growing for small business via digital platforms.

The broker's submission is the core information package for underwriting.

docs.title: The Submission Process
docs.text: Step Description Broker/agent gathers data Applications, loss runs, financials, values, photos, engineering reports Submission to market The insurer reviews and may request additional data Underwriting analysis COPE, exposure assessment, experience review Indication/quote Preliminary indication or firm quote subject to conditions Binder / binding Coverage attaches; pending receipt of documents and premium Issuance Final policy documentation

docs.title: Underwriting Data for Commercial Lines
docs.text: Data Source Applications ACORD applications by line (property, GL, auto, WC) Loss runs Prior carrier loss history (typically 3–5 years) Financial statements Business financials; credit report; bankruptcy search Values Statement of values (SOV), property schedules Inspections Risk engineering reports, photos COPE data Construction, occupancy, protection, exposure MVRs For commercial auto Class codes / payroll For workers compensation Contracts Lease, purchase, hold-harmless agreements

docs.title: Package vs. Mono-Line
docs.text:
Structure Description Mono-line Separate policy for each coverage (property, GL, auto, WC) Package (BOP) Simplified combined form for small businesses; property + liability + selected extras in one policy Commercial Package Policy (CPP) Two or more coverage parts in one policy, with common declarations and conditions

Packaging benefits:

  • Fewer documents and easier compliance.
  • Interline discounts and credits.
  • One renewal and service relationship.

docs.title: The Underwriting Cycle in Commercial Lines
docs.text:
Commercial lines are subject to the same underwriting cycle as personal lines, but amplified for larger risks:

  • Soft market — broad terms, low rates, high capacity.
  • Hard market — reduced capacity, higher rates, reduced limits, more exclusions.

Large commercial accounts are individually negotiated; terms vary by account. Portfolio management matters: concentration by territory, class, and catastrophe exposure.

docs.title: Regulation of Commercial Lines
docs.text:
• US: state rate and form regulation; large commercial accounts often exempt from rate filing (file-and-use/manual exceptions); surplus lines market for non-admitted.
  • UK: FCA/PRA; Solvency II; fairness and consumer duty apply but corporate customers have fewer conduct protections than consumers.
  • Cross-border: global programs require local policies (admitted) plus a master policy (non-admitted or London).

docs.title: Role of the Commercial Underwriter
docs.text:
The commercial underwriter:

  1. Assesses the risk — exposures, hazards, controls, management quality.
  2. Selects — accepts, declines, or modifies.
  3. Prices — using manual rates, experience rating, and judgment.
  4. Sets terms — limits, deductibles, exclusions, warranties.
  5. Documents — the file rationale.
  6. Manages — the portfolio and the account at renewal.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Commercial lines cover business and professional risks across property, liability, auto, WC, package, and specialty.
  • The broker's submission and data quality drive underwriting.
  • Packages simplify small business coverage; large accounts require bespoke structures.
  • The cycle, portfolio management, and regulation shape commercial underwriting.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Commercial property insurance protects business-owned real and personal property against physical loss and resulting business interruption. It covers:

  • Buildings — the structure and permanent fixtures.
  • Business personal property — contents, stock, equipment, and improvements.
  • Business income (BI) / extra expense — lost revenue and continuing expenses after a covered loss.
  • Additional coverages — debris removal, ordinance/law, loss of rents, etc.

docs.title: The Commercial Property Program (ISO)
docs.text:
The ISO commercial property program consists of:

Component Purpose Building and Personal Property Coverage Form (BPP) Core direct damage coverage Business Income (and Extra Expense) Coverage Form Lost revenue and extra costs Cause of Loss Forms Basic, Broad, Special — define covered perils Conditions and Endorsements Coinsurance, valuation, deductibles, ordinance/law, etc.

docs.title: Building and Personal Property (BPP)
docs.text: Coverage What It Covers Building The structure, fixtures, permanently installed machinery (owned or insured under a lease), additions under construction, and building materials/equipment Business personal property Furniture, fixtures, machinery, equipment, stock, and other personal property owned or held in trust while on the described premises Property of others Personal property of others in the insured's care, custody, or control Additional coverages Debris removal, preservation of property, fire department charges, pollutant clean-up, etc.

docs.title: Business Income / Extra Expense
docs.text:
• Business income — net income the business would have earned plus continuing normal operating expenses during the period of restoration.
  • Extra expense — necessary costs to continue operations (e.g., renting temporary space).
  • Period of restoration — from the loss until repaired/replaced/business reopened with reasonable speed.
  • Extended business income — protects against loss of income after reopening due to slow recovery of customers.
  • Loss of rents / rental value — for landlord exposures.

docs.title: Cause of Loss Forms
docs.text:
Form Covered Perils Basic Fire, lightning, explosion, windstorm/hail, smoke, riot, vandalism, sprinkler leakage, etc. (named) Broad Basic plus falling objects, weight of snow/ice, water damage, etc. (named) Special (Open Perils) All risks of physical loss unless excluded — the most common for commercial

Common exclusions: flood, earthquake, ordinance/law, wear and tear, rust/corrosion, mold, pollution (limited), nuclear, war, government action, and business interruption without direct physical damage (e.g., utility outage contingent BI requires endorsement).

docs.title: Valuation
docs.text: Basis Meaning Replacement Cost Cost to replace with like kind and quality, no depreciation Actual Cash Value Replacement cost less depreciation Functional Replacement Cost Cost of a modern equivalent that serves the same function Market Value / Agreed Value Stated or appraised value; used for special property

docs.title: Coinsurance
docs.text:
The coinsurance clause requires the insured to carry insurance equal to a stated percentage (usually 80%, 90%, or 100%) of the property's value at the time of loss:

Payment = Loss × (Insurance Carried ÷ Insurance Required)

If the insured under-insures, the claim is proportionately reduced. Example:

  • Building value: \$1,000,000; 90% coinsurance requires \$900,000.
  • Insured carries \$600,000.
  • Loss: \$300,000.
  • Payment: \$300,000 × (\$600,000 ÷ \$900,000) = \$200,000.

Underwriters must ensure values are adequate at inception and on change; agreed value endorsements waive coinsurance where the insurer has approved the stated values.

docs.title: COPE — The Core Underwriting Factors
docs.text: Factor Explanation Construction Fire-resistive, masonry, frame, wood, unprotected steel; building materials and finish Occupancy What the building is used for; hazards of operations (cooking, chemicals, storage) Protection Public fire protection (hydrants, fire department), private protection (sprinklers, alarms, extinguishers) Exposure Surrounding buildings and external hazards (wildfire, flood, wind, exposure from neighbors)

docs.title: Key Underwriting Steps
docs.text:
1. Verify values — SOV accuracy; replacement cost estimation; coinsurance compliance.
  2. Assess COPE — construction, occupancy, protection, exposure.
  3. Review loss history — frequency, severity, and causes of prior losses.
  4. Evaluate management — housekeeping, maintenance, safety culture, and risk engineering implementation.
  5. Identify catastrophes — flood zone, wildfire, wind/hail, earthquake; require appropriate deductibles or separate coverage.
  6. Check occupancy controls — hazardous operations, hot work, storage density, equipment maintenance.
  7. Set terms — limits, deductibles, coinsurance, valuation, special conditions (e.g., sprinkler warranty, protection requirements).

docs.title: Underwriting Red Flags
docs.text:
• Underinsurance or a SOV that has not been updated.
  • Frame construction with no sprinklers.
  • Poor housekeeping; blocked exits; overloaded storage.
  • Deferred maintenance (roof, electrical, HVAC).
  • High fire load (combustibles) without protection.
  • Flood or wildfire zone exposure without required coverage/deductible.
  • Frequent small claims suggesting behavioral issues.

docs.title: Protection Requirements
docs.text:
Conditions often warrant that fire protection systems be maintained in service:

  • Sprinkler warranty — require sprinkler system operational; breakage penalty.
  • Alarm requirements — fire/burglary alarms monitored.
  • Inspections and testing — mandated fire protection system testing and records.

docs.title: Business Income Underwriting
docs.text:
• Review financial statements to verify exposure and determine appropriate period of restoration.
  • Assess dependence on a single location, supplier, or customer.
  • Contingent business income — covers losses from suppliers' or customers' premises (requires endorsement and specific exposure data).
  • Check utility dependence — power, water, data (endorsements for utility interruption).

docs.title: Endorsements and Special Forms
docs.text: Endorsement Purpose Ordinance or Law Demolition, increased cost of construction, loss of business income due to code compliance Flood / Earthquake Add coverage or provide separate policy Equipment Breakdown Mechanical/electrical breakdown (boiler and machinery) Spoilage Refrigerated stock loss Builder's Risk Property under construction Installation Floater Property in transit/at site Difference in Conditions (DIC) Broadens coverage beyond primary (often for flood/earthquake gap) Peak season / seasonal limits Adjust limits for seasonal inventory

docs.title: UK Commercial Property
docs.text:
• Commercial combined insurance typically covers buildings, contents/stock, business interruption, and liability in one policy.
  • Sum insured for buildings is the rebuild cost; contents/stock at full value.
  • Average clause — similar to coinsurance: under-insurance reduces claims payment (e.g., 80% average).
  • Business interruption — indemnity period (e.g., 12, 24, 36 months), gross profit basis.
  • Property owners/landlord policies, shop/office policies, and commercial combined are common market products.
  • Flood is a standard covered peril in UK commercial property (no general flood exclusion), but high-flood-risk addresses are rated/located risk or may be declined.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Commercial property covers buildings, contents, and business income.
  • COPE (construction, occupancy, protection, exposure) is the core analysis framework.
  • Coinsurance (average) penalizes underinsurance; value adequacy is critical.
  • Open perils (special) is the dominant cause of loss form.
  • Business interruption requires financial analysis and careful period-of-restoration setting.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
