  • 4.4 Risk Assessment & COPE
  • 5.6 Rating by Line

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Commercial General Liability (CGL) protects businesses against third-party claims for bodily injury (BI) and property damage (PD), plus personal and advertising injury, arising from the insured's premises, operations, products, and completed work. CGL also covers the cost of defending such claims.

CGL is the foundation of commercial liability coverage:

  • Premises liability — injury to visitors on the insured's premises.
  • Operations liability — injury or damage arising from ongoing operations.
  • Products liability — injury or damage caused by products sold or distributed.
  • Completed operations — injury or damage from work completed by the insured.
  • Personal and advertising injury — libel, slander, false arrest, copyright infringement in advertising.

docs.title: The CGL Policy Structure (ISO CG 00 01)
docs.text:
The standard ISO CGL has two coverage forms:

Form Coverage Occurrence (CG 00 01) Covers BI/PD caused by an occurrence (an accident) during the policy period, including for bodily injury that manifests after the period Claims-made (CG 00 02) Covers claims first made during the policy period (and reported within the extended reporting period) Claims-made (CG 00 33) Simplified claims-made variant

docs.title: Coverage A — Bodily Injury and Property Damage Liability
docs.text:
• Who is insured: the named insured, employees (for acts within the scope of employment), partners/members/executives, and others as defined.
  • What is covered: sums the insured is legally obligated to pay as damages due to BI or PD caused by an occurrence.
  • Defense: the insurer has the right and duty to defend suits seeking such damages — defense costs are typically outside the limit for most CGL policies (though some are "defense within limits").

docs.title: Coverage B — Personal and Advertising Injury
docs.text:
• Covers injury arising from offenses such as libel, slander, defamation, false arrest, wrongful eviction, invasion of privacy, and misappropriation of advertising ideas.
  • Subject to the insured's advertising activities; many exposures excluded for certain professions.

docs.title: Coverage C — Medical Payments
docs.text:
• Pays medical expenses for bodily injury caused by an accident on the premises or arising from the insured's operations, regardless of fault.
  • Limited amounts (e.g., \$5,000 per person); no admission of liability.

docs.title: Key Definitions
docs.text: Term Meaning Occurrence An accident, including continuous or repeated exposure to substantially the same general harmful conditions Bodily injury Bodily injury, sickness, or disease sustained by a person, including death Property damage Physical injury to tangible property, or loss of use of tangible property not physically injured Personal injury Injury arising from specified offenses (libel, slander, false arrest, etc.) Advertising injury Injury from specified offenses in the course of advertising Products-completed operations BI/PD arising from products sold/distributed or work completed after possession is transferred; excluded from the general aggregate Insured The named insured and others as defined

docs.title: Coverage Triggers
docs.text: Trigger Meaning Occurrence Injury/damage must occur during the policy period Claims-made Claim must be first made during the policy period (and reported within the ERP) Retroactive date Claims-made policies only cover claims from events after the retroactive date

docs.title: Occurrence vs. Claims-Made — Underwriting Implications
docs.text:
Factor Occurrence Claims-made Tail Insurer remains on risk for claims arising later from events during the policy period No tail unless the ERP is purchased (e.g., 1, 3, 5 years) Pricing Must anticipate long-tail development Pricing based on current claims made Risk Greater uncertainty for the insurer Greater certainty but tail risk transferred to the insured Best for Low-to-moderate tail lines (GL, auto) Long-tail and professional lines (malpractice, E&O, D&O, environmental)

The choice between occurrence and claims-made is a significant underwriting and pricing decision.

docs.title: Aggregate Limits
docs.text:
• General aggregate — the maximum the insurer pays for all BI/PD (except products-completed operations) during the policy period.
  • Products-completed operations aggregate — separate cap for products/completed ops claims.
  • Per-occurrence limit — the maximum for any one occurrence.
  • Personal and advertising injury limit — per person/organization.

Example limits: \$1,000,000 per occurrence / \$2,000,000 general aggregate.

docs.title: Exclusions (Key)
docs.text: Exclusion Effect Expected or intended injury Not covered Contractual liability Only covered if assumed in an "insured contract" Liquor liability Excluded unless endorsements are added (host liquor, etc.) Workers compensation Excluded; covered by WC Pollution Broadly excluded; limited coverage for specific operations Aircraft, auto, watercraft Excluded; covered under other policies Mobile equipment Not covered as auto; covered as premises/operations Damage to your work / product Your own defective work/product not covered Damage to impaired property Your work/product that damages other property is limited Professional services Excluded; requires separate professional liability Product recall Excluded; requires recall coverage Punitive damages Not covered in many states

docs.title: Key Underwriting Questions
docs.text:
1. What are the operations? — class code, description of business.
  2. Where are the premises? — territory, condition, hazards on site.
  3. What products are sold or work completed? — products exposure; completed operations.
  4. Who are the customers/end users? — adjacent risk; contractual requirements.
  5. What is the claims experience? — loss runs (frequency and severity).
  6. What contractual obligations exist? — hold-harmless, additional insured requirements.
  7. What is the management quality? — safety culture, loss-control execution.

docs.title: Exposure Analysis
docs.text: Exposure Underwriting Information Needed Premises Square footage, occupancies, business operations on site, visitors/customers Operations Off-site work (contractors), supervision, subcontracting Products Product type, hazards, distribution, recalls history, quality control Completed operations Duration of exposure, warranties, statute of repose Personal/advertising Advertising practices, intellectual property exposure

docs.title: Underwriting Data Sources
docs.text:
• Application (ACORD GL).
  • Loss runs (5 years preferred).
  • Financial statements.
  • Inspection/risk engineering report.
  • Contracts and certificates of insurance (for additional insured requirements).
  • Subcontractor agreements (for contractors).

docs.title: Rating the CGL
docs.text:
• Premises/operations — rated on payroll, square footage, gross receipts, or number of units.
  • Products/completed operations — rated on gross receipts or sales.
  • Class codes — ISO/NCCI classification of the business operations.
  • Experience modification — relates to the insured's own loss experience.
  • Limits and deductibles — ILF (Increased Limits Factor) tables and SIR options.
  • Territory — litigation climate and hazard location.

docs.title: CGL Endorsements
docs.text: Endorsement Purpose Additional Insured Adds parties (owners, contractors, lessors) to coverage Primary and Noncontributory States the CGL is primary and does not contribute with the additional insured's policy Waiver of Subrogation Waives the insurer's right to recover from the additional insured Contractual Liability Broadens assumed contract coverage (limited/blanket) Liquor Liability Adds coverage for the sale of alcohol Pollution Adds limited or full pollution coverage for specific operations Employee Benefits Liability Covers errors in administering employee benefits Hired and Non-Owned Auto Provided when no commercial auto exists Cyber Liability Data breach response and liability (often separate program) Product Withdrawal/Recall Adds recall expense coverage

docs.title: Contractors' Liability (Special Focus)
docs.text:
Contractors have a distinctive profile:

  • Operations exposure — worksites, supervision, tools.
  • Subcontracting — ensure downstream coverage and certificates.
  • Completed operations — long-tail exposure; statute of repose.
  • Contractual requirements — additional insureds, indemnity agreements.
  • X-C-U exclusions — known hazards (explosion, collapse, underground).
  • OCP (Owners and Contractors Protective) policies for owner-contractor relationships.

docs.title: UK Commercial Liability
docs.text:
• Public and Products Liability (PL/Products) — similar to CGL; covers third-party BI/PD claims.
  • Employers' Liability (EL) — compulsory; covers employee injuries not covered by the state system.
  • Claims-made vs. occurrence — both used; PL often occurrence-based; professional and some liability lines claims-made.
  • Principal's Liability and Contractor's All Risks are used in construction.
  • FCA rules — fair value and consumer duty apply to smaller commercial customers; brokers must disclose.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• CGL covers BI, PD, personal/advertising injury, and medical payments for third parties.
  • Occurrence vs. claims-made is a fundamental coverage and underwriting choice.
  • Aggregates cap per-period exposure; products/completed operations are separately aggregated.
  • Underwriting analyzes premises, operations, products, completed ops, contracts, and claims experience.
  • Class codes, gross receipts, payroll, and experience drive rating.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 3.2 Commercial Property
  • 3.4 Commercial Auto
  • 4.4 Risk Assessment & COPE
  • 5.6 Rating by Line
  • 7.4 Loss Evaluation

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Commercial auto insurance covers vehicles owned, hired, or used in business. It protects against:

  • Liability — third-party BI/PD from auto accidents.
  • Physical damage — collision and comprehensive for owned vehicles.
  • Medical payments / PIP — occupant injuries.
  • Uninsured/underinsured motorist — where applicable.

Commercial auto is needed by any business that owns vehicles, hires vehicles, or has employees driving personal vehicles on business.

docs.title: The Business Auto Policy (BAP)
docs.text:
The standard ISO Business Auto Coverage Form (CA 00 01) includes:

Section Coverage Coverage Symbols Defines which autos are covered (1–9, 19, etc.) Liability Coverage BI/PD, defense, covered autos Physical Damage Collision, comprehensive, specified causes Medical Payments Occupant medical expense Uninsured/Underinsured Motorists By state requirements Covered Auto Conditions Duties, valuation, other insurance

docs.title: Coverage Symbols
docs.text:
The symbols determine which autos are covered:

Symbol Autos Covered 1 Any auto 2 Owned autos only 3 Owned private passenger autos only 4 Owned autos other than private passenger (trucks) 5 Owned autos subject to no-fault 6 Owned autos subject to compulsory insurance 7 Specifically described autos 8 Hired autos only 9 Non-owned autos only 19 Mobile equipment subject to compulsory insurance

Choosing the correct symbols is critical — symbol 7 covers only listed vehicles; symbol 1 (any auto) is the broadest but most expensive.

docs.title: Commercial Auto Exposures
docs.text: Exposure Description Owned autos Vehicles owned by the business, including private passenger, trucks, trailers Hired autos Vehicles leased, rented, or borrowed by the business Non-owned autos Vehicles owned by employees used in the business (e.g., salespeople driving personal cars) Garage operations For auto dealers, repair shops, and service stations (Garage Coverage Form) Motor carrier / trucking Fleet operations, owner-operators, cargo liability Public livery Taxis, limousines, for-hire passenger transport

docs.title: Key Underwriting Data
docs.text: Data Source Application Vehicle schedule, garaging location, use, radius MVRs All authorized drivers Loss runs Prior auto losses (frequency/severity) Financials Credit, business stability Fleet information Vehicle types, values, mileage, maintenance Driver files CDL (commercial driver's license) status, training

docs.title: Underwriting Considerations
docs.text:
1. Fleet composition — vehicle types (autos, trucks, trailers, special equipment).
  2. Radius of operations — local vs. long-haul.
  3. Driver quality — CDL holders, training, accident/violation history.
  4. Use — business, delivery, transportation of goods, passengers.
  5. Garaging — secure parking, territory, crime rate.
  6. Maintenance — vehicle condition and maintenance records.
  7. Safety program — driver training, telematics, policies.
  8. Contractual requirements — additional insureds, certificates.

docs.title: Underwriting Red Flags
docs.text:
• High driver turnover or unlicensed drivers.
  • MVR violations (speeding, DUI).
  • Frequent at-fault accidents.
  • Poor vehicle maintenance.
  • Long-haul routes through high-risk territories.
  • Uninsured operation or lapsed coverage.

docs.title: Trucking and Motor Carrier
docs.text:
Motor carrier underwriting is specialized:

Topic Underwriting Focus FMCSA authority Operating authority, safety ratings Driver qualifications CDL, medical certificates, drug/alcohol testing Hours of service Compliance with HOS rules Vehicle maintenance Inspection records, DOT inspections Cargo Type (general freight, hazardous, refrigerated), liability, cargo insurance Owner-operators Status (independent contractor vs. employee) Physical damage Truck/trailer values, deductibles Excess liability Umbrella/truckers excess for high limits

The Truckers Coverage Form (ISO CA 00 20) is designed for motor carriers; the Motor Carrier Coverage Form (CA 00 20/21 variants) addresses owner-operators and leased vehicles.

docs.title: Garage Coverage
docs.text:
The Garage Coverage Form (ISO CA 00 05) is used for:

  • Auto dealers, repair shops, service stations.
  • Covers garage operations liability (premises and operations), auto liability (symbols), and garagekeepers (customer vehicles).
  • Dealers physical damage covers inventory (new/used vehicles) while on the lot.

docs.title: Rating Commercial Auto
docs.text: Factor Basis Liability Vehicle type, radius, use, territory, driver class, fleet size Physical damage Vehicle value, make/model, territory, deductibles Cargo Cargo type, value, radius Experience Loss ratio / experience modification Limits Increased limits factors Deductible Choice of deductible Fleet discount Volume credit

docs.title: UK Commercial Motor
docs.text:
• Fleet policies — multiple vehicles on one policy; rated by vehicle class, usage, drivers, claims history, territory.
  • Own goods — vehicles used to carry the insured's own goods (e.g., delivery vans).
  • Hired/rental — vehicles hired with driver or without.
  • Trade (garage) — motor traders insurance for vehicles in the dealer's custody.
  • FCA rules — fair value, pricing rules, and conduct for commercial customers.

docs.title: Claims Considerations
docs.text:
• Coverage — symbol check, driver authorization, use.
  • Liability investigation — fault determination, police reports.
  • Physical damage — appraisal, total loss, salvage.
  • Cargo claims — loss/damage in transit, carrier liability.
  • Subrogation — recover from at-fault third parties.
  • Fraud — staged accidents, inflated claims, fake cargo losses.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Commercial auto covers owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles for liability and physical damage.
  • Symbols define coverage scope and are a frequent source of errors.
  • Trucking, garage, and public livery are specialized exposures with separate forms.
  • Underwriting focuses on fleet, drivers, use, radius, maintenance, and claims history.
  • MVRs, loss runs, and safety programs are the core data sources.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Workers compensation (WC) is a compulsory, no-fault insurance system that provides statutory benefits to employees for work-related injuries and occupational diseases, in exchange for which employees generally surrender the right to sue the employer for negligence.

WC is a social contract:

  • The employee receives medical care and wage replacement without proving fault.
  • The employer receives limited liability — employees cannot sue for pain and suffering or punitive damages (subject to exceptions).

In the US, WC is state-regulated (state statutes, state funds, private carriers, or monopolistic state funds). In the UK, the system differs: employers have a statutory liability under the Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969 for employee injuries, but benefits are provided through the state social security system and common-law negligence claims — there is no no-fault WC benefit scheme as such.

docs.title: Benefits Provided (US WC)
docs.text: Benefit Description Medical care Full medical treatment for work-related injury/illness, no limit in most states Temporary total disability (TTD) Wage replacement while the employee is disabled and recovering (typically 2/3 of average weekly wage, subject to state maximums) Temporary partial disability (TPD) Wage replacement when the employee can work in a limited capacity Permanent partial disability (PPD) Scheduled or unscheduled awards for permanent impairment (e.g., loss of a limb, hearing loss) Permanent total disability (PTD) Lifetime benefits for total and permanent disability Death benefits Burial and weekly benefits to dependents Vocational rehabilitation Retraining and return-to-work services

docs.title: The Structure of WC Insurance (US)
docs.text: Component Description Monopolistic states The state fund is the exclusive carrier (e.g., ND, OH, WA, WV, WY) Competitive states Private carriers compete with state funds where they exist Assigned risk / residual market Employers unable to obtain voluntary coverage are assigned to a pool Self-insurance Large employers may self-insure with state approval Group self-insurance Small employers pool to self-insure in some states NCCI The National Council on Compensation Insurance develops rates and experience rating in most states

docs.title: Class Codes
docs.text:
Every occupation and operation is assigned an NCCI class code with a rate per \$100 of payroll:

  • Manual rates — state-specific, class-specific rates.
  • Payroll audit — actual payroll by class determined at audit.
  • Premium = (Payroll ÷ 100) × Class Rate × Experience Modifier × (1 + Ex-Mod Taxes/Assessments)

docs.title: Experience Rating
docs.text:
• Experience modification (Ex-Mod / EMR) — compares actual losses to expected losses over a period (typically 3 policy years, excluding the most recent) and produces a modifier:
  • Below 1.00 — better than average experience (credit).
  • Above 1.00 — worse than average experience (debit).
  • Experience rating rewards safe employers and penalizes poor loss experience.
  • Large deductibles / SIR — employers assume risk in exchange for lower premium; claims are reimbursed to the insurer above the deductible.

docs.title: Payroll and Exposure
docs.text:
• WC premium is driven by payroll by class code, so accurate payroll reporting is essential.
  • Owners/officers — may be included or excluded under state rules.
  • Independent contractors — must be correctly classified (misclassification is a compliance and premium issue).
  • Subcontractors — certificates of insurance and coverage verification required.

docs.title: Key Underwriting Questions
docs.text:
1. What operations? — class codes, job hazards, materials.
  2. Who are the employees? — payroll, tenure, experience, training.
  3. What is the loss history? — frequency, severity, types of claims.
  4. What is the safety culture? — safety programs, return-to-work, management commitment.
  5. What is the financial stability? — payroll accuracy, credit, premium payment history.
  6. What is the state environment? — benefit levels, litigation culture, medical costs.

docs.title: Hazard Assessment
docs.text: Hazard Examples Underwriting Impact Physical Manual handling, machinery, falls, vehicles Frequency/severity of injuries Chemical Exposure, flammability, inhalation Occupational disease claims Ergonomic Repetitive motion, lifting Soft-tissue claims Psychosocial Stress, workplace conflict Mental health claims (in some states) Organizational Safety program weakness, training gaps General frequency

docs.title: Underwriting Data
docs.text: Data Source Application Class codes, payroll, ownership, operations Loss runs 3–5 years WC loss history Experience mod NCCI/state rating bureau Safety program Documentation, inspections, training records Financial statements Payroll verification, credit Prior carrier Coverage verification, claims handling performance Drug-free workplace Testing program (discounts in many states) Return-to-work program Documented modified duty program

docs.title: Underwriting Red Flags
docs.text:
• High frequency of minor injuries (indicative of poor safety).
  • Severity spikes (large indemnity or permanent disability awards).
  • Misclassification of employees or payroll.
  • Poor safety documentation or no safety program.
  • High turnover, seasonal employees, or inexperienced workforce.
  • Claims of fraud or abuse.
  • Weak financial condition of the employer.

docs.title: Controlling WC Loss
docs.text: Control Description Safety programs Hazard identification, training, PPE Return-to-work (modified duty) Reduces duration of TTD Medical management Early intervention, choice of physician panel Claims management Prompt reporting, investigation, litigation control Drug-free workplace Testing reduces frequency Ergonomics Prevents soft-tissue injuries Safety culture Management commitment, employee engagement

docs.title: Fraud in Workers Compensation
docs.text:
• Employer fraud — misclassification, underreporting payroll, failure to carry coverage.
  • Employee fraud — malingering, exaggeration, off-work activities.
  • Provider fraud — unnecessary treatment, billing scams.
  • SIU — special investigation units investigate red flags: Monday-morning injuries, weekend accidents, inconsistent medical narratives.

docs.title: UK Employers' Liability (EL)
docs.text:
The UK system:

  • Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969 — every employer must have EL insurance for employee injuries/diseases (civil liability).
  • State benefits — statutory sick pay, industrial injuries disablement benefit, and NHS treatment are funded by the state.
  • Common law claims — employees can sue employers for negligence; EL insurance funds awards and defense.
  • EL rating — based on payroll, occupation (class), and claims history; excesses are generally prohibited or limited for EL.
  • FCA conduct — EL is regulated; renewals require disclosure of claims history.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• WC is a statutory, no-fault system providing medical and wage benefits.
  • Premium is driven by class codes, payroll, and experience modification.
  • Underwriting focuses on hazards, loss history, safety culture, financial stability, and state environment.
  • Return-to-work, medical management, and claims handling control WC severity.
  • UK EL is a civil-liability system, not a no-fault benefit scheme.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Many businesses need more than one coverage. Commercial packages combine property and liability coverages under one policy, and the Businessowners Policy (BOP) is a simplified package designed for small businesses.

Structure Description Best For BOP Simplified, standardized package: property + liability + selected extras in one form Small businesses (retail, offices, apartments, small contractors) Commercial Package Policy (CPP) Two or more coverage parts (property, GL, auto, crime, inland marine) in one policy with common declarations and conditions Middle market businesses needing flexible, customized coverages

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The CPP (ISO) consists of:

  • Common Declarations — insured, policy period, locations.
  • Common Policy Conditions — cancellation, examination of books, changes, etc.
  • Coverage Parts — one or more of:
  • Commercial Property
  • Commercial General Liability
  • Commercial Crime
  • Boiler & Machinery (Equipment Breakdown)
  • Inland Marine
  • Commercial Auto
  • Farm (in some programs)
  • Supplemental Declarations and Forms — per coverage part.

docs.title: Interline Conditions
docs.text:
• Liberalization — coverage automatically broadened if forms are revised.
  • Non-renewal conditions — common notice requirements.
  • Policy period and territory — common to all parts.

docs.title: Advantages of Packaging
docs.text:
• One policy document, one premium, one renewal.
  • Interline discounts — premium credits for combining coverages.
  • Consistent terms and conditions — gaps between coverage parts reduced.
  • Simpler administration — for both insurer and insured.

docs.title: The Businessowners Policy (BOP)
docs.text: The BOP (ISO BP 00 03) is designed for small businesses that meet eligibility criteria. It provides a broad, standardized set of coverages:

docs.title: Section I — Property
docs.text:
• Buildings and business personal property at described premises.
  • Business income and extra expense (included, not optional).
  • Perils — open perils (special) for covered property (with exclusions).
  • Valuation — replacement cost on buildings and most contents.
  • Included extras — debris removal, fire department charges, pollutant cleanup, etc.
  • Optional coverages — outdoor property, glass, signs, spoilage, etc.

docs.title: Section II — Liability
docs.text:
• Bodily injury and property damage liability (occurrence-based).
  • Personal and advertising injury.
  • Medical payments.
  • Defense costs (outside limits).

docs.title: Other Coverages
docs.text:
• Loss of income — included.
  • Crime — optional (employee dishonesty, theft of money/securities).
  • Equipment breakdown — optional.
  • Hired/non-owned auto — optional.
  • Umbrella/excess — optional BOP umbrella.

docs.title: BOP Eligibility
docs.text:
Eligible Not Eligible Retail/wholesale (non-high-risk) Manufacturing with significant hazards Offices (non-professional services) Professional services (law, medicine, accounting) Apartments (limited units) High-risk occupancies (bars, nightclubs) Small contractors (limits on size) Auto/trucking operations Service businesses (low hazard) Hazardous materials Restaurants (with conditions) Large, complex risks

Eligibility is defined by class/occupancy and size (square footage, receipts, employees). The BOP is not available for risks that require special forms or high limits.

docs.title: BOP vs. CPP
docs.text: Factor BOP CPP Forms Standardized Customizable Eligibility Strict occupancy/size limits Any qualifying commercial risk Property Open perils, business income included As desired (basic/broad/special; BI optional) Liability Occurrence only Occurrence or claims-made Pricing Manual rates, simplified Manual + judgment + experience Best for Small, simple risks Larger or unusual risks

docs.title: Interline Underwriting
docs.text:
The package should be underwritten as a whole, not line by line:

  • Check consistency — limits, premises, operations across coverage parts.
  • Verify eligibility for BOP vs. CPP choice.
  • Assess cross-line hazards — a restaurant has property (grease, fire), GL (slip/trip, food liability), and crime exposures.
  • Manage interline credits — packaging discounts are justified by combined economics.

docs.title: BOP Underwriting Checklist
docs.text:
• Eligibility (occupancy, size).
  • Property values and condition (COPE).
  • Business income adequacy.
  • Liability exposures (premises, operations, products).
  • Hired/non-owned auto needs.
  • Crime exposure (cash handling, employees).
  • Prior losses (frequency/severity).
  • Management quality and housekeeping.

docs.title: Rating the Package
docs.text: Factor BOP CPP Property Rating by occupancy, construction, protection, territory Manual plus judgment Liability Based on receipts, payroll, square footage Class rates on exposure bases Packaging discount Included in BOP pricing Interline credits applied Experience Limited or none Experience rating available Minimum premium Fixed per class As developed

docs.title: UK Equivalent
docs.text:
• Commercial combined policies bundle property, contents, business interruption, public/products liability, and employers' liability.
  • Shop, office, and trade policies are standard small-business products.
  • Ratings typically based on sum insured, class of trade, and claims experience.
  • Average clauses apply to property sections.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The BOP is a standardized small-business package; the CPP is a flexible multi-part package.
  • Eligibility governs which product applies.
  • Packages are underwritten holistically across lines.
  • Interline discounts and simplified terms drive package economics.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Businessowners Policy (BOP) is a simplified package for small businesses. It combines property, business income, and liability coverage into one standardized form, with optional coverages available by endorsement.

This chapter deepens the BOP discussion from 3.6, focusing on rating, endorsements, underwriting detail, and claims considerations.

docs.title: BOP Structure
docs.text:
The ISO BOP (BP 00 03) is built around:

  • Eligibility — occupancy class and size criteria.
  • Section I — Property (Building, Business Personal Property, Business Income/Extra Expense).
  • Section II — Liability (BI/PD, Personal & Advertising Injury, Medical Payments).
  • Conditions and Definitions common to both sections.
  • Endorsements — adding coverages as needed.

docs.title: Coverage Summary
docs.text: Coverage Included? Buildings Only if elected (property limit) Business personal property Included Business income / extra expense Included Outdoor property & signs Limited, included Glass Included as part of property Crime (employee dishonesty, theft of money/securities) Option Equipment breakdown Option Hired/non-owned auto liability Option Professional liability Option (limited classes) Umbrella / excess Option

docs.title: BOP Rating
docs.text:
The BOP is rated using class/occupancy rates rather than pure manual property and liability components:

Component Rating Basis Property Building value, contents value, construction, protection, territory Business income Based on property values and class factors Liability Receipts, payroll, square footage, number of apartments/units Optional coverages Flat charges or stated exposure bases Deductibles Choice of general/GL deductible; percentage wind/hail deductible Minimum premium Fixed by class/territory

docs.title: Rating Example (Illustrative)
docs.text:
• Class: 5,000 sq ft retail store; contents \$250,000; no building owned.
  • Base liability premium from class rate × exposure.
  • Contents premium: \$250,000 × rate per \$1,000 at 80% coinsurance.
  • Business income: factor on contents limit.
  • Optional crime: flat charge per location.
  • Deductible: \$1,000 property; \$500 GL.
  • Result: annual premium with BOP pricing already including package credits.

docs.title: Core Underwriting Steps
docs.text:
1. Eligibility check — occupancy, size, receipts; ensure the risk qualifies.
  2. Property values — verify building/contents values; replacement cost adequacy; coinsurance.
  3. COPE analysis — construction, occupancy, protection, exposure.
  4. Liability review — premises conditions, operations, products, contracts.
  5. Business income — verify revenue and recovery time.
  6. Loss history — 3–5 years loss runs.
  7. Management/housekeeping — visit or inspection where indicated.
  8. Optional coverages — quote and endorse; ensure no gaps.

docs.title: Key BOP Underwriting Questions
docs.text: Question Purpose Is the occupancy eligible? BOP eligibility controls Are values current and adequate? Coinsurance and adequacy Is there a significant products exposure? BOP liability limits may be insufficient Are there hired/non-owned autos? Add coverage if employees drive on business Is there a cash/asset handling risk? Crime coverage need Are there special hazards (restaurant cooking, flammable storage)? Endorsements or decline Is there a business interruption exposure? BI adequacy; verify revenue

docs.title: BOP Underwriting Red Flags
docs.text:
• Underinsured values (values below coinsurance requirement).
  • Ineligible occupancy or size.
  • Poor housekeeping; fire hazards.
  • Claims frequency (small claims pattern).
  • Products/completed operations needing higher limits than BOP offers.
  • Multi-vehicle operations (BOP auto coverage is limited).
  • Professional services that require separate E&O.

docs.title: BOP Endorsements (Common)
docs.text: Endorsement Effect Ordinance or Law Adds code upgrade coverage Spoilage Refrigerated stock Money and Securities (Crime) Employee dishonesty, theft of money/securities Equipment Breakdown Mechanical/electrical Hired/Non-Owned Auto Auto liability for hired/non-owned Umbrella/Excess Higher limits Professional Liability Adds specific professional coverage (limited) Employment Practices Adds EPLI Cyber Adds data breach Flood / Earthquake Adds CAT perils Additional Insured Endorses additional parties

docs.title: BOP Claims Considerations
docs.text:
• Prompt notice — the BOP requires prompt notice of loss; failure may prejudice coverage.
  • Duties after loss — protect property, cooperate, submit sworn statement, allow inspection.
  • Valuation — replacement cost (buildings and contents) subject to coinsurance compliance.
  • Business income — actual loss sustained during the period of restoration.
  • Reservation of rights / coverage questions — eligibility and occupancy misrepresentation can void BOP coverage.

docs.title: When a BOP Is Not the Right Product
docs.text: Situation Preferred Solution Large or complex exposure CPP or specialty High-risk occupancy (bars, nightclubs) Specialty program or surplus lines Manufacturing with major hazards CPP with tailored protections Professional practice (law, medicine, accounting) Professional liability + CPP Trucking/fleet operations Commercial auto + cargo + GL High limits (>\$1M–\$2M GL) CPP + umbrella

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The BOP is a standardized small-business package with property, BI, and liability included.
  • Rating is class-based with package credits built in.
  • Underwriting centers on eligibility, values, COPE, loss history, and optional coverage needs.
  • Endorsements extend the BOP; some exposures require moving to a CPP or specialty market.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Businesses purchase a range of life, accident, and health (LA&H) products to protect their employees, their owners, and the business itself. These products fall into two broad categories:

  • Group benefits — medical, life, disability, and accident coverages for employees.
  • Business protection — key person, buy-sell, and business expense coverages.

This chapter covers the commercial LA&H products an underwriter meets, with emphasis on underwriting considerations.

docs.title: Group Benefits
docs.text: Product Purpose Group life Term life for employees, often a multiple of salary (e.g., 1–2×) Group medical/health Medical expense coverage for employees and their families Group short-term disability (STD) Wage replacement during short absences Group long-term disability (LTD) Wage replacement for extended disability Group accident (AD&D) Accidental death/dismemberment benefits Vision and dental Supplemental benefits Voluntary (worksite) benefits Employee-paid supplements (life, critical illness, accident)

docs.title: Underwriting Group Benefits
docs.text:
Group underwriting is fundamentally different from individual underwriting:

  • No individual medical selection for most groups (guaranteed issue).
  • The group as a whole is rated on:
  • Participation rate (percentage of eligible employees).
  • Employer size and stability.
  • Industry and occupation class.
  • Claims history (experience-rated groups).
  • Employee demographics (age, gender, salary distribution).

docs.title: Participation and Anti-Selection
docs.text:
• Guaranteed issue requires high participation (e.g., 75%+ of eligible).
  • Low participation invites anti-selection — only unhealthy employees enroll.
  • Voluntary products are especially exposed; insurers set participation minimums.

docs.title: Group Underwriting Tiers
docs.text: Tier Description Fully insured Insurer assumes the risk; premium fixed for the period Experience-rated Large groups' premiums reflect their own claims (loss ratio) Self-funded Employer funds claims; insurer provides ASO (administrative services only) and stop-loss Stop-loss Insurer reimburses claims above an attachment point (specific and aggregate)

docs.title: Stop-Loss Insurance
docs.text:
Stop-loss (excess medical) covers self-funded employers:

  • Specific stop-loss — reimburses claims above a per-person attachment (e.g., \$100,000).
  • Aggregate stop-loss — reimburses claims above the expected total for the group.
  • Underwriting factors: group size, demographics, plan design, prior claims (rx and medical), financial condition of the employer.

Stop-loss underwriting is data-heavy:

  • Prior claims (medical and pharmacy) for 2–3 years.
  • Census data — age/gender distribution.
  • Plan design — deductibles, out-of-pocket maximums.
  • Laser underwriting — specific high-cost individuals are "lasered" (excluded or lowered attachment).

docs.title: Key Person Insurance
docs.text:
Key person (keyman) insurance covers the business against financial loss from the death or disability of a key person — an owner, executive, or essential employee whose loss would damage the business.

  • The business is the owner and beneficiary.
  • Coverage: term or whole life on the key person; disability income or buy-out cover.
  • Underwriting: the key person's health and income; the business's financial dependence on them; the amount needed (revenue loss, replacement, debt).

docs.title: Underwriting Data
docs.text:
• Financial statements of the business.
  • Description of the key person's role and value.
  • Insurance needs calculation (replacement, debt, loss of profits).
  • Key person's medical/lifestyle underwriting (as individual life).

docs.title: Buy-Sell (Shareholder Protection)
docs.text:
Buy-sell agreements fund the purchase of a deceased or disabled owner's shares:

  • Cross-purchase — remaining owners each insure the others; proceeds fund share purchase.
  • Entity purchase — the company insures each owner; proceeds fund company purchase of the deceased's shares.
  • Funding: life insurance and disability buy-out policies on each owner.

docs.title: Underwriting Considerations
docs.text:
• Valuation — the agreement must specify how shares are valued.
  • Funding amount — insurance must match the buy-sell obligation.
  • Proceeds use — must be documented to avoid taxable or unintended outcomes.
  • Individual underwriting — each owner's health and lifestyle.

docs.title: Business Travel Accident and Accident Products
docs.text:
• Business travel accident (BTA) — covers employees on business trips (death, dismemberment, medical).
  • Group AD&D — accidental death/dismemberment for employees.
  • Occupational accident — for non-subscriber employers or high-hazard trades, provides benefits similar to WC in some jurisdictions.
  • Underwriting: travel patterns, destination risk, occupations, and participation.

docs.title: Voluntary / Worksite Products
docs.text:
Employees pay premiums (often via payroll deduction) for:

  • Term life.
  • Critical illness.
  • Accident.
  • Hospital indemnity.
  • Cancer or specified disease.

Small premium amounts can support small groups. Insurers rely on participation thresholds and simplified underwriting (health questions) to control anti-selection.

docs.title: Underwriting Data and Governance
docs.text: Topic Data / Control Census data Age, gender, salary, location Claims data Prior claims/usage (medical, rx) Plan design Benefits, cost-sharing, networks Participation Enrollment percentages Financial Employer financials for self-funded Compliance HIPAA/ERISA (US); FCA conduct (UK) Reinsurance Catastrophic and morbidity cover

docs.title: Compliance and Conduct
docs.text:
• US: ERISA governs employer plans; HIPAA privacy; ACA market reforms; state stop-loss and product regulation.
  • UK: FCA regulation; consumer duty and fair value for group risk products; advised distribution.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Commercial LA&H includes group benefits (life, medical, disability, accident) and business protection (key person, buy-sell).
  • Group underwriting rates the group as a whole; participation control prevents anti-selection.
  • Stop-loss protects self-funded employers; underwriting is data-heavy.
  • Key person and buy-sell are individually underwritten on the insured lives, with the business as owner.
  • Compliance (ERISA, HIPAA, FCA) shapes products and governance.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Specialty lines is the umbrella term for insurance coverages that do not fit neatly into standard property, liability, auto, or WC lines. They often require specialized forms, specialized underwriting expertise, and a distinct market (surplus lines, London market, MGAs).

This chapter surveys the principal specialty lines and their underwriting considerations.

docs.title: Categories of Specialty Lines
docs.text: Category Coverages Marine Ocean marine (hull, cargo, freight) and inland marine Aviation Aircraft hull, aviation liability, airport liability, space Surety Performance bonds, payment bonds, fidelity bonds Professional liability Medical malpractice, lawyers' E&O, architects, accountants, brokers Directors & Officers (D&O) Management liability Cyber Data breach, cyber liability, network security Environmental Pollution liability, remediation Energy Onshore/offshore energy, power plants Financial lines D&O, E&O, crime, employment practices, fiduciary Construction Builders risk, project-specific liability, wrap-ups Political risk / trade credit Expropriation, contract frustration, credit default

docs.title: Ocean Marine
docs.text:
Coverage Underwriting Focus Hull Vessel value, age, type, flag, condition, P&I club, navigation limits Cargo Commodity, packing, route, carrier, port conditions, declaration basis Freight Length of voyage, vessel suitability Protection & Indemnity (P&I) Crew, liability to third parties, pollution; often through P&I clubs Marine liability Wreck removal, pollution, collision (running-down clause)

Key considerations: vessel condition surveys, crew competence, route hazards (piracy, war zones), cargo packing and fragility, and cargo values declared.

docs.title: Inland Marine
docs.text:
• Domestic transit — goods in transit within the country.
  • Bailees' customers — property in the insured's care (dry cleaners, repair shops).
  • Contractors' equipment — machinery and tools at job sites.
  • Builders risk — construction in progress.
  • Installation floaters — equipment being installed.
  • Electronic data processing (EDP) — computers and media.
  • Accounts receivable / valuable papers — records and receivables.
  • Fine arts / collections — for businesses.
  • Motor truck cargo — goods carried by truckers.

Inland marine is one of the fastest-growing and most flexible lines because it covers property that is movable or in transit, which the standard property policy does not.

docs.title: Aviation
docs.text:
Coverage Exposure Aircraft hull Physical damage to the aircraft Liability Bodily injury/property damage to third parties and passengers Airport premises Ground operations, hangars, fuel Products liability Manufacturer liability Space Satellite launch and in-orbit

Underwriting factors: pilot qualifications and hours, aircraft type and maintenance, use (private/business/charter), flight routes, ground risk, and passengers.

docs.title: Surety
docs.text:
Surety is not insurance in the traditional sense — it is a three-party guarantee:

Party Role Principal The party required to perform (contractor, principal) Obligee The party receiving the guarantee (owner, government) Surety The guarantor (insurer)

docs.title: Types of Bonds
docs.text: Bond Purpose Bid bond Guarantees the bidder will enter the contract if awarded Performance bond Guarantees completion of the contract Payment bond Guarantees payment to subcontractors and suppliers Maintenance bond Guarantees workmanship for a period License & permit bonds Compliance with regulations Court bonds Appeal, fiduciary, injunction bonds Fidelity bonds Employee dishonesty (commercial crime)

docs.title: Underwriting Surety
docs.text:
• The surety underwrites the principal's ability to perform, not the hazard of loss.
  • Financial strength — balance sheet, working capital, liquidity, credit.
  • Capacity — the contractor's aggregate bond program vs. net worth.
  • Experience — prior success on similar contracts.
  • Claims history — completed contracts, litigation.
  • Aggregate exposure — concentration risk on a single contractor.

Surety underwriting is a credit underwriting discipline; unlike insurance, the surety expects zero loss. A performance bond loss is a default, not an expected claim frequency event.

docs.title: Professional Liability (E&O / Malpractice)
docs.text:
Market Underwriting Focus Medical malpractice Specialty, claims history, peer review, hospital privileges, limits Lawyers' professional liability Practice areas (litigation, securities, real estate), claims history, firm size Accountants' E&O Client size, services (audit, tax, advisory), SEC exposure Architects & engineers Project size, discipline, contractual terms, claims history Insurance agents/brokers E&O Volume, lines, claims, procedures Technology E&O Software/services, data exposure, contractual liability Miscellaneous E&O Consultants of all types

These are claims-made policies; underwriting focuses on professional qualifications, risk management procedures, claims history, and exposure metrics (revenue, headcount, project size).

docs.title: Directors & Officers (D&O) Liability
docs.text:
Covers management for claims alleging wrongful acts in the management of the company:

  • Side A — personal coverage for directors/officers when the company cannot indemnify.
  • Side B — reimbursement to the company for indemnifying directors/officers.
  • Side C — securities claims against the entity (entity coverage).

Underwriting focus: company financials, industry, governance, prior litigation, securities exposure, IPO status, and D&O claims history.

docs.title: Cyber Insurance
docs.text:
Covers data breaches, network security failures, and liability from compromised data:

Coverage Description First-party Breach response (forensics, notification, credit monitoring), business interruption, data restoration, ransomware Third-party Network security and privacy liability, regulatory defense, media liability Extras Social engineering (fraud), cyber extortion, contingent business interruption

docs.title: Cyber Underwriting
docs.text:
• Sector and data sensitivity (PII, PHI, payment data).
  • Security controls (MFA, encryption, patching, backups).
  • Prior breaches / claims.
  • Revenue dependence on IT systems.
  • Ransomware defense posture.
  • Compliance (GDPR, HIPAA, state breach laws).
  • Use of technical questionnaires or assessments.

Cyber is a fast-evolving risk; underwriting standards tighten as threat landscapes change (ransomware, supply-chain attacks, cloud dependence).

docs.title: Environmental and Pollution
docs.text:
Coverage Underwriting Property/GL pollution Limited cleanup, remedial action CGL pollution exclusion Broad exclusion; separate environmental policy Site pollution Known sites, remediation costs Contractors pollution Construction operations Environmental impairment liability (EIL) Gradual pollution, third-party claims

Underwriting involves Phase I/Phase II environmental assessments, site history, operations, waste handling, regulatory status, and financial strength for clean-up obligations.

docs.title: Financial Lines (Other)
docs.text:
• Employment Practices Liability (EPLI) — discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination; underwriting focuses on HR practices, claims history, headcount.
  • Fidelity (Crime) — employee dishonesty, forgery, theft; underwriting focuses on internal controls, cash handling, segregation of duties.
  • Fiduciary liability — ERISA plans; underwriting focuses on plan administration, investment policies, and claims history.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
• Builders risk — property under construction; underwriting focuses on project value, schedule, contractors, fire protection during construction.
  • Contractor's liability — GL, wrap-ups (OCIP/CCIP) for large projects.
  • Construction professional liability — design and CM risks.
  • Surety — performance and payment bonds for contractors.

docs.title: The Specialty Market
docs.text:
Specialty lines are often written in the surplus lines / London market:

  • Non-admitted carriers — not regulated by state rates/forms; flexibility for unusual risks.
  • MGAs/covers — delegated authority under clear guidelines for niche programs.
  • Reinsurance — essential capacity for catastrophe-heavy specialty lines.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Specialty lines cover marine, aviation, surety, professional, financial, cyber, environmental, energy, and construction risks.
  • Underwriting is line-specific and often requires specialist expertise.
  • Surety is a credit discipline — zero-loss expectation.
  • Cyber, D&O, and professional lines are claims-made and evolving quickly.
  • The surplus lines/London market provides capacity for non-standard risks.

docs.text:

  • 4.6 Underwriting by Line
  • 5.4 Pricing Techniques
  • 5.6 Rating by Line

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Risk management is the discipline of identifying, analyzing, and controlling the risks that could prevent a business from achieving its objectives. For the commercial insurer, risk management is both:

  • The subject of what is insured — managing the risks the policy covers.
  • The professional practice of the insured — how businesses assess, retain, transfer, and mitigate risk.

This chapter frames commercial risk management from the perspective of both the risk manager (the buyer) and the underwriter (the insurer).

docs.title: The Risk Management Process
docs.text:
The classic risk management process (RIMS / ISO 31000) has five steps:

Step Description 1. Identify Identify all exposures to loss (property, liability, personnel, financial, strategic) 2. Analyze Measure frequency and severity; quantify potential impact 3. Control Reduce frequency (prevention) and severity (protection) 4. Finance Decide how to pay for losses (retention, transfer, insurance, captives) 5. Monitor Review and update the program continuously

docs.title: Risk Identification
docs.text:
Sources of exposure:

  • Physical — property, equipment, inventory, vehicles.
  • Liability — third-party injury/damage, products, contracts.
  • Personnel — employees, key people, benefits.
  • Financial — credit, currency, interest rates, liquidity.
  • Operational — supply chain, IT, fraud.
  • Strategic — competition, regulation, reputation.
  • Catastrophic — natural perils, terrorism, pandemic.

docs.title: Risk Control Techniques
docs.text: Technique Example Avoidance Discontinuing a hazardous product line Reduction (prevention) Safety training, machine guards, cybersecurity controls Reduction (protection) Sprinklers, firewalls, backups, business continuity planning Contractual transfer Hold-harmless agreements, indemnities Risk retention Deductibles, self-insurance, captives Risk transfer (insurance) Purchased insurance

docs.title: The Risk Manager's Role
docs.text:
The risk manager:

  1. Identifies and analyzes risks across the enterprise.
  2. Implements loss prevention and safety programs.
  3. Designs the insurance program — coverages, limits, deductibles, carriers.
  4. Manages claims — coordination with carriers, litigation control.
  5. Budgets for risk — retentions, premiums, loss control costs.
  6. Coordinates with brokers — submission, marketing, negotiation.
  7. Monitors coverage adequacy — valuations, changes in exposure, endorsements.
  8. Communicates to leadership — risk reporting, board presentations.

docs.title: Risk Retention vs. Transfer
docs.text: Approach Description Full insurance Transfer all risk to insurers Deductibles Insured assumes losses below the deductible SIR (self-insured retention) Insured handles claims up to the SIR; insurer above Captive Owned insurer absorbs retained losses Self-insurance Formal self-funded program (common for WC in large employers)

docs.title: Layered Programs
docs.text:
Large programs use layers:

  • Primary layer — first limit (e.g., \$1M per occurrence).
  • Excess layers — subsequent layers (e.g., \$25M excess of \$1M).
  • Umbrella — broad excess over underlying lines.
  • Total program limit — combined across layers.

docs.title: Program Considerations
docs.text:
• Consistency — coverage gaps between layers; drop-down provisions.
  • Carrier quality — AM Best ratings; claims service; financial strength.
  • Territory — global vs. domestic operations; admitted vs. non-admitted.
  • Statutory requirements — WC, auto compulsory, EL in the UK.
  • Contractual requirements — certificates, additional insureds, waivers of subrogation.
  • Claims control — who handles claims at each layer.

docs.title: Captives
docs.text:
A captive is a wholly owned insurance company formed to insure the risks of its owner(s):

Type Description Pure captive One owner; insures the parent's risks Group captive Multiple owners in similar businesses share risk Rent-a-captive Unrelated businesses rent capital and administration Protected cell company (PCC) Separate cells with segregated assets

docs.title: Why Form a Captive?
docs.text:
• Cost — access to reinsurance at wholesale rates.
  • Tax — premium deductions and investment returns (subject to jurisdiction rules).
  • Coverage flexibility — cover hard-to-place risks.
  • Claims control — direct handling and settlement management.
  • Profit retention — underwriting profit and investment return stay in the group.
  • Risk management incentive — measured loss costs drive safety behavior.

docs.title: Captive Administration
docs.text:
• Domicile — offshore (Bermuda, Cayman, Guernsey) or onshore (Vermont, Delaware, etc.).
  • Fronting — a licensed insurer issues policies; the captive reinsures (fronting fee).
  • Capital and solvency — regulated minimum capital; letters of credit.
  • Reinsurance — captives typically buy stop-loss or quota-share reinsurance.

docs.title: Enterprise Risk Management (ERM)
docs.text:
ERM is a holistic approach to managing all risks across the organization:

Risk Category Examples Strategic Competition, M&A, regulatory change Operational Process failures, IT outages, fraud Financial Credit, market, liquidity Hazard Property, liability, personnel Compliance Law, regulation, contracts

ERM frameworks (COSO, ISO 31000) help organizations:

  • Set risk appetite — how much risk to take.
  • Identify and assess risks consistently.
  • Prioritize by likelihood and impact.
  • Implement responses — avoid, reduce, transfer, accept.
  • Monitor and report — board-level visibility.

docs.title: Claims Management
docs.text:
Effective claims management reduces cost and protects the program:

  • Prompt reporting — early notice improves investigation and defense.
  • Reserve adequacy — proper case reserves and IBNR.
  • Litigation management — panel counsel, settlement authority, appeal strategy.
  • Subrogation — recover from third parties.
  • Data analytics — claims patterns drive safety and pricing.
  • Fraud detection — SIU protocols.

docs.title: Loss Control and Risk Engineering
docs.text:
The insurer's risk engineering function supports underwriting and the insured:

Service Purpose Property surveys COPE assessment, protection evaluation Safety inspections Workplace safety, ergonomics Business continuity reviews Resilience to interruption Cybersecurity assessments Controls, response readiness Contract reviews Liability transfer, additional insureds Training Driver safety, hot work, hazard communication

Good loss control is the shared interest of both parties: fewer losses mean lower premiums and better outcomes.

docs.title: The Underwriter's View of Risk Management
docs.text:
The underwriter assesses the quality of the insured's risk management:

Indicator Strong Weak Safety program Documented, resourced, trained None or informal Claims management Prompt reporting, return-to-work Late reporting, litigation-prone Maintenance Scheduled, documented Reactive, deferred Business continuity Tested plans No plan Risk ownership Risk manager / C-suite focus No single owner Data Uses data to reduce losses No metrics

A strong risk management culture is a positive underwriting factor — it justifies broader terms and better pricing.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Risk management is a five-step process: identify, analyze, control, finance, monitor.
  • The risk manager designs the program, manages claims, and drives loss control.
  • Retention tools (deductibles, SIRs, captives) balance risk transfer with cost.
  • ERM connects hazard risk to strategic, operational, and financial risks.
  • The underwriter rewards strong risk management culture with better terms.

docs.title: Volume 4 — Underwriting
docs.text: Volume 4 is the practical core of the handbook: how insurance risk is analyzed, selected, and priced. It covers the underwriting process, information sources, risk assessment frameworks, risk engineering, the role of the underwriter, line-specific underwriting, and portfolio management.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Chapter Title Contents 4.1 The Underwriting Process Steps from submission to issuance; file documentation; declinations 4.2 Information Sources Applications, loss runs, inspections, MVR, CLUE, financials, public records 4.3 Underwriting Principles Selection, adverse selection, classification, pricing discipline, appetite 4.4 Risk Assessment & COPE Physical and moral hazard analysis; COPE for property; qualitative assessment 4.5 Risk Engineering & Loss Control Surveys, protection, control recommendations, engineering data 4.6 Underwriting by Line Line-specific considerations for property, GL, auto, WC, specialty, life/health 4.7 Portfolio Management Aggregation, CAT limits, concentration, planning, cycle management 4.8 Automation & Data in Underwriting Straight-through processing, predictive models, telematics, regulatory constraints

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this volume you should be able to:

  1. Describe the underwriting process from submission to issuance.
  2. Identify and use the principal information sources.
  3. Apply underwriting principles: selection, classification, pricing discipline, and appetite.
  4. Assess physical and moral hazard, including COPE.
  5. Explain the role of risk engineering in underwriting.
  6. Apply line-specific underwriting considerations.
  7. Manage an underwriting portfolio: aggregation, concentration, and cycle discipline.
  8. Describe how automation and data reshape underwriting.

docs.title: Suggested Reading
docs.text:
• For the practical workflow start with 4.1 The Underwriting Process.
  • For the analytical core see 4.3 Underwriting Principles and 4.4 Risk Assessment & COPE.
  • Cross-reference line underwriting with Volumes 2 and 3, and pricing with Volume 5.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The underwriting process is the disciplined workflow by which an insurer evaluates, selects, prices, and documents a risk. It begins with the receipt of a submission and ends with issuance of the policy (or a declination). The process must be:

  • Consistent — same standards applied to every risk.
  • Documented — the file must support every decision.
  • Timely — quoted and issued within service standards.
  • Compliant — meeting regulatory and internal governance rules.

docs.title: The Underwriting Workflow
docs.text:
Submission Received
       ↓
1. Data Collection & Validation
       ↓
2. Risk Analysis
       ↓
3. Risk Selection (Accept / Modify / Decline)
       ↓
4. Pricing & Rating
       ↓
5. Terms, Conditions & Documentation
       ↓
6. Issuance & Post-Issuance

docs.title: Step 1 — Data Collection & Validation
docs.text:
Activity Description Review the submission Application completeness; broker/agent cover note Validate data Consistency checks; missing or conflicting information Order reports MVR, CLUE, inspections, financials, environmental, etc. Request supplements Additional data needed for a decision Confirm authority Does the risk fit the underwriter's authority level?

Common validation issues:

  • Overstated/understated values.
  • Inconsistent loss runs.
  • Missing signatures or dates.
  • Occupancy/use mismatch with cover requested.

docs.title: Step 2 — Risk Analysis
docs.text:
• Physical hazard — condition, construction, occupancy, protection, exposure (COPE).
  • Moral hazard — intent, claims history, financial distress, prior fraud.
  • Morale hazard — indifference, poor housekeeping, lack of care.
  • Information quality — completeness and reliability of data.
  • Experience — loss runs, frequency, severity, trend.

docs.title: Step 3 — Risk Selection
docs.text:
Decision Basis Accept as presented Meets appetite and standards Accept with modification Terms adjusted: limits, deductibles, exclusions, conditions Refer Above authority; unusual; borderline Decline Outside appetite or unacceptable risk

Modification tools:

  • Limits — reduce the offered limit.
  • Deductibles / retentions — require the insured to retain more.
  • Exclusions / sub-limits — remove or cap specific exposures.
  • Warranties / conditions — require protection, inspections, safety programs.
  • Premium loading — price the additional risk.
  • Reporting requirements — scheduled statements of values.

docs.title: Step 4 — Pricing & Rating
docs.text:
Pricing is covered in detail in Volume 5. Key principles:

  • Price to the risk, not to the market or competition alone.
  • Apply manual rates, experience rating, schedule rating, or judgment as appropriate.
  • Reflect cost of risk (expected loss + expenses + capital) and profit margin.
  • Ensure adequacy — premium must cover expected loss and expenses with margin.
  • Ensure compliance — rates filings, discrimination rules.

docs.title: Step 5 — Terms, Conditions & Documentation
docs.text:
• Draft the policy — forms, endorsements, declarations, schedules.
  • Issue binders or quotations — confirm coverage subject to terms.
  • Document the file — rationale, data, authority level, decisions.
  • Record the risks — for portfolio monitoring and regulatory returns.

docs.title: Step 6 — Issuance & Post-Issuance
docs.text:
• Issue policy documents — delivery, audit, and payment terms.
  • Post-issuance obligations — premium audits, inspections, endorsements.
  • Inspection conditions — complete required surveys within limits.
  • Renewal planning — set reminders for mid-term reviews and renewal dates.

docs.title: File Documentation
docs.text:
The underwriting file is the record of the decision. A proper file includes:

Item Purpose Application and supplements Basis of information Loss runs and reports Experience evidence Inspections and engineering reports Physical risk evidence Pricing worksheet Rate and premium basis Authority record Who decided what, when Rationale Why accepted, modified, or declined Correspondence Broker/agent/insured communications Policy documentation Form, endorsements, declarations

Good file discipline protects the insurer in disputes, audits, and regulatory reviews.

docs.title: Declinations
docs.text:
A declination is a written refusal to offer coverage. Rules include:

  • Adverse action notices — required where consumer reporting (MVR, credit, CLUE) influenced the decision.
  • Fair access — cannot decline based on prohibited factors (race, religion, national origin, etc.).
  • Documentation — record the reason honestly and completely.
  • Broker notification — communicate promptly and clearly.

docs.title: Underwriting Authority
docs.text:
Authority is the level of risk an underwriter may accept without referral:

Level Scope Junior / line underwriter Small, standard risks within guidelines Senior / lead underwriter Larger or complex risks; exceptions Regional / chief underwriter Major accounts; portfolio decisions

Authority is defined by limits, premium size, class, territory, and unusual features. Exceeding authority without referral is a serious governance breach.

docs.title: Workflow and Turnaround
docs.text:
Metric Description Turnaround time (TAT) Time from submission to quote Clear-to-close Percentage of submissions that can be completed without referral Hit ratio Quoted premiums written vs. quoted Referral rate Percentage routed to higher authority Declination rate Percentage declined Issuance accuracy Correct policy issuance on time

Service expectations matter: brokers reward fast, clear decisions; slow underwriting loses business.

docs.title: Governance and Clean Underwriting
docs.text:
• Underwriting guidelines — documented appetite and rules.
  • Pricing tools and manuals — consistent rating.
  • Peer review — referrals and audits.
  • Quality assurance (QA) — file audits; error tracking.
  • Regulatory compliance — fair discrimination; adverse action notices; anti-fraud controls.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The process runs from submission to issuance through six disciplined steps.
  • Analysis, selection, pricing, terms, and documentation are the core.
  • Authority and referral control risk-taking.
  • File documentation is the record that protects the insurer.
  • Service metrics (TAT, hit ratio) balance speed with discipline.

docs.text:

  • 4.2 Information Sources
  • 4.3 Underwriting Principles
  • 5.1 Pricing Fundamentals
  • 6.1 Policy Issuance

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Underwriting decisions are only as good as the information supporting them. The underwriter gathers data from the submission, third-party databases, inspections, and company records, then validates and interprets it.

This chapter catalogs the main information sources and the questions each answers.

docs.title: Core Information Sources
docs.text: Source Information Provided Application Risk description, coverage requested, values, operations Loss runs Prior claims history (frequency, severity, type) MVR (Motor Vehicle Report) Driver licensing, violations, accidents CLUE / A-Plus Personal/commercial property loss history Inspections / surveys Physical condition, COPE, protection Financial statements Business financial health, payroll, assets Credit / insurance scores Payment and loss-propensity indicators Public records Litigation, liens, judgments, bankruptcy Prior carrier records Coverage history, claims handling, cancellations Broker/agent reports Relationship, knowledge of the insured

docs.title: The Application
docs.text:
The application is the primary document — but only as accurate and complete as the person who completes it.

Section Typical Contents Named insured Legal entity, address, ownership Operations Class, products, processes, locations Coverage requested Limits, forms, deductibles Exposure data Values, payroll, receipts, vehicles, units Prior losses Description and history Financial data For commercial risks Signatures Application is part of the policy basis

docs.title: Validating the Application
docs.text:
• Is the information internally consistent?
  • Does the occupancy match the coverage requested?
  • Are values realistic (not under/overstated)?
  • Was the application signed and dated?

Where an application is part of the policy, misrepresentation can void coverage. Underwriters must ensure the basis of the contract is accurate.

docs.title: Loss Runs
docs.text:
Loss runs are the prior claims record. They reveal:

  • Frequency — how often claims occur.
  • Severity — average and maximum paid/incurred.
  • Cause patterns — theft, fire, liability, WC.
  • Trend — improving or deteriorating.

docs.title: Loss Run Details
docs.text: Field Meaning Policy period The year of coverage Claim number Identity Date of loss When it occurred Cause / description What happened Paid amount What has been paid Incurred amount Paid + reserves Status Open, closed, reopened Months of disability (WC) Duration Subrogation recovered Recoveries

docs.title: Loss Run Analysis
docs.text:
• Compare loss ratio (incurred ÷ premium) to expected by line.
  • Review large losses individually; avoid over-reacting to one-off events.
  • Watch for small claims frequency — a behavioral warning.
  • Consider reserves — high open reserves indicate active claims.

docs.title: Motor Vehicle Reports (MVR)
docs.text:
MVRs provide the driving record:

Data Use Violations Speeding, DUI, reckless driving Accidents At-fault and not-at-fault License status Valid, suspended, revoked CDL Commercial driver's license status

docs.title: MVR Underwriting
docs.text:
• Points systems — assign severity to violations and accidents.
  • DUI/CUI — significant surcharge or declination.
  • Multiple violations — indicates risky driving behavior.
  • Unlicensed drivers — auto coverage generally excluded.

MVR use is regulated: adverse action notices are required where MVR affects the decision (US Fair Credit Reporting Act and state laws).

docs.title: Claim History Databases
docs.text:
Database Contents CLUE (Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange) Personal and commercial property/auto claims (LexisNexis) A-PLUS Auto and property loss database (Verisk) Index systems Insurance claims history (ISO index) Medical information databases Life/health history (MIB, medical information bureau)

These databases identify claims not disclosed in the application — a key anti-fraud and accuracy tool.

docs.title: Inspections and Surveys
docs.text:
Risk inspections provide physical evidence:

Type Purpose Photo inspections Condition, occupancy, exterior Drive-by Neighborhood, property condition Full survey COPE, protection, construction, occupancy details Engineer survey Complex property, machinery, process hazards Liability inspection Premises condition, hazards, exposures

docs.title: When Inspections Are Required
docs.text:
• New business above a value threshold.
  • Older or high-value dwellings.
  • Commercial risks with complex operations.
  • Vacant or special occupancies.
  • Following large losses (to verify controls).

docs.title: Financial Data
docs.text:
For commercial lines and high-value personal, financials matter:

Document Use Financial statements Profitability, solvency, net worth Tax returns Income verification (personal and business) Payroll records WC exposure verification Bank statements Cash flow, creditworthiness Budget/forecast Forward-looking assessment

Financial strength affects terms and pricing: financially distressed insureds may cut maintenance, under-insure, or commit fraud.

docs.title: Credit and Insurance Scores
docs.text:
• Credit-based insurance scores — proprietary scores used in personal auto and property to predict loss propensity (where legally permitted).
  • Payment history — consistent premium payment correlates with lower loss frequency.
  • Regulatory constraints — some states and countries restrict credit use (e.g., some US states ban or limit; UK insurance pricing rules cap the "loyalty penalty").

The underwriter must know what data is permissible in their jurisdiction and when adverse action notices are required.

docs.title: Public Records and Litigation
docs.text:
Data Source Lawsuits Court records, judgment searches Liens Property liens, tax liens Bankruptcy Bankruptcy filings Licenses Professional licenses, complaints OSHA/DOT Workplace safety, transportation violations Regulatory actions Fines, consent orders

Public records identify litigation-prone insureds, fraud risk, and compliance problems.

docs.title: Prior Carrier and Broker Records
docs.text:
• Prior policies — coverage history, gaps, cancellations.
  • Cancellation reasons — for cause, for underwriting, for non-payment.
  • Claims handling — litigated claims, coverage disputes.
  • Broker relationship — track record of the producer, loss ratio, professionalism.

docs.title: Privacy and Compliance
docs.text:
Jurisdiction Key Rules US FCRA (consumer reports, adverse action), GLBA (privacy), HIPAA (medical), state laws UK GDPR/UK GDPR (data protection), FCA (fair treatment, pricing rules) General Data minimization, consent, retention, security

The underwriter must understand what can be collected, how it can be used, and what disclosures are required when adverse decisions are based on third-party data.

docs.title: Information Quality and Reliability
docs.text:
Criterion Question Accuracy Is the data verifiable from sources? Completeness Are gaps in the submission filled? Timeliness Is the data current? Relevance Does it bear on the risk? Permissibility Is collection/use legal?

When information is missing or unreliable, the underwriter must request more data or make a conservative assumption — never guess.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The application, loss runs, MVR, claim databases, inspections, financials, credit, and public records are the core data sources.
  • Each answers a different question about the risk.
  • Validation and consistency checks guard against errors and fraud.
  • Privacy and adverse action rules govern data use.
  • Information quality determines the quality of the underwriting decision.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
