  • 4.3 Underwriting Principles
  • 4.4 Risk Assessment & COPE
  • 5.2 Data & Loss Reserving

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Underwriting rests on a set of principles that guide consistent, profitable risk selection. These principles are the intellectual framework beneath the process described in 4.1 and the data described in 4.2.

docs.title: The Core Underwriting Principles
docs.text: Principle Meaning Selection Choose risks that fit the insurer's appetite; decline or modify those that do not Classification Group similar risks so that pricing reflects differences in expected loss Anti-selection control Prevent adverse selection by those who know their risk is worse than average Pricing discipline Charge what the risk costs, regardless of market pressure Adequacy and margins Premium must cover expected losses, expenses, capital, and profit Portfolio balance Diversify; avoid dangerous concentrations Documentation Record the basis of each decision Fairness and legality Apply consistent, non-discriminatory standards

docs.title: Selection and Adverse Selection
docs.text:
Adverse selection occurs when those most likely to claim are most motivated to buy insurance. Without underwriting control:

  • The insured knows more about their risk than the insurer.
  • High-risk individuals buy more coverage; low-risk individuals buy less or none.
  • The pool deteriorates and premiums must rise, driving more low-risks away (the "death spiral").

docs.title: Underwriting Responses to Adverse Selection
docs.text: Response Example Screening Applications, questionnaires, medical underwriting Third-party data MVR, CLUE, MIB, credit scores Inspection Property surveys, medical exams Classification and rating Higher rates for higher risk groups Restrictions Limits, exclusions, deductibles Participation requirements Group insurance minimum enrollment Waiting periods / moratoriums Pre-existing condition clauses

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
Classification groups risks by factors that predict loss, such as:

  • Age, gender, territory.
  • Construction, occupancy, protection, exposure.
  • Class code and occupation.
  • Vehicle type and usage.
  • Health and lifestyle.
  • Claims experience.

docs.title: Classification Criteria
docs.text: Criterion Requirement Statistical credibility Factor is supported by data Causal relevance Factor relates to expected loss Practicality Easy to collect, objective, verifiable Fairness Not unfairly discriminatory or prohibited

docs.title: Prohibited Classification
docs.text:
• Race, religion, national origin, color.
  • Gender (in some lines and jurisdictions, e.g., EU gender directive).
  • Genetic information (US GINA).
  • Marital status (in some jurisdictions).
  • Medical history (in some cases, e.g., ACA individual health plans).

The underwriter must know what factors are lawful in each line and jurisdiction.

docs.title: Pricing Discipline
docs.text:
Pricing discipline means:

  • Price the risk, not the competition — do not sacrifice adequacy to win business.
  • Use the pricing tools — manual rates, experience, schedule rating, modeling.
  • Understand the cost structure — loss costs, LAE, acquisition, fixed expenses, capital.
  • Set and respect minimum premiums — small policies have fixed costs.
  • Review adequacy continuously — rate levels, loss trends, model outputs.

Pricing discipline is undermined by:

  • Soft-market competition (rate cutting to gain share).
  • Commission pressure.
  • Misleading loss experience (immature data).
  • Ignoring IBNR (incurred but not reported).
  • Underestimating tail risk (long-tail lines).

docs.title: Risk Appetite
docs.text:
Risk appetite is the insurer's stated willingness to accept risk, defined by:

Dimension Example Lines and classes What we write Territories Where we write Limits How much per risk Aggregate exposure Total CAT limit Acceptance criteria Eligibility rules, minimum standards Reinsurance Net retained exposure

Appetite is documented in underwriting guidelines and enforced through authority levels and referral rules.

docs.title: Portfolio Balance
docs.text:
Individual risk selection is not enough — the portfolio must be managed:

  • Concentration — avoid excess exposure in one class, territory, or account.
  • Correlation — losses that occur together (wind + flood in the same event).
  • Aggregation — sum of individual limits across a CAT zone.
  • Cycle management — write at adequate rates in soft markets; protect capital.

Portfolio management is covered in detail in 4.7.

docs.title: Moral Hazard and Fraud
docs.text:
Moral hazard is the risk that the insured will cause or exaggerate a loss because they benefit from it.

Signal Response Overinsurance (sum >> value) Cap limits; verify values Recent large purchases + claims Investigate; document Financial distress Review credit; payables/underinsurance Claims history out of proportion Verify loss runs; inspection Recent policy changes before a loss Investigate date-of-loss coverage Vague or inconsistent information Request specifics; verify independently

Fraud control complements underwriting: SIU referrals, data analytics, and claims scrutiny.

docs.title: Fairness, Non-Discrimination, and Compliance
docs.text:
• Unfair discrimination — charging materially different rates for the same risk without data support, or treating equals unequally.
  • Fair discrimination — charging actuarially justified differences.
  • Regulated lines — rates and forms must be filed and approved (US) or satisfy fair value (UK FCA).
  • Adverse action notices — consumer-report-based decisions trigger disclosure rules.

The underwriter's duty is to classify on risk factors with evidence, and to document the support.

docs.title: Judgment and Its Limits
docs.text:
Underwriting involves professional judgment, but discipline requires:

  • Structured frameworks — COPE, exposure analysis, decision checklists.
  • Calibration — compare your decisions to outcomes; learn from claims.
  • Peer review — referrals, audits, committee review.
  • Bias awareness — avoid anchoring, overconfidence, and recency bias.
  • Consistency — same standards for identical risks.

Judgment without discipline produces inconsistent, unprofitable results.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The principles are selection, classification, anti-selection control, pricing discipline, adequacy, portfolio balance, documentation, and fairness.
  • Adverse selection is controlled through screening, data, classification, and restriction.
  • Classification must be actuarially supported and legally permissible.
  • Risk appetite and authority translate principles into rules.
  • Moral hazard and fraud are managed through verification and investigation.
  • Judgment is valuable only within a disciplined framework.

  • 4.4 Risk Assessment & COPE
  • 4.7 Portfolio Management
  • 5.1 Pricing Fundamentals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Risk assessment is the underwriter's analysis of the probability and severity of loss for a given risk. It blends:

  • Physical hazard — the tangible features that affect loss (construction, occupancy, condition).
  • Moral hazard — the behavioral risk that the insured will cause or exaggerate loss.
  • Morale hazard — indifference or carelessness because insurance exists.
  • Legal/contractual exposure — liability, contractual obligations.
  • Financial exposure — the size and adequacy of limits and values.

For property risks the classic framework is COPE: Construction, Occupancy, Protection, Exposure.

docs.title: Physical Hazard
docs.text: Category Examples Construction Frame, masonry, fire-resistive; roof; building systems Occupancy Business type, processes, storage, people Housekeeping Clutter, blocked exits, waste handling Maintenance Roof, electrical, plumbing, HVAC condition Protection Sprinklers, alarms, extinguishers, hydrants Exposure Adjacent buildings, wildfire, flood, crime Contrast Vehicle type and safety features Condition Age, wear, prior damage, deferred maintenance

docs.title: Moral Hazard
docs.text:
Moral hazard is the risk of intentional or exaggerated loss:

Signal Assessment Financial distress Debts, bankruptcy, declining business Overinsurance Sum insured far above value Claims history Frequency out of proportion; prior fraud Behavioral patterns Recent large purchases, policy changes before loss Vague information Incomplete, inconsistent, or evasive responses

docs.title: Morale Hazard
docs.text:
Morale hazard is carelessness enabled by insurance:

  • Lack of basic loss prevention (no locks, no extinguishers).
  • Poor housekeeping and maintenance.
  • Failure to follow loss control recommendations.
  • Indifference to claims frequency (small claims repeatedly).

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
Type Fire Characteristics Frame (wood) Highest combustibility; rapid fire spread Joisted masonry Exterior masonry, combustible interior; good but less than fire-resistive Masonry non-combustible Exterior and structure non-combustible; lower risk Fire-resistive Protected steel/concrete; best fire performance Metal Fast heat conduction; not fire rated itself

Other construction factors:

  • Roof — materials (metal, asphalt, wood shake), condition, age.
  • Occupancy load — height, area, openings.
  • Building systems — electrical, heating, HVAC; age and condition.
  • Maintenance — evidence of deferred maintenance.

docs.title: Occupancy
docs.text: Consideration Underwriting Questions Hazard What operations, materials, processes? Density People load; storage concentration Fire load Combustible inventory and packaging Special hazards Cooking, chemicals, welding, dust, flammable liquids Vehicles on premises Parking, loading, repair operations Tenants Multiple occupancies; tenant operations Hours Operations while unoccupied (night risk)

docs.title: Protection
docs.text:
Public protection:

  • Fire department distance, staffing, water supply.
  • Response time and capability.

Private protection:

System Effect Automatic sprinklers The single most effective fire control Fire alarms Early detection; monitored vs. local Standpipes/hydrants Water supply for firefighting Extinguishers First-aid firefighting Special systems Kitchen hood suppression, alarm verification Security systems Burglar alarms, video, doors

Protection conditions are often policy warranties — if the insured disconnects protection, coverage may be voided at the loss.

docs.title: Exposure
docs.text:
External exposures:

  • Adjacent properties — proximity, construction, occupancy of neighbors.
  • Wildfire — Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) zones.
  • Flood — FEMA flood zones; floodways; storm surge.
  • Wind — hurricane, tornado zones.
  • Earthquake — seismic zones.
  • Crime — burglary/theft territory.
  • Other — airports, railroads, chemical plants, dense commercial.

The underwriter assesses the neighborhood effect: what is around the risk determines frequency and severity of certain losses.

docs.title: Underwriting the Liability Risk
docs.text:
Liability is assessed differently than property:

Exposure Assessment Premises Condition, visitors, hazards (slip/trip), security Operations Processes off/on site, supervision, subcontracting Products Nature, distribution, hazard, recall history Completed operations Duration of exposure, contract terms Contracts Indemnity, additional insured, waiver of subrogation Litigation climate Territory, legal environment, claim trends

docs.title: Financial Exposure Assessment
docs.text: Question Purpose Is the limit adequate for the worst credible loss? Determine whether the requested limit is sensible Are values adequate (coinsurance)? Validate premium and coverage adequacy Can the insured sustain a deductible/SIR? Financial retentions must be credible Is the premium affordable and payment reliable? Lapse and non-payment risk Are there moral hazard signals in the financials? Distress → fraud/lapse risk

docs.title: Qualitative Assessment
docs.text:
Underwriters also weigh qualitative factors:

  • Management quality — experience, safety culture, responsiveness.
  • Housekeeping — physical reflection of management attitude.
  • Information quality — a clean, complete submission signals professionalism.
  • Broker/agent relationship — track record and reliability.
  • Risk improvement receptiveness — willingness to act on recommendations.

docs.title: The Risk Assessment Output
docs.text:
The assessment should conclude:

Element Example Risk classification Acceptable / borderline / unacceptable Exposure analysis Worst credible loss, frequency drivers Loss control needs Conditions, warranties, inspections Recommended terms Limits, deductibles, exclusions, endorsements Pricing indication Rate basis, loadings, credits Documentation Basis of the decision recorded

docs.title: Common Assessment Errors
docs.text: Error Correction Overweighting recent large loss Analyze trend and cause, not just a single event Ignoring small claim frequency Recognize behavior signals Anchoring on the submitted values Independently estimate values Under-estimating CAT exposure Model and check aggregates Relying on one information source Triangulate application, loss runs, inspection Confusing moral and morale hazard Treat causes separately in response

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Risk assessment blends physical, moral, morale, legal, and financial analysis.
  • COPE (construction, occupancy, protection, exposure) is the framework for property.
  • Liability and financial exposure require separate analytical lenses.
  • Qualitative factors (management, housekeeping, information quality) distinguish good risks from bad.
  • The output is a documented classification, terms, and pricing decision.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:

  • 4.3 Underwriting Principles
  • 4.5 Risk Engineering

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Risk engineering (also called loss control or risk improvement) is the technical discipline that identifies and mitigates the physical and operational causes of loss. It supports underwriting by:

  • Validating the information in the submission.
  • Identifying hazards not visible from paper.
  • Recommending controls that reduce frequency and severity.
  • Supporting price — better protected risks deserve better terms.
  • Meeting policy conditions — inspections required by guidelines or reinsurance.

docs.title: The Risk Engineering Process
docs.text:
Screening → Survey/Inspection → Analysis → Report → Follow-up
Step Activity Screening Decide if the account requires a survey (value, occupancy, hazard) Survey On-site inspection by engineer or trained surveyor Analysis Evaluate COPE, exposures, controls, management Report Document findings, recommendations, PIR scores Follow-up Track recommendation implementation

docs.title: Types of Surveys
docs.text: Survey Type Scope Photo survey Exterior and basic interior condition; no engineering detail Drive-by Neighborhood, construction, exterior hazards Basic property survey COPE fields, protection, housekeeping Full engineering survey Detailed systems, fire protection, occupancy, process hazards Boiler & machinery Pressure vessels, electrical, mechanical systems Liability survey Premises, operations, products exposure Environmental assessment Phase I/II site assessments

docs.title: Fire Protection Engineering
docs.text:
The core of property loss control:

System Engineering Focus Sprinkler systems Design standard, water supply, coverage density, maintenance Fire pumps Capacity, reliability, testing Water supply Hydrant flow, storage, reliability Fire alarms Detection, monitoring, response Special suppression Kitchen hoods, foam, gas systems Fire doors Compartmentation, closures Egress Exit paths, signage, capacity

docs.title: Occupancy and Process Hazards
docs.text:
• Wet processes, machining, heat treating.
  • Flammable and combustible liquid storage.
  • Dust collection and housekeeping (combustible dust).
  • Welding and hot work programs.
  • Storage height and racking stability.
  • Material handling and conveyors.

docs.title: Natural Hazards
docs.text:
• Wind — roof systems, glazing, tie-downs.
  • Earthquake — structural bracing, anchorage.
  • Flood — elevation, barriers, wet location storage.
  • Wildfire — defensible space, combustible vegetation.

docs.title: Crime and Security
docs.text:
• Perimeter security (fencing, lighting, locks).
  • Alarm systems, video surveillance.
  • Cash handling and safe procedures.
  • Employee screening (pre-employment checks).

docs.title: Liability Engineering
docs.text:
• Premises maintenance (walkways, parking, stairs).
  • Slip/trip hazards and housekeeping.
  • Product quality control.
  • Contractor qualification and supervision.
  • Signage and warnings.

docs.title: The Engineering Report
docs.text:
A professional report includes:

Section Content Executive summary Overall risk quality, key findings Risk description Construction, occupancy, protection, exposure Loss history analysis Claims drivers and trends Evaluations Systems, processes, controls Recommendations Prioritized improvements PIR (Protection Impairment Rating) Where applicable

docs.title: The PIR Score
docs.text:
The Protection Impairment Rating (PIR) qualifies the reliability of fire protection:

PIR Meaning 0–10 Superb protection availability and reliability 11–20 Good protection with minor impairments 21–30 Fair; significant impairments or reliance on public fire 31–50 Poor; substantial protection deficiencies Over 50 Unacceptable; requires major improvement

PIR affects pricing and acceptance. A high PIR may require rectification before binding or a premium loading.

docs.title: Recommendations and Penalties
docs.text:
Recommendation Type Example Required before binding Install sprinkler system; correct electrical hazard Required during term Fix fire door closure; implement hot work permit Recommended Improve housekeeping; add extinguishers Advisory Consider water leak detection; business continuity

Warranties and conditions formalize required improvements. Failure to comply can:

  • Void coverage (warranty breach).
  • Increase deductible (PIR penalty).
  • Trigger cancellation or non-renewal.

docs.title: Risk Engineering Data and Analytics
docs.text:
Modern risk engineering uses data:

Data Source Use Sensor/IoT data Water leaks, temperature, equipment vibration Aerial imagery Roof condition, wildfire fuel, exposure Geospatial analytics Flood, wind, wildfire scoring Claims analytics Cause-of-loss patterns, cost drivers Inspection data Benchmarking by class and account

Underwriters integrate engineering findings with pricing models and portfolio analytics.

docs.title: Engineering vs. Underwriting
docs.text: Issue Handling Major deficiency Requirement, warranty, or decline Minor deficiency Recommendation; price consideration Excellent protection Credit; broaden terms Impairment of protection PIR penalty; require rectification Management resistance Underwrite the attitude, not just the building

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Risk engineering validates the risk and identifies improvement opportunities.
  • Surveys range from photos to full engineering assessments.
  • Fire protection reliability (PIR) and protection conditions drive terms.
  • Recommendations become warranties when required.
  • Data and analytics increasingly augment the engineer's judgment.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Every insurance line has its own risk profile, loss drivers, and underwriting techniques. This chapter provides a cross-line reference of the key underwriting considerations that were developed in Volumes 2 and 3.

docs.title: Property — Personal and Commercial
docs.text: Factor Personal Commercial Core framework COPE COPE Primary perils Fire, theft, wind, water Fire, water, business interruption Valuation Replacement cost (owner-occupied); ACV for rentals Replacement cost; coinsurance; agreed value Main data Application, CLUE, inspection Application, SOV, loss runs, engineering Key loss control Mitigation devices, construction Sprinklers, alarms, maintenance programs

docs.title: Auto — Personal and Commercial
docs.text: Factor Personal Commercial Rating basis Driver + vehicle + territory Symbol + fleet + radius + use Main data MVR, CLUE, telematics MVRs, loss runs, fleet schedule, CDL files Key exposures Teen drivers, high-value vehicles Long-haul, cargo, hired/non-owned Loss control Driver education, telematics Driver training, telematics, maintenance

docs.title: General Liability
docs.text: Exposure Underwriting Emphasis Premises Condition, visitors, slip/trip, security Operations Contractors, supervision, subcontracting Products Product type, distribution, recall history, QC Completed operations Long-tail; statute of repose Contracts Indemnity, additional insureds Litigation climate Territory, legal environment

docs.title: Workers Compensation
docs.text:
• Payroll and class codes drive premium.
  • Experience modification reflects loss history.
  • Underwriting emphasizes safety culture, return-to-work, drug-free workplace, and claims management.
  • State benefit levels and litigation environment matter.

docs.title: Specialty Lines
docs.text: Line Key Underwriting Factors Ocean marine Vessel, route, cargo, P&I Inland marine Transit, bailees, installation, EDP Aviation Pilot, aircraft, use, maintenance Surety Financial strength, capacity, experience Professional liability Qualifications, claims history, risk controls D&O Financials, governance, securities exposure Cyber Security controls, data sensitivity, prior losses Environmental Site assessments, operations, remediation

docs.title: Life and Health
docs.text: Product Underwriting Emphasis Individual life Age, health, lifestyle, insurable interest, amount Disability Occupation, income, health, financial motivation Critical illness Health history, family history, age Long-term care Age, health, cognitive/functional status Group benefits Participation, group demographics, employer stability

docs.title: The Underwriting "Toolbox" by Line
docs.text: Tool Lines Where Most Used COPE analysis Property (personal and commercial) MVR Auto (personal and commercial) CLUE / loss databases Property, auto, package Loss runs All commercial Financial statements Commercial, surety, D&O, key person Credit-based scores Personal lines where lawful Medical underwriting Life, health, disability Engineering surveys Commercial property, energy, marine Technical questionnaires Cyber, professional, environmental Inspection requirements Property, high-value personal

docs.title: Line-Specific Red Flags
docs.text: Line Red Flags Property Underinsurance, no sprinklers in high hazard, poor housekeeping, deferred maintenance Auto DUI, violations, unlicensed drivers, long-haul exposure, poor maintenance GL Frequent small claims, products exposure without QC, litigation history WC High frequency, misclassification, no return-to-work, fraud indicators Specialty Inadequate controls (cyber), prior securities claims (D&O), weak financials (surety) Life/health Hazardous avocations, substance abuse, oversized requests, financial motivation

docs.title: Integrated (Package) Underwriting
docs.text:
Packages must be underwritten across lines:

  • Verify coverage consistency (limits, premises, operations).
  • Look for cross-line signals (e.g., frequent auto claims in a commercial account with labor issues).
  • Use package credits only where booking economics justify them.
  • Ensure no coverage gaps between property, liability, auto, and specialty needs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Each line has distinct loss drivers and techniques.
  • Data sources and tools map to lines (MVR → auto, CLUE → property, loss runs → all).
  • Red flags are line-specific but share a behavioral theme.
  • Packages require integrated underwriting.
  • The underwriter develops line expertise on top of core principles.

docs.text:

  • 3.x Commercial Lines

  • 5.6 Rating by Line

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Portfolio management is the discipline of shaping and monitoring the aggregate book of business. Individual risk selection alone is not enough: losses are driven not only by how many bad risks are written, but by how risks correlate and concentrate.

The underwriting portfolio must be managed to meet:

  • Profitability targets — combined ratio, return on capital.
  • Capital constraints — solvency capital, reinsurance attachment.
  • Appetite — lines, territories, classes, limits.
  • Diversification — across causes of loss, geography, and accounts.

docs.title: Key Portfolio Concepts
docs.text: Concept Meaning Aggregation Total exposure from many policies that can be lost in one event Concentration Heavy dependence on a class, territory, account, or peril Correlation Losses that rise together (wind and flood; cyber and cloud) Diversification Spreading risk across uncorrelated exposures Catastrophe limit (CAT) Maximum modeled loss the company will retain (net of reinsurance) Natural catastrophe model Probabilistic model of hurricanes, earthquakes, flood, etc. Worst-case / PML Probable maximum loss at various return periods

docs.title: Monitoring the Portfolio
docs.text: Metric Description Exposure by territory Sum insured by zone (flood, wind, wildfire, earthquake) Limit concentration Largest accounts as % of surplus Class concentration % premium from a single class Geographic concentration % exposure in one territory Reinsurance ceded % of limit ceded; retention levels Loss ratio trends Actual vs. expected by segment Rate adequacy Price monitoring vs. benchmark New business mix Growth segments and their profitability

docs.title: The PML Process
docs.text:
For CAT perils:

  1. Exposure accumulation — sum insured by peril zone.
  2. Probabilistic modeling — run event sets (hurricane, earthquake, flood).
  3. Determine PML — worst-case loss at return periods (e.g., 1-in-100, 1-in-250).
  4. Compare to appetite — net of reinsurance vs. capital.
  5. Act — limit new business, buy reinsurance, adjust retentions.

docs.title: Aggregation Controls
docs.text: Control Example Per-risk limits Max sum insured per location Per-event limits Max exposure in a flood/wind zone Per-account limits Cap on any one insured Zone blocks Stop writing when a zone capacity is reached Reinsurance program Cat XL, per-risk XL, proportional cover

docs.title: Concentration Analysis
docs.text:
Concentration Risk Single account Loss of a major account undermines profit Single class Systemic claims (e.g., all restaurants) Single territory One CAT event hits the whole book Single peril Wind-only book; flood-only book Single producer Broker distribution risk Single reinsurer Counterparty credit risk

Concentration limits are set in underwriting guidelines and enforced by the portfolio manager.

docs.title: Setting Appetite
docs.text:
• Risk tolerance — what the company will accept (return period, PML).
  • Capital allocation — how much capital each line consumes.
  • Return targets — required ROE; pricing floor.
  • Line capacity — limits per risk, per event, per account.

docs.title: The Business Plan
docs.text:
The underwriting plan translates strategy into numbers:

Element Content Premium plan New business, renewal retention, rate change Mix plan By line, class, territory Capacity plan Limits, aggregate exposures Reinsurance plan Structure, retention, cost Pricing plan Rate levels, credits, debits

The plan is monitored monthly/quarterly against actual results; variances trigger action.

docs.title: Cycle Management
docs.text:
The insurance cycle drives portfolio decisions:

Phase Underwriting Response Soft market Rates fall; consider reducing exposure; maintain discipline; avoid writing at inadequate rates Hard market Rates rise; capacity returns; re-underwrite; write to improved terms Transition Watch loss trends; adjust appetite before the cycle turns

Cycle discipline means not mistaking volume for profit in the soft phase and not losing relationships in the hard phase.

docs.title: Reinsurance and Portfolio Protection
docs.text:
Reinsurance protects the portfolio:

Type Purpose Proportional (quota share, surplus) Share risk and premium with a reinsurer Excess of loss (per risk) Protect individual large losses Catastrophe XL Protect against single-event aggregation Stop loss Protect the loss ratio of the whole portfolio Facultative Specific risk-by-risk protection

The underwriter must understand the net position — what the company retains after reinsurance — and write within it.

docs.title: Emerging Risks and the Portfolio
docs.text:
Trend Portfolio Impact Climate change Rising flood/wildfire frequency; model uncertainty Cyber aggregation Systemic risk through common cloud providers Social inflation Liability severity rising; litigation funding Litigation funding More claims; larger settlements Supply chain Contingent BI concentration Pandemic Business interruption correlation

Portfolio managers incorporate forward-looking risk into appetites and models.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Portfolio management shapes the aggregate risk of the book.
  • Monitoring uses exposure, concentration, loss ratio, and rate adequacy metrics.
  • CAT limits, PML, and aggregation controls prevent catastrophe concentration.
  • The business plan and appetite translate strategy into limits.
  • Cycle discipline balances growth and profit.
  • Reinsurance manages the net retained position.
  • Emerging risks (climate, cyber, social inflation) are portfolio-level threats.

docs.text:

  • 5.8 Reinsurance

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Insurance underwriting is being transformed by automation, data, and analytics. Technology does not replace the underwriter — it changes the job:

  • Routine, repetitive decisions are automated (straight-through processing).
  • Complex risks are augmented by models, data, and tools.
  • The underwriter's role shifts to judgment, exception handling, and portfolio thinking.

docs.title: Degrees of Automation
docs.text:
Level Description Manual The underwriter reviews every submission and prices by judgment Assisted Systems score, flag, and price; underwriter decides Automated (STP) Eligible risks are bound and issued without human review Fully algorithmic The whole decision is made by a model, supervised by rules

Most personal lines and small commercial benefit from straight-through processing (STP). Large commercial and specialty remain actively underwritten with decision support.

docs.title: What Automates Well vs. What Does Not
docs.text: Automates Well Requires Human Judgment Standard personal lines (auto, home) Complex commercial accounts Small BOP/package Specialty lines (marine, aviation, surety) Eligibility and rules checks Moral hazard evaluation Rating and issuance Coverage design and negotiation Renewal re-pricing Exception handling Claims triage and data entry Large loss and coverage disputes

docs.title: Key Technologies
docs.text: Technology Use Rules engines Eligibility, acceptance criteria, referral logic Predictive models Pricing, retention, conversion, fraud Machine learning Claims reserving, propensity models, anomaly detection Telematics Usage-based auto insurance, driver feedback IoT sensors Water leak detection, property risk mitigation Geospatial data Flood, wildfire, wind scoring Aerial imagery Roof condition, property features, exposure APIs and data exchange Instant quoting from external data RPA (robotic process automation) Document processing, data entry, reconciliation Generative AI Summarizing submissions, drafting correspondence, document extraction Portfolio dashboards Real-time concentration and performance

docs.title: The Data-Driven Underwriting Stack
docs.text:
Submission Data
      ↓
Enrichment (MVR, CLUE, credit, geospatial)
      ↓
Models & Scores (pricing, risk, fraud)
      ↓
Decision Engine (rules + referral)
      ↓
Underwriter Review (exceptions)
      ↓
Issuance & Monitoring

docs.title: Telematics and Usage-Based Insurance (UBI)
docs.text:
Application How It Works Personal auto App/device records driving; discounts for safe behavior Commercial fleet Driver coaching, route optimization, claim verification Pay-per-mile Premium based on distance driven Post-crash Crash detection and verification

Telematics changes the nature of auto insurance: pricing moves from demographic proxies to actual driving behavior, and insurers gain a loss-prevention channel.

docs.title: IoT and Smart Homes
docs.text:
Sensor Use Water leak Early detection prevents water damage claims Smoke/CO Faster fire response Security cameras Theft prevention and claim verification Temperature Freeze and spoilage prevention

Loss prevention data directly improves underwriting and claims; some insurers offer premium discounts for connected devices.

docs.title: Predictive Models in Underwriting
docs.text:
Model Purpose Frequency model Expected number of claims Severity model Expected cost per claim Pricing model Indicated premium Retention model Likelihood of renewal Conversion model Likely acceptance of a quote Fraud model Risk of fraudulent claim Reserving model Estimate outstanding liabilities Propensity model Cross-sell potential

Models are built on historical data; they must be validated, monitored, and governed (see Model Risk below).

docs.title: Model Risk and Governance
docs.text:
Risk Mitigation Bias Fairness testing; prohibited factors excluded Overfitting Holdout validation; backtesting Data quality Data lineage, quality checks Drift Performance monitoring; refresh cycles Opacity Documentation, explainability for decisions Regulatory Approved rate filings; adverse action notices

A model governance framework includes development standards, independent validation, version control, and audit.

docs.title: Regulatory Constraints on Data and Automation
docs.text:
Jurisdiction Key Rules US FCRA (adverse action), state rate/fairness laws, GLBA privacy EU/UK GDPR, AI Act (high-risk classification), FCA fair value and pricing rules General Prohibited factors (race, religion, gender where barred), transparency, human review for material decisions

Automation must not create unfair discrimination or deny rights that a human process would provide.

docs.title: The Changing Role of the Underwriter
docs.text:
Then Now / Future Clerical data entry and rating Judgment, exception handling Manual file review Model-driven prioritization Silent risk selection Broker/insured dialogue on exposures After-the-fact portfolio checks Real-time concentration dashboards Document-based Data-based with documents for context

The underwriter's core skills — risk assessment, judgment, communication, and portfolio thinking — remain essential, but they are applied to exceptions and complexity rather than routine processing.

docs.title: Ethics and Fairness in Automated Underwriting
docs.text:
• Transparency — applicants should understand the basis of decisions where required.
  • Fairness — models must not use prohibited factors or proxy them.
  • Explainability — decisions must be explainable to regulators and consumers.
  • Human oversight — material adverse decisions should allow human review.
  • Accountability — there must be clear ownership of model outcomes.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Automation handles standard, rules-based decisions; judgment handles exceptions.
  • Predictive models, telematics, IoT, and geospatial data enrich underwriting.
  • Model governance controls bias, drift, and opacity.
  • Regulation (FCRA, GDPR, AI Act, FCA) constrains how data and models are used.
  • The underwriter's role shifts to judgment, complexity, and portfolio management.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Underwriting guidelines translate an insurer's strategy and risk appetite into practical, day-to-day rules for selecting and pricing risks. They ensure consistency, compliance, and discipline across underwriters, delegated authority holders, and automated systems.

docs.title: Purpose of Guidelines
docs.text: Purpose Description Consistency Same risk treated the same way Risk appetite Explicit criteria for acceptance and declinature Compliance Adherence to law, filings, and conduct rules Delegation Authority granted consistent with guidelines Automation Rules that straight-through processing can apply Audit Clear basis for underwriting decisions

docs.title: Structure of Guidelines
docs.text:
Introduction (purpose, scope, governance)
Risk Appetite (accept, refer, decline)
Eligibility (classes, territories, minimum standards)
Coverage Rules (limits, terms, exclusions)
Pricing Rules (rates, factors, minimums)
Referral & Escalation (authority levels)
Delegated Authority (MGA/binder rules)
Compliance (regulatory, sanctions, fairness)
Documentation & File Standards

docs.title: Key Components
docs.text: Component Description Eligibility Who/what can be considered Exposure limits Maximum per risk, per account Referral triggers When a senior underwriter must decide Declinature rules Prohibited classes or hazards Pricing latitude Discounts, credits, minimum premiums Coverage flexibility Optional coverages and endorsements Documentation What must be in the file

docs.title: Risk Appetite Statements
docs.text: Statement Example Accept Within guidelines and authority Refer Requires escalation or referral Decline Outside appetite or eligibility Special terms Acceptable with restrictions or pricing

docs.title: Authority Levels
docs.text: Level Authority Underwriter Binds within guidelines Senior underwriter Exceptions, referrals, higher limits Head of underwriting New products, strategic deviations Underwriting committee Portfolio and appetite changes

docs.title: Guidelines by Line
docs.text: Line Typical Rules Property Construction, occupancy, protection, TIV limits General liability Class, operations, limits, prior losses Auto Fleet size, usage, drivers, MVR Workers comp Classification, payroll, employer controls Marine Vessel, cargo, voyage, crew Specialty Per-product guidelines and appetite

docs.title: Delegated Authority Guidelines
docs.text: Rule Purpose Binder limits Authority cap Minimum standards Data, documentation, eligibility Referral rules What must go to the insurer Bordereaux Reporting requirements Audit rights Insurer review of decisions

docs.title: Guidelines and Rating
docs.text: Element Relationship Rate minimums Floor below which referral is required Rating factors Pre-defined multipliers by class Schedule credits Discretion within limits Experience rating Large-account adjustments Deviations Justified exceptions, documented

docs.title: Compliance in Guidelines
docs.text: Requirement Practice No unfair discrimination No protected-basis rules Filing consistency Rules match approved rates/forms Conduct rules Fair treatment, consumer duty Sanctions No business with sanctioned parties Privacy Data use within legal boundaries

docs.title: Governance and Maintenance
docs.text: Control Practice Ownership Document owner per line Approval Formal sign-off on changes Version control Review cycle and edition control Training Underwriters trained on updates Audit Adherence monitored Exception tracking Referrals and overrides logged

docs.title: Failure Modes
docs.text: Failure Impact Outdated guidelines Writing risks no longer in appetite Unclear referral rules Inconsistent decisions No pricing latitude Missed market opportunities Guideline gaps Arbitrary or inconsistent judgment Weak enforcement Portfolio drift

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Guidelines translate strategy into selection rules.
  • They define eligibility, appetite, authority, and pricing latitude.
  • Referral and escalation manage larger or unusual risks.
  • Compliance and governance keep guidelines lawful and current.
  • Effective guidelines drive consistency, discipline, and auditability.

docs.title: Volume 5 — Rating & Pricing
docs.text: Volume 5 covers how insurance premiums are calculated: from the fundamentals of pricing to the data, techniques, and models used across lines. It explains the difference between rating (applying approved rates) and pricing (setting the level of rates), and how actuaries and underwriters work together.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Chapter Title Contents 5.1 Pricing Fundamentals Pure premium, loss ratio, combined ratio, expenses, profit, rate components 5.2 Data & Loss Reserving Data quality, triangles, IBNR, development, reserving methods 5.3 Classification & Rating Rating factors, manual rates, class rates, territories, ILF, schedules 5.4 Pricing Techniques Loss cost method, loss ratio method, trending, credibility, fit 5.5 Predictive Analytics GLMs, machine learning, telematics, model validation, fairness 5.6 Rating by Line Auto, property, GL, WC, package, life/health, specialty 5.7 Experience Rating Experience modification, schedule rating, retrospective rating 5.8 Reinsurance Proportional, non-proportional, pricing, retention, portfolio use 5.9 Pricing Governance & Compliance Rate filings, discrimination, fair value, monitoring, documentation

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this volume you should be able to:

  1. Explain the components of premium and the pricing equation.
  2. Understand loss reserving, triangles, and IBNR.
  3. Describe classification and rating factors across lines.
  4. Apply the loss cost and loss ratio pricing methods.
  5. Describe predictive modeling in pricing and its governance.
  6. Rate the principal property/casualty lines.
  7. Explain experience, schedule, and retrospective rating.
  8. Describe reinsurance structures and pricing.
  9. Explain pricing governance: filings, fairness, and monitoring.

docs.title: Suggested Reading
docs.text:
• Start with 5.1 Pricing Fundamentals.
  • For the practical methods see 5.3 Classification & Rating and 5.4 Pricing Techniques.
  • Cross-reference underwriting with Volume 4, and line coverage with Volumes 2 and 3.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Pricing is the determination of the rate (and therefore premium) that an insurer must charge to cover expected losses, expenses, capital costs, and profit — while remaining competitive. Pricing is distinct from rating: rating applies the approved rate structure to a specific risk; pricing sets the level of the rate structure itself.

docs.title: The Insurance Pricing Equation
docs.text:
The basic pricing identity:

Premium = Pure Premium ÷ (1 − Expense Ratio − Profit & Contingency Loading)

Pure Premium = Loss Cost = (Frequency × Severity)
Component Definition Pure premium The portion of premium needed to pay losses (and loss adjustment expenses) Frequency Expected number of claims per exposure unit Severity Expected average cost per claim Expense ratio Acquisition, general, and premium taxes as % of premium Profit & contingency Target underwriting profit and provisions for deviation

docs.title: Loss Ratio Form
docs.text: Indicated Rate Change = (Experience Loss Ratio − Target Loss Ratio) ÷ Experience Loss Ratio × 100%

docs.title: Ratio Concepts
docs.text: Ratio Formula Meaning Loss ratio Incurred Losses ÷ Earned Premium Claims (% of premium) LAE ratio Loss Adjustment Expense ÷ Earned Premium Claims handling cost Expense ratio Acquisition + General Expense ÷ Written Premium Operating cost Combined ratio Loss + LAE + Expense Ratio Underwriting profitability (<100% = profit) Operating ratio Combined Ratio − Investment Income Ratio Net of investment earnings Retention ratio (Written − Ceded) ÷ Written Net premium

docs.title: Combined Ratio Example
docs.text:
Loss ratio (incl. LAE):        65.0%
Expense ratio:                 30.0%
Combined ratio:                95.0%  ← profitable
Investment income ratio:        3.0%
Operating ratio:               92.0%

A combined ratio below 100% means an underwriting profit; above 100% means losses and expenses exceed premium, offset only by investment income or capital.

docs.title: Components of Rate
docs.text: Component Description Expected (pure) loss cost The actuarial best estimate of losses per exposure Loss adjustment expense (LAE) Allocated (ALAE) and unallocated (ULAE) claims costs Acquisition expense Commissions, distribution costs General expense Overhead, other operating costs Premium taxes and assessments Statutory levies Risk / profit margin Compensation for uncertainty and capital

docs.title: Ratemaking vs. Pricing
docs.text:
Concept Description Ratemaking Actuarial determination of the rate level for a class/book (manuals, filings) Pricing Business-level decision on rates: discounting, underwriting judgment, market conditions Rating Application of the approved rate structure to an individual risk

The underwriter prices individual risks within the framework the actuary develops; discipline requires the underwriter to respect the indicated rate unless justified.

docs.title: Rate Levels and Exposures
docs.text:
• Rate is premium per unit of exposure:
Line Exposure Unit Commercial property \$100 of value (building/contents) Auto (liability) Car year General liability \$1,000 of receipts / \$100 of payroll Workers comp \$100 of payroll Life/health \$1,000 of sum assured

docs.title: The Underwriting Cycle and Pricing
docs.text: Phase Pricing Behavior Soft Rates fall below indicated; capacity is ample; loss ratios deteriorate Hard Rates rise; capacity tightens; underwriting profit returns Discipline Maintain adequate rates through the cycle; don't chase volume

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Premium = pure premium plus expenses, taxes, profit, and contingency.
  • The combined ratio measures underwriting profitability.
  • Frequency and severity drive loss cost; exposure bases convert loss cost to rates.
  • Ratemaking sets the manual; rating applies it; pricing adjusts for judgment and market.
  • Pricing discipline through the cycle protects solvency.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 5.2 Data & Loss Reserving
  • 5.3 Classification & Rating
  • 5.4 Pricing Techniques
  • 5.9 Pricing Governance

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Pricing and reserving both depend on loss data. Loss reserving estimates the outstanding liability for claims already incurred; pricing uses historical loss data to project expected future losses. Both are built on claim triangles.

docs.title: Data Quality
docs.text:
Dimension Considerations Completeness All claims captured, no gaps Consistency Definitions stable across years Granularity Claim-level detail for analysis Timeliness Data as of evaluation dates Accuracy Correct payments, reserves, recoveries

Poor data produces unreliable prices and reserves.

docs.title: Loss Development Triangles
docs.text:
A triangle tracks cumulative paid or incurred losses by accident year (or report year) as they develop over time.

Accident Year 12 mo 24 mo 36 mo 48 mo 60 mo 2020 5,000 8,000 9,000 9,500 9,800 2021 5,500 9,000 10,200 10,800 2022 6,000 10,000 11,500 2023 6,500 11,000 2024 7,000
  • Rows = accident years.
  • Columns = development periods (evaluation age).
  • Cumulative — each cell includes all prior payments.
  • The diagonal (last cell per row) is the current estimate.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text: Term Meaning IBNR Incurred But Not Reported — claims not yet reported IBNER Incurred But Not Enough Reported — revisions to known claims Case reserve Estimate for a known open claim Development factor Projection of how losses grow as they mature Tail factor Development beyond the last observed period Ultimate losses Final total cost of claims for a period

docs.title: Reserve Methods
docs.text: Method Use Strengths Chain Ladder Project paid/incurred by development factors Simple, standard Bornhuetter-Ferguson (B-F) Combine expected ultimate with actual development Good for immature/volatile data Expected loss ratio Ultimate = expected LR × earned premium When data insufficient Frequency-severity Project counts and averages separately More granular Stochastic methods Distributions of outcomes (bootstrapping, Mack) Range, uncertainty

docs.title: Chain Ladder Example (Illustrative)
docs.text:
• Accident year 2024 losses at 12 months: 7,000.
  • Average 12→24 development factor from prior years: 1.60.
  • Estimated 24-month: 7,000 × 1.60 = 11,200.
  • Continue applying factors to reach ultimate.

docs.title: Reserves in the P&L
docs.text:
• Reserves are liabilities on the balance sheet.
  • Loss reserve development — changes in estimates flow through the income statement.
  • IBNR must be estimated for pricing adequacy; underestimating reserves understates prices.

docs.title: Pricing Data Adjustments
docs.text:
For pricing, historical data must be adjusted:

Adjustment Reason Trend Inflation, claims cost growth, social inflation Exposure changes Payroll, receipts, values changes Policy form changes Coverage differences across years Reinsurance Net vs. gross analysis Large losses Separate attritional from shock losses Underlying rate changes Rate level movements distort comparisons

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Triangles and development factors are the foundation of reserving and pricing.
  • IBNR/IBNER capture unrealized liabilities.
  • Chain ladder, B-F, and stochastic methods are the core techniques.
  • Pricing adjustments (trend, exposure, large loss) turn raw data into projections.
  • Data quality determines the credibility of everything downstream.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 5.1 Pricing Fundamentals
  • 5.4 Pricing Techniques
  • 7.5 Reserving & Settlement

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Classification groups risks into classes with similar expected loss. Rating applies rates to a specific risk using rating factors. The combination of classification and rating produces the manual premium for a risk.

docs.title: The Rating Structure
docs.text:
Base Rate (per exposure unit)
      × Class/Table Factors
      × Territory Factors
      × Limit / Deductible Factors
      = Manual Premium
      ± Experience / Schedule Adjustments
      = Final Premium

docs.title: Rating Factors by Line
docs.text: Line Main Classifications Personal auto Age, sex (where lawful), marital status, driving record, vehicle, territory, annual mileage, credit/insurance score Homeowners Construction, protection class, age, territory, deductibles, coverage amounts Commercial property Construction, occupancy, protection, exposure, values Commercial auto Vehicle type/use, radius, fleet size, driver records General liability Class code by operation, receipts/payroll, territory, products exposure Workers comp Class code by occupation, payroll, experience modification Life/health Age, sex, health class, smoker status, occupation, avocation

docs.title: Key Rating Concepts
docs.text: Concept Meaning Base rate Rate for a standard risk before factors Relativity Multiplier reflecting relative risk vs. base (e.g., 1.25 territory) Limits profile (ILF) Increase in loss cost per additional limit; diminishing factor Increased limits factor (ILF) Multiplier for higher policy limits Deductible credit Premium reduction for higher deductibles Territory Geographic rated area Class code Occupation/business classification (WC, GL, workers comp) Experience modification (E-mod) Credibility-weighted loss experience factor for WC

docs.title: Manual Rate
docs.text:
The manual rate is the filed rate for a class/territory before individual risk adjustments. Manual rates are built from:

  • Expected loss cost per exposure × expense/profit loading.
  • Adjusted for trend and rate level.

docs.title: Example — Commercial Property
docs.text:
Base rate:                     $0.85 per $100 of value
Construction factor (masonry):  0.80
Protection factor (sprinkler):  0.90
Limit factor:                   1.00
Territory factor:               1.10
Manual rate = 0.85 × 0.80 × 0.90 × 1.00 × 1.10 = $0.673/$100
Premium on $1,000,000 = $6,730

docs.title: Schedule Rating
docs.text:
Schedule rating adjusts the manual rate for individual account characteristics beyond the classification:

Debit/Credit Basis Management quality Safety programs, training, expertise Housekeeping/maintenance Physical condition evidence Loss control programs Engineering, safety, return-to-work Claims management Cooperation, loss history, mitigation Financial strength Deductible credibility, insolvency risk Special hazards Operations outside the class norm

Schedule factors apply within a range (e.g., ±25%); they must be justified and documented.

docs.title: Increased Limits Factors
docs.text:
As limits rise, loss cost rises less than proportionally:

Limit ILF $100,000 1.00 $250,000 1.25 $500,000 1.45 $1,000,000 1.60

ILFs are filed and applied consistently; the underwriter does not re-derive them in a standard risk.

docs.title: Rating vs. Pricing
docs.text:
Function Who Output Ratemaking Actuary Manual rates, ILFs, schedules Rating System/underwriter Applied premium for the risk Pricing Underwriter Final terms: debits, credits, judgment

The underwriter may make discretionary adjustments within authority; large deviations require referral.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Classification and rating translate risk characteristics into premium.
  • Factor multiplicatives (class, territory, ILF, deductible) build the manual rate.
  • Schedule rating reflects account-specific quality.
  • Experience rating (E-mod) reflects historical losses (see 5.7).
  • Ratemaking, rating, and pricing are distinct but connected functions.

docs.text:

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Pricing techniques convert historical loss experience and exposure data into an indicated rate level. The two classic approaches are the loss cost method and the loss ratio method. Both are built on the concepts from 5.2 Data & Loss Reserving.

docs.title: The Loss Cost (Pure Premium) Method
docs.text:
Step 1: Calculate trended, developed loss cost per exposure
Step 2: Divide by expense + profit allowance
Step 3: Compare to current rate level
Step 4: Apply credibility
Step 5: Set indicated rate change

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text: Item Value Developed losses (per exposure) $45.00 Trend factor (2 years) 1.10 Trended loss cost $49.50 Expense ratio target 30% Profit & contingency 5% Variable expense allowance 35% Indicated rate 49.50 ÷ (1 − 0.35) = $76.15 Current average rate $70.00 Indicated rate change (76.15 − 70.00) ÷ 70.00 = +8.8%

docs.title: The Loss Ratio Method
docs.text:
Indicated Rate Change = (Experience Loss Ratio − Target Loss Ratio) ÷ Target Loss Ratio × 100%
Item Value Experience loss ratio (trended, developed) 72% Target loss ratio 65% Indicated change (72 − 65) ÷ 65 = +10.8%

The loss ratio method compares actual incurred to expected target, with adjustments for trend, development, and rate level.

docs.title: Components of Both Methods
docs.text: Adjustment Purpose Development Bring historical losses to ultimate Trend Project loss costs to the policy period Rate level adjustment Index premiums to current rate levels Experience period Selection of credible years Credibility Blend company data with industry data

docs.title: Credibility
docs.text:
Credibility (Z) measures how much weight to give actual experience vs. expected/industry data:

Indicated = Z × (Experience-based indication) + (1 − Z) × (Expected/Industry indication)
Z (Credibility) Interpretation 0.00–0.30 Low — rely on industry/expected 0.31–0.70 Partial — blend 0.71–1.00 High — rely on own data

Full credibility is typically set where the data volume gives a stable estimate (e.g., a certain number of claims or exposures). Complementary credibility uses the industry/prior rate as the complement.

docs.title: Simple vs. Weighted
docs.text: Method Use Simple average Equal weight to all years Weighted average More weight to recent years (they are more representative) Exponential smoothing Decay weights

docs.title: Large Loss Treatment
docs.text:
Approach Description Cap/limit losses Cap individual losses at a level; add a loading for the excess Separate modeling Model severity distribution for the tail Reinsurance credit Reflect net-of-reinsurance losses

Large losses (catastrophes, single shocks) are treated separately so they do not distort the attritional loss cost.

docs.title: Fit and Rate Level
docs.text:
Term Meaning Loss trend Annual change in loss cost (frequency + severity) Premium trend Change in exposure base and rate level On-level premium Premium as if current rates applied historically Rate level index Measure of rate changes over time

On-leveling aligns historical premiums to current rates so that loss ratios are comparable across years.

docs.title: Off-Balance and Classification Relativity
docs.text:
• Off-balance factors — adjust overall rate level while keeping class relativities constant.
  • Classification relativity — update relativities (e.g., age, territory) independently of the overall level.

Both must be monitored to preserve equity between classes.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Loss cost method builds the indicated rate from loss cost per exposure.
  • Loss ratio method compares experience to target.
  • Development, trend, rate level, and credibility are the core adjustments.
  • Large losses are handled separately.
  • On-leveling makes historical data comparable.
  • The output is an indicated rate change with a documented basis.

docs.text:

  • 5.2 Data & Loss Reserving
  • 5.3 Classification & Rating
  • 5.5 Predictive Analytics

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Predictive analytics uses statistical and machine-learning models to estimate loss propensity, pricing, retention, and fraud. In pricing, models replace many manual classification tables with continuous, data-driven risk scores.

docs.title: Models in Insurance Pricing
docs.text: Model Type Use Generalized Linear Model (GLM) The workhorse: frequency, severity, pure premium Decision trees / gradient boosting Non-linear interactions, fraud, retention Random forests Ensemble robustness, feature importance Neural networks / deep learning Complex patterns (claims triage, imagery) Cluster analysis Risk segmentation Survival models Lapse, claim duration, tail

docs.title: The GLM in Pricing
docs.text:
The GLM models the expected value of the response (e.g., claim count, severity) as a function of predictors:

E(Y) = g⁻¹(β₀ + β₁X₁ + ... + βₖXₖ)
Choice Common Option Why Distribution Poisson / negative binomial (frequency), Gamma (severity) Counts and positive-skewed severity Link Log link Multiplicative factors, positivity Offset log(exposure) Rate per unit exposure

docs.title: GLM Output
docs.text:
• Coefficients become rating relativities.
  • Model can be validated on holdout data.
  • Interactions can be added if supported by data and credible.

docs.title: The Modeling Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Data assembly (claims, exposures, policy, external)
2. Feature engineering (transformation, missing values, encoding)
3. Split data (train / validation / test)
4. Model fitting
5. Model validation (lift, AIC, holdout performance)
6. Implementation (rating factors, score)
7. Monitoring (drift, fairness, performance)

docs.title: Validation and Selection
docs.text:
Metric Purpose AIC / BIC Model comparison (lower is better) Lift / gain chart How well the model separates risk Gini coefficient Discrimination of the score Holdout performance Out-of-sample accuracy Calibration Predicted vs. actual ratios

A model must be predictive, explainable, and stable.

docs.title: Telematics and Usage-Based Pricing
docs.text:
Source Feature Examples GPS Distance, time of day, road type, route Accelerometer Hard braking, acceleration, cornering Phone use Distraction indicators Crash data Impact detection and verification

Telematics pricing shifts from proxies (age, territory) toward actual behavior. It also enables pay-per-mile or pay-how-you-drive products.

docs.title: IoT, Imagery, and External Data
docs.text: Data Pricing Use IoT sensors (water, smoke, temp) Property risk, loss prevention discounts Aerial imagery Roof condition, vegetation, wildfire proximity Geospatial analytics Flood, wind, wildfire, crime scoring Social media / web Limited and regulated; mostly avoidance Credit / insurance scores Where lawful, personal lines

docs.title: Fairness and Governance
docs.text: Risk Mitigation Proxy discrimination Test for indirect use of prohibited factors Bias in training data Review, reweight, document Opacity Explainability tools; human review for decisions Regulatory Filed rates, adverse action, fair value

docs.title: Model Governance Framework
docs.text:
• Standards for development and documentation.
  • Independent validation.
  • Version control and approval gates.
  • Ongoing monitoring for drift and fairness.
  • Audit trail for regulatory review.

docs.title: Implementation into Pricing
docs.text: Step Description Scoring Model produces a predicted pure premium Rating structure Map scores to rating factors where suitable Filed rates Where required, submit with justification Underwriter override Judgment adjustments within authority Monitoring Compare actual to predicted; revisit model

docs.title: The Future of Predictive Pricing
docs.text:
• Real-time pricing — instant quotes using live data.
  • Continuous underwriting — telematics updates mid-term.
  • Personalized products — microsegmentation and tailored terms.
  • Explainable AI — regulatory pressure for transparency.
  • Fairness-aware models — constraints to prevent prohibited outcomes.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• GLMs and machine learning replace manual tables with data-driven scores.
  • The pipeline (data → features → fit → validate → implement → monitor) governs quality.
  • Telematics, IoT, and external data enrich predictors.
  • Fairness and governance are mandatory for regulatory acceptance.
  • Pricing moves toward personalization and real-time underwriting.

docs.text:

  • 5.2 Data & Loss Reserving
  • 5.4 Pricing Techniques
  • 5.9 Pricing Governance

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Each line of business has its own rating structure and exposure base. This chapter summarizes the rating approach for each of the principal lines covered in Volumes 2 and 3.

docs.title: Personal Auto
docs.text:
Premium = (Liability + Collision + Comprehensive + UM/UIM + Medical) × Territory × Vehicle × Driver Factors
Component Exposure Base Main Factors Liability Car year Territory, driver record, age, mileage Collision Car year Vehicle value, symbol, deductible Comprehensive Car year Vehicle, territory (theft), deductible UM/UIM Car year Limits, state Medical/PIP Per person State, limits
  • Vehicle symbol reflects cost to repair/replace.
  • Telematics adds actual driving data.

docs.title: Homeowners
docs.text:
Premium = Base Rate × Construction × Protection × Territory × Coverage Limits × Deductible
Factor Description Dwelling limit Reconstruction cost, not market value Protection class Fire district rating Territory Hail, wind, crime, wildfire Construction Frame vs. masonry vs. fire-resistive Deductible Percentage or flat Endorsements Contents, replacement cost, water backup

docs.title: Commercial Property
docs.text:
Premium = (Building Rate × Building Value + Contents Rate × Contents Value) × COPE Factors
Factor Description COPE Construction, occupancy, protection, exposure Coinsurance Penalty if insured below stated % of value SOV Statement of values per location BI Business income exposure: gross earnings × period Deductibles Time (BI), flat, percentage

docs.title: Commercial General Liability
docs.text:
Premium = Class Rate × Exposure Base (per $1,000 receipts or $100 payroll)
Component Basis Premises/operations Receipts, payroll, area Products/completed ops Gross sales Occurrence vs. claims-made Different coverage periods, different rating ILF Increased limits factor Per-occurrence aggregate Exposure measure

docs.title: Commercial Auto
docs.text:
Premium = (Liability Symbol × Radius × IA) + (Physical Damage Symbol × Vehicle Value)
Factor Description Symbol Vehicle cost group Radius Mileage/territory of operation IA (interstate authority) Operating scope Fleet size Experience becomes credible MVR Driver risk

docs.title: Workers Compensation
docs.text:
Premium = (Payroll ÷ 100) × Class Rate × Experience Mod × Premium Discount
Element Description Class code Occupation; highest-paying principal class governs where allowed Experience mod (E-mod) Credibility-weighted loss history Premium discount Volume-based expense reduction Deductible programs Large account retention State Benefit levels, rates, classifications

docs.title: Business Owners Policy (BOP)
docs.text:
• Package credit — property + liability bundled.
  • Simplified rating: size, occupancy, territory, protection.
  • Eligibility rules (occupancy, size, limits) restrict qualifying risks.

docs.title: Life / Health
docs.text:
Product Premium Basis Term life Age, sex, health class, smoker status, amount Whole life Same + cash value and dividend assumptions Annuities Age, sex, interest assumptions Disability Occupation, income, elimination period, benefit period Health/medical Age, geography, plan design, risk adjustment

Life pricing uses mortality tables, interest, and expenses (see Volume 2 chapter 6).

docs.title: Package and Multi-Line Pricing
docs.text:
• Package discount reflects expense savings (single policy, single premium).
  • Must be justified by actual cost savings, not across-the-board subsidy.
  • Multi-line accounts are underwritten line-by-line first; the package credit is applied last.

docs.title: Specialty Lines
docs.text: Line Rating Basis Inland marine Equipment values, transit exposure, coverage limits Ocean marine Vessel value, hull rate, cargo, P&I Aviation Aircraft value, pilot, use, territory Surety Contract size, financial strength, capacity Cyber Revenue, records, industry, security controls, limits D&O Assets, market cap, class D claims, limits Professional liability Revenue, headcount, discipline, limits Environmental Site type, operations, coverages

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Exposure bases differ by line: values, receipts, payroll, car years, headcount.
  • Rating structures are built from base rates × classification factors × limit/deductible adjustments.
  • Experience (E-mod, fleet, schedule) adjusts for account-specific history.
  • Packages discount only justified expense savings.
  • Specialty lines use bespoke exposure measures and technical factors.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 2.x Personal Lines
  • 3.x Commercial Lines
  • 5.3 Classification & Rating
  • 5.7 Experience Rating

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Experience rating adjusts a risk's premium based on its own loss history, rather than class-wide averages. It rewards good risks and penalizes poor ones, and it is most reliable where the insured is large enough to have credible experience.

docs.title: When Experience Rating Applies
docs.text:
Line Mechanism Workers comp Experience modification (E-mod) — universal Commercial auto Large fleet experience rating General liability Large accounts; schedule/experience Commercial property Large accounts; loss sensitive plans Package Combined experience across lines

Small risks lack credibility and use manual rates only.

docs.title: The Experience Modification (E-mod)
docs.text:
The E-mod compares the insured's actual losses to expected losses for its class, adjusted for credibility.

Component Meaning Primary limit Claims up to this amount count fully (e.g., first $X per claim) Excess ratio Claims above primary count with less weight Ballast Stabilizes small accounts Credibility (Z) Weight on actual vs. expected E-mod value 1.00 = average; <1.00 = better; >1.00 = worse

docs.title: E-mod Example (Illustrative)
docs.text:
Expected primary losses:     $50,000
Expected excess losses:      $30,000
Actual primary losses:       $40,000
Actual excess losses:        $20,000
Credibility (Z):             0.60

Primary mod = (40,000 / 50,000) = 0.80
Excess mod  = (20,000 / 30,000) = 0.67
E-mod = Z × (0.80) + (1 − Z) × (1.00)  (simplified)
     = 0.6 × 0.80 + 0.4 × 1.00 = 0.48 + 0.40 = 0.88

The E-mod is applied to the manual premium; a 0.88 E-mod reduces premium 12%.

docs.title: Schedule Rating
docs.text:
Schedule rating adjusts the manual/E-mod premium for qualitative account factors:

Debit (+) Credit (−) Poor housekeeping/maintenance Strong safety programs High management turnover Experienced management Lack of training Training and return-to-work Poor claims cooperation Engaged claims management Hazardous operations Loss control engineering

Schedule adjustments are limited in range (e.g., ±25%) and must be documented.

docs.title: Retrospective Rating
docs.text:
Retrospective rating ties the final premium to actual losses during the policy period:

Final Premium = Basic Premium + (Converted Losses × Loss Conversion Factor) ± Tax

Where:

  • Basic premium — fixed expense/profit component.
  • Converted losses — losses adjusted by the LCF (loss conversion factor covers LAE).
  • Minimum and maximum premiums — cap the downside and upside.
  • Standard premium — the manual premium before the retro plan.

docs.title: Retro Rating Characteristics
docs.text: Feature Description Loss sensitive Refunds or additional premiums based on losses Cash flow Retained loss fund for self-insured accounts Minimum/maximum Insurer and insured share risk Used for Large risks with credible experience

docs.title: Loss Sensitive Plans
docs.text: Plan Description Deductible Insured pays first losses; insurer administers SIR (self-insured retention) Insured defends and pays up to SIR Paid loss retro Premium adjusts as losses are paid Qualified plan Tax-approved large deductible programs

docs.title: Credibility in Experience Rating
docs.text:
Credibility determines how much weight the insured's own experience receives:

  • Larger accounts — more credibility, more experience-based pricing.
  • Small accounts — more weight to class averages.
  • New businesses — no experience; manual rates only.

docs.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
docs.text: Aspect Notes Fairness Rewards good experience, penalizes poor Incentive Encourages loss prevention Anti-selection Prevents good risks from leaving a pooled book Volatility Large claims create premium swings Complexity Requires loss data, thresholds, filings Small risk limit Little credibility for small insureds

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Experience rating ties premium to the insured's own losses.
  • E-mod (WC) compares actual to expected with credibility and primary/excess weighting.
  • Schedule rating adds qualitative factors.
  • Retrospective rating adjusts premium based on policy-period losses within min/max bounds.
  • Deductibles and SIRs transfer loss exposure to the insured.
  • Experience rating is credible only for larger risks.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Reinsurance is insurance for insurers — the transfer of risk (and premium) from a primary insurer (the cedent) to a reinsurer. Reinsurance protects against:

  • Individual large losses — single risk severity.
  • Aggregate catastrophe losses — many risks in one event.
  • Volume of risk — expanding capacity.
  • Volatility — smoothing results.

docs.title: Why Reinsurance
docs.text: Purpose Example Capacity Enable writing limits beyond own resources Catastrophe protection Hurricane, earthquake, flood events Earnings stability Smooth large single losses Capital management Reduce required solvency capital Portfolio transfer Exit a line or territory Expertise Reinsurer provides underwriting insight

docs.title: 1. Proportional (Pro Rata)
docs.text:
Structure Description Quota share (QS) Fixed % of every risk ceded; premium and losses shared in same % Surplus share Cede only risk above retention; proportional per risk

Features:

  • Reinsurer shares premium, losses, and expenses proportionally.
  • Ceding commission compensates the cedent for acquisition and admin.
  • Used for capacity and portfolio sharing.

docs.title: 2. Non-Proportional (Excess of Loss)
docs.text:
Structure Description Per risk XL Reinsurer pays losses per risk above a retention Catastrophe XL (Cat) Reinsurer pays losses from one event above an aggregate retention Stop loss Protects the annual aggregate loss ratio

Features:

  • Premium is independent of individual risk premium.
  • Uses loss rate or burning cost pricing.
  • Retention = company's retained loss per event/risk.

docs.title: Proportional Pricing
docs.text: Reinsurer's premium = Ceded % × Gross Premium (minus ceding commission)

docs.title: Non-Proportional Pricing
docs.text:
Burning cost = Expected losses to the layer ÷ Premium input

Rate on Line (ROL) = Layer Limit ÷ Layer Premium × 100%

Technical price = Expected loss cost + LAE + expense + profit loading

docs.title: Pricing Components
docs.text: Component Description Expected loss cost Historical loss experience, trended, projected Burning cost Simple average of past losses to the layer Rate on line (ROL) Premium as % of limit Exposure rating Based on exposure data (e.g., PML) Experience rating Cedent's own claims experience Expense loading Acquisition, admin, brokerage Risk/return loading CAT models, capital cost

docs.title: The Retention Decision
docs.text:
Choosing the retention (what the cedent keeps) balances:

Factor Lower Retention Higher Retention Premium cost Higher reinsurance cost Lower reinsurance cost Earnings volatility Lower volatility Higher volatility Capital requirement Lower required capital Higher required capital Frequency of claims to layer More frequent recovery Less frequent recovery

The optimal retention aligns with capital tolerance and earnings targets.

docs.title: Facultative vs. Treaty
docs.text:
Type Description Facultative Individual risk-by-risk reinsurance; full underwriting each time Treaty Automatic coverage for a defined class of risks; bordereau reporting

Treaties are cheaper and more seamless; facultative is used for large or unusual risks outside the treaty.

docs.title: Reinsurance Program Design
docs.text:
A typical commercial program combines layers:

Layer 3: Catastrophe excess (e.g., $100M xs $100M)
Layer 2: Mid excess (e.g., $50M xs $50M)
Layer 1: Working / per risk XL (e.g., $10M xs $5M)
Retention: Net retained by cedent (e.g., $5M)

docs.title: Reinsurance and Underwriting
docs.text:
• Underwriters must know the reinsurance program: what is retained, what is ceded.
  • Facultative decisions require underwriter input on each risk.
  • Ceding limits and recovery terms vary by treaty.
  • Credit risk — reinsurance recoverables are assets; they must be secure.

docs.title: Reinsurance Administration
docs.text: Activity Purpose Bordereau Monthly premium/loss reporting per treaty Cash calls Quick recovery of large claims Accounts Premium, claims, commissions, profit commission Audit Reinsurer audits cedent records; rights of access

docs.title: Regulation and Security
docs.text:
• Trust funds — reinsurer collateral for US cedents.
  • Collateral requirements — letters of credit, funds withheld.
  • Licensing — admitted vs. non-admitted reinsurers.
  • IFRS 17 / Solvency II — reinsurance assets and contract boundaries.
  • Credit for reinsurance — regulator recognition only if the reinsurer is secure.

docs.title: Emerging Issues
docs.text: Issue Consideration Cyber aggregation Systemic, correlated losses; model uncertainty Secondary perils Severe convective storms, wildfire — frequency rising Retrocession Reinsurers buying reinsurance; market capacity ILS (insurance-linked securities) Cat bonds, collateralized reinsurance — capital market capacity Climate stress testing Model scenarios beyond historical

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Reinsurance transfers risk and premium for capacity, catastrophe, and stability.
  • Proportional shares risk in %; non-proportional responds above retentions.
  • Pricing uses burning cost, exposure, and experience methods with expense and capital loadings.
  • Retention levels balance cost against volatility and capital.
  • Underwriters must know the net position and the treaty terms.
  • Security and collateral protect recoverables.

  • 5.4 Pricing Techniques
