docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Pricing is regulated and must be documented, fair, and sustainable. Governance ensures that rates are adequate, not unfairly discriminatory, and comply with law. It also protects the insurer from pricing errors that undermine solvency or reputation.

docs.title: Why Pricing Governance Matters
docs.text: Risk Consequence Inadequate rates Losses exceed premium; insolvency Unfair discrimination Regulatory action, litigation, reputational harm Rate filing non-compliance Fines, forced refunds, license issues Model error Inaccurate classes and prices Undocumented judgment Inconsistent decisions, audit failures

docs.title: Rate Regulation — US Model
docs.text:
Concept Description Prior approval Rates must be filed and approved before use File and use Filed and effective immediately; regulator can object Use and file Used, then filed Open competition Minimal filing; market disciplines rates

All US states require rates that are not excessive, not inadequate, and not unfairly discriminatory.

docs.title: Rate Filing Content
docs.text:
A filing demonstrates:

  • Data — premium, exposure, loss experience.
  • Method — loss cost or loss ratio method.
  • Adjustments — development, trend, credibility.
  • Relativities — class, territory, limit, deductible.
  • Expense provisions — acquisition, general, profit.
  • Support — actuarial memoranda, exhibits, validation.

docs.title: Fairness and Discrimination
docs.text:
Term Meaning Unfair discrimination Same risk charged different rates without actuarial justification Fair discrimination Different rates justified by expected loss differences Prohibited factors Race, religion, national origin, gender (where barred), genetic info

Pricing must avoid direct and indirect use of prohibited factors (e.g., proxies in models).

docs.title: Adverse Action and Consumer Notices
docs.text:
• Adverse action — denial, non-renewal, higher premium based on consumer report triggers notice requirements.
  • FCRA (US) — adverse action notice; right to dispute.
  • State laws — notices for credit-based scores, MVR use.
  • UK FCA — fair value assessments; no "loyalty penalty" for renewals.

docs.title: UK Regulatory Approach
docs.text: Requirement Description Fair value Product and price must deliver fair value (Consumer Duty) Risk-based pricing Prices reflect risk; no unjustified cross-subsidy Pricing practices Renewal pricing must not penalize loyalty Data protection GDPR — lawful basis, minimization Model governance AI Act — high-risk systems require oversight

docs.title: Pricing Monitoring
docs.text: Metric Use Actual vs. indicated rate Discipline of underwriters Rate realization Average premium vs. manual Loss ratio by class Relative profitability Retention by segment Customer behavior Price monitoring Adherence to guidelines Model drift Performance over time Complaint rates Consumer harms

docs.title: Documentation Standards
docs.text:
A pricing file should support every decision:

Element Standard Memo Basis of the indicated rate Data Source, period, definitions Assumptions Trend, expenses, credibility Judgment Where discretion was used Approval Sign-off by actuarial/management Retention Maintained per policy

docs.title: Pricing Committees and Controls
docs.text:
• Pricing committee — approves rate changes, discount programs, exceptions.
  • Underwriting authority — sets limits on discretionary deviation.
  • Independent validation — actuaries validate models and ratings.
  • Audit — internal and external audit of pricing processes.
  • Regulatory reporting — rates ROR (rates, rules, and forms) documentation.

docs.title: Cycle Discipline and Market Conduct
docs.text: Theme Practice Soft market Do not chase volume below indicated rates Fair competition Price on merits, not predatory behavior Transparency Clear explanations of pricing to customers Sustainability Rates must be self-supporting over time

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Pricing must be adequate, not unfairly discriminatory, and lawful.
  • Rate filings document data, methods, and assumptions.
  • Adverse action rules protect consumers using third-party data.
  • Fair value (UK) and anti-discrimination (US) govern the same goal: fair pricing.
  • Monitoring and documentation maintain discipline and auditability.
  • Model governance (AI Act, FCRA) constrains automated pricing.

docs.title: Volume 6 — Policy Administration
docs.text: Volume 6 covers the policy administration function — from the initial policy lifecycle through issuance, endorsements, renewals, cancellations, and servicing. It explains how policies are created, maintained, and terminated, and the systems, premium handling, and compliance standards that keep the process accurate and lawful.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Chapter Title Contents 6.1 Policy Lifecycle Stages, binders, issuance, renewals 6.2 Policy Issuance Documents, delivery, effective dates, evidence 6.3 Endorsements Changes, additional insureds, processing 6.4 Renewals Renewal process, notices, non-renewal 6.5 Cancellations & Non-Renewals Grounds, notices, refunds, statutory rules 6.6 Premium Handling & Audits Billing, collections, premium audits, adjustments 6.7 Systems & Data Policy administration systems, data, automation 6.8 Servicing & Compliance Customer service, certificates, compliance

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this volume you should be able to:

  1. Explain the policy lifecycle from quote to renewal.
  2. Issue accurate policy documents with proper evidence.
  3. Process endorsements and policy changes correctly.
  4. Manage renewals and statutory notices.
  5. Handle cancellations and non-renewals in compliance.
  6. Manage premium billing, collection, and audits.
  7. Use policy administration systems and data.
  8. Apply servicing and compliance standards.

docs.title: Suggested Reading
docs.text:
• Start with 6.1 Policy Lifecycle.
  • For the regulated process see 6.5 Cancellations & Non-Renewals.
  • Cross-reference underwriting (Volume 4), pricing (Volume 5), and claims (Volume 7).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Every insurance policy follows a lifecycle — from quotation and issuance through mid-term changes, renewal, and final expiry or cancellation. The policy administration function ensures each stage is processed accurately and on time.

docs.title: The Policy Lifecycle
docs.text:
Quote → Issue → In-force → Mid-term change → Renewal / Expiry / Cancellation
Stage Key Activities Quotation Data capture, rating, terms offered Issuance Policy documents issued; premium collected; coverage begins In-force Endorsements, billing, claims, servicing Mid-term change Adjust limits, values, drivers, premises; premium correction Renewal Re-underwrite, re-rate, issuance of renewal documents Expiry Policy ends; claims reporting period Cancellation Mid-term termination; refund or additional premium

docs.title: Quotation to Issuance
docs.text: Step Description 1. Submission Application data from agent/broker or customer 2. Rating Apply rate table or model; determine premium 3. Underwriting Eligibility, referral, terms 4. Bind Agreement to provide coverage as of a date 5. Issue Generate policy documents and schedule 6. Collect Premium payment or installment plan 7. Deliver Send policy to insured/producer 8. Verify Confirm data and documents correct

docs.title: Key Policy Data
docs.text: Data Element Example Named insured Legal entity and address Policy period Effective and expiry dates Coverages & limits Per coverage and policy limits Exposures Vehicles, locations, payroll, values Deductibles Per coverage Premium Base, taxes, fees, payment plan Forms & endorsements Applicable policy forms Insurer & producer Underwriting company, agency

docs.title: The In-Force Period
docs.text:
During the term, policy administration supports:

  • Endorsements — mid-term changes.
  • Billing — installments, renewals, adjustments.
  • Claims — notification and handling (Volume 7).
  • Audits — premium audits for exposure-based policies.
  • Compliance — cancels, notices, regulatory filings.
  • Customer service — questions, certificates, evidence.

docs.title: Renewal
docs.text:
• Renewal notice — sent before expiry (typically 30–60 days).
  • Re-underwriting — review current data, claims, and risk changes.
  • Re-rating — new rate level, exposure base, terms.
  • Declination — notice of non-renewal with reasons where required.
  • Retention — ensure continuous coverage and no gaps.

See 6.4 Renewals.

docs.title: Cancellation and Expiry
docs.text:
Event Description Expiry Term ends naturally; coverage ceases; report period for claims Cancellation by insured Mid-term cancellation; short-rate refund Cancellation by insurer Non-payment, material misrepresentation, fraud, risk deterioration Non-renewal Insurer declines to renew at expiry Rescission/void Coverage void ab initio (fraud)

Refunds and additional premiums are calculated per the cancellation provisions of the policy and state law.

See 6.5 Cancellations & Non-renewals.

docs.title: Lifecycle Control Points
docs.text: Control Purpose Effective date validation Proper binding and retroactivity Document generation Issued vs. pending tracking Premium verification Collect or bill before bind where required Audit trail Every change logged with user, date, reason Reconciliation Premiums, endorsements, and documents match Compliance checks Notices, cancellations, state rules

docs.title: Common Lifecycle Errors
docs.text: Error Impact Wrong effective date Coverage gap or retroactive exposure Incorrect exposure basis Wrong premium and potential coinsurance Missing endorsement Coverage mismatch at claim Delayed renewal Lapse and reinstatement issues Improper cancellation notice Regulatory violation and coverage challenge Unreconciled premium Accounting and audit issues

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The lifecycle is quote → issue → in-force → change → renewal/cancellation.
  • Issuance, endorsements, renewal, and cancellation each have strict data and timing requirements.
  • Controls (effective dates, documents, premiums, audit trail) protect accuracy.
  • Errors at any stage produce coverage, premium, or compliance problems.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Policy issuance converts a bound submission into a valid, documented insurance contract. The policy documents define exactly what is covered, for whom, for what period, at what premium, and subject to what conditions.

docs.title: The Policy Document Set
docs.text: Document Purpose Declarations page (Dec page) Summary of insured, period, coverages, limits, premium Policy form / wording The full contractual terms and conditions Schedules Lists of locations, vehicles, items, values Forms & endorsements Amendments to the base form Certificates of insurance Evidence of coverage for third parties Insuring agreement Statement of what is covered Conditions Duties, cancellation, claims provisions Exclusions What is not covered

docs.title: The Declarations Page
docs.text:
The Dec page is the summary of the contract:

Field Example Policy number CP-1001234 Named insured ABC Manufacturing Inc. Policy period 01/01/2026 – 01/01/2027 Coverages Building, Contents, BI, Liability Limits $2,000,000 / $500,000 / $250,000 Deductibles $10,000 property Premium $18,500 plus taxes/fees Forms CP 00 10, CP 10 30, etc. Insurer/agency Company, agency, contact

docs.title: Policy Form / Wording
docs.text:
The form contains:

  • Insuring agreement — the promise to pay.
  • Definitions — key terms and their meaning.
  • Exclusions — what is not covered.
  • Conditions — duties, cancellation, suit, subrogation.
  • Deductibles and coinsurance — the insured's retention.
  • Limits of liability — per occurrence, aggregate, per person.

docs.title: Issuance Process
docs.text:
1. Bind coverage (authority + data complete)
2. Verify underwriting conditions met (inspection, payment)
3. Generate documents (system or manual)
4. Quality check (data, forms, premium)
5. Deliver to insured/producer
6. Record issuance (policy file, system, documents)
7. Confirm premium collection/billing

docs.title: Issuance Timing and Effective Dates
docs.text: Situation Rule Standard new business Coverage effective at 12:01 AM local time of effective date Backdated binders Allowed only with authority; date on binder Retroactive cover Requires specific underwriting approval Evidence of insurance Certificate issued; does not amend policy terms

docs.title: Delivery and Evidence
docs.text: Method Notes Paper Mailed or hand-delivered; proof of delivery retained Electronic Email or portal; consent for e-delivery may be required Certificate Not a policy; evidence only Binder Temporary contract pending policy issue

docs.title: Quality Checks
docs.text: Check Purpose Named insured Correct legal entity and spelling Date Effective/expiry, no gaps Limits Match application and underwriting Exposures Correct premises, vehicles, values Premium Rate × exposure = charged premium Forms Correct editions and endorsements Taxes/fees Proper statutory charges

docs.title: Issuance Errors and Corrections
docs.text: Error Type Correction Clerical Corrective endorsement; evidence of correction Underwriting miss Endorse to correct terms; notify insured Premium error Additional or return premium Coverage gap Endorse retroactively if covered under binder authority Wrong form Replace form from inception if within authority

docs.title: Recordkeeping
docs.text:
• Policy file retains the complete document set.
  • Audit trail — every version, change, and activity logged.
  • Retention per regulatory and corporate schedule.
  • Indexing — searchable by policy number, insured, date.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Issuance produces the declarations, form, schedules, and endorsements.
  • The Dec page is the summary; the form is the contract.
  • Quality checks verify data, dates, limits, exposures, premium, and forms.
  • Delivery, records, and audit trail support compliance.
  • Errors must be corrected and documented promptly.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:

  • 6.3 Endorsements
  • 6.6 Premium Handling
  • 6.7 Policy Systems & Data

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: An endorsement is a written modification to the insurance contract during the policy period. Endorsements keep the policy aligned with the insured's actual risk as circumstances change. Incorrect or missing endorsements are a leading source of coverage disputes.

docs.title: Types of Mid-term Changes
docs.text: Type Examples Exposure change Add/remove vehicle, location, employee Coverage change Increase/decrease limits, add coverage Value change Change insured values, SOV update Named insured change Entity, name, address Deductible change Increase/decrease retention Forms change Add/remove endorsements Payment change Payment plan, billing information Policyholder service Certificate requests, evidence

docs.title: Endorsement Process
docs.text:
1. Receive request (insured/producer; verify authority)
2. Review terms and conditions (eligible? within authority?)
3. Re-rate / re-underwrite if required
4. Apply the endorsement with effective date
5. Calculate premium adjustment (AP/RP)
6. Issue amended documents
7. Deliver and record

docs.title: Effective Date Handling
docs.text: Situation Rule Prospective Endorsement effective from a future date Retroactive Effective before the current date; requires authorization and consideration Backdated binders Coverage may be retroactive from a binder; must align Loss in progress No coverage for known losses; clarify at effective date

docs.title: Premium Adjustments
docs.text:
• Additional premium (AP) — when exposure or limits increase.
  • Return premium (RP) — when exposure or limits decrease.
  • Adjustments are pro-rata by time unless short-rate applies.
  • AP/RP must be transparent and documented on the endorsement.
Change Effect Add vehicle AP from the effective date Remove driver RP from the effective date Increase limits AP; ILF difference Reduce coverage RP; pro-rata Change deductible AP or RP per rate difference

docs.title: Underwriting Referral
docs.text:
Some changes require underwriting review:

  • Specialty lines — adding high-hazard exposures.
  • Large value increases — property or liability.
  • Change of occupancy — different class.
  • Named insured changes — new legal entity.
  • Changes outside guidelines — discretionary authority.

docs.title: Documentation Requirements
docs.text:
Each endorsement must show:

Element Example Endorsement number Endt. 2 Policy number CP-1001234 Effective date 03/01/2026 Named insured ABC Manufacturing Inc. Description of change Added forklift; $25,000 AP Forms referenced CP 12 18 – Coverage change Issued by/e-signature System/user

docs.title: Common Endorsement Errors
docs.text: Error Impact Wrong effective date Coverage gap or retroactive exposure Incorrect limit Claim underpaid or uninsured exposure Missing endorsement Policy doesn't match expectation at claim Wrong form edition Legal interpretation issues AP/RP error Premium dispute; audit finding No signature/authority Unauthorized change

docs.title: Endorsement vs. New Policy
docs.text: Situation Endorsement New Policy Add a vehicle Yes No Change ownership entity Possibly (review) Possibly Major restructuring No Yes End of policy period change Renewal Yes Change carrier No Yes

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Endorsements modify the contract mid-term; accuracy is critical.
  • Effective dates, premium adjustments, and documentation must be precise.
  • Underwriting referral applies to material changes.
  • AP/RP calculations must be transparent and correct.
  • Errors produce coverage disputes and premium issues.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 6.1 Policy Lifecycle
  • 6.2 Policy Issuance & Documentation
  • 6.4 Renewals
  • 6.6 Premium Handling

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Renewal is the continuation of coverage for a new policy period. It is the point at which the insurer re-underwrites the risk, re-rates the premium, and either renews, non-renews, or restructures the policy. Renewal is also a key retention event.

docs.title: The Renewal Cycle
docs.text:
Pre-renewal review → Offer → Re-underwriting → Rate → Issue → Deliver → Retain
Stage Activity Pre-renewal review Claims, changes, loss runs, market check Re-underwriting Current exposures, risk improvement, guidelines Rating Updated rate level, exposure base, credits/debits Offer Renewal terms to producer/insured Issue Renewal documents before expiry Retain Ensure acceptance; avoid coverage gaps

docs.title: Key Renewal Inputs
docs.text: Input Use Claims history Loss ratio, frequency, severity, large losses Current policy data Limits, forms, exposures Risk changes New operations, locations, values Underwriting guidelines Appetite, capacity, current stance Rate changes Approved rate level and classification Market conditions Pricing pressure, capacity Inspection updates New engineering or survey reports

docs.title: Re-Underwriting the Renewal
docs.text:
The underwriter decides:

Decision Basis Renew as is Risk within appetite; loss experience acceptable Renew with changes Conditions, warranties, rates, deductibles Renew with restrictions Limit, coverage, or territory changes Non-renew Deterioration, claims, outside appetite

docs.title: Renewal Underwriting Checklist
docs.text:
• Current loss runs and trend
  • Exposure changes (payroll, receipts, values, vehicles)
  • Compliance with previous warranties/conditions
  • Inspections and engineering recommendations
  • Financial health of the insured
  • Coverage adequacy (limits vs. exposures)
  • Rate adequacy vs. current data

docs.title: Rating the Renewal
docs.text:
Element Description Rate level change Filed rate movement Experience adjustment E-mod, schedule, retro changes Exposure change Updated payroll, receipts, values Premium change compared to prior Retention conversation

The renewal premium should be explained — rate × exposure changes and any underwriting adjustments.

docs.title: Renewal Documentation and Timing
docs.text: Requirement Typical Rule Notice of renewal Sent before expiry (e.g., 30–60 days) Renewal policy issued On or before effective date Non-renewal notice Statutory notice period (varies by line/state) New dec page Updated limits, premium, forms

docs.title: Retention and Lapse Prevention
docs.text:
• Retention — keep good business through competitive, accurate renewal pricing.
  • Lapse — coverage ends without renewal; may require reinstatement or new application.
  • Grace period — auto-renewal terms or late payment options.
  • Renewal contact — reminders, quotes, service.

docs.title: Loss Ratio and Profitability at Renewal
docs.text:
Renewal decisions balance:

View Consideration Individual account Is this account profitable? Portfolio Does the class remain in appetite? Market Is pricing competitive or is the account over/under-priced? Long-term relationship Does the account have growth or claims potential?

docs.title: Non-Renewal
docs.text:
• Must follow statutory notice periods and reasons.
  • Producers and insured must be notified in writing.
  • Evidence of alternative coverage may be required.
  • Non-renewal differs from cancellation (expiry vs. mid-term).

See 6.5 Cancellations & Non-renewals.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Renewal is a re-underwriting and re-rating event.
  • Use claims, exposures, inspections, and guidelines to decide terms.
  • Timing and notices are regulatory and contractual.
  • Retention and lapse prevention keep the book stable.
  • Renewal decisions balance account, portfolio, and market.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 4.1 The Underwriting Process
  • 6.1 Policy Lifecycle
  • 6.2 Policy Issuance & Documentation
  • 6.5 Cancellations & Non-renewals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Cancellation terminates a policy before its expiration. Non-renewal allows the policy to expire without renewal. Both are highly regulated: insurers must follow statutory grounds, notice periods, and refund calculations, while insureds typically retain broader rights.

docs.title: Cancellation Basics
docs.text: Party Grounds Insurer Statutory grounds only: non-payment, fraud/material misrepresentation, substantial change in risk, license suspension, catastrophic exposure, loss of reinsurance Insured Any reason; written notice; may be subject to short-rate penalty

docs.title: Insurer Cancellation Grounds
docs.text:
Ground Example Non-payment of premium Missed installment; covered if policy terms met Material misrepresentation False application answers; discovered after binding Fraud Fraudulent claim or application Substantial change in risk Physical change increasing hazard beyond underwriting intent Loss of license Insured's professional license revoked Catastrophe exposure Multi-peril crop, catastrophe concentration Reinsurance termination Underlying capacity withdrawn

Grounds vary by state law and line of business. Some lines (e.g., personal auto, workers comp) have strict statutory restrictions.

docs.title: Notice Requirements
docs.text:
Element Requirement Insurer cancellation Statutory notice: typically 10–60 days Non-payment Shorter notice allowed (often 10 days) Non-renewal Typically 30–60 days before expiry Insured cancellation Usually written request; effective on receipt Notice form Written, mailed; some states allow electronic

Notices must state the effective date, reason (where required), and often the right to appeal.

docs.title: Non-Renewal
docs.text:
Aspect Description Meaning Policy not continued at expiry Timing Notice within statutory period before expiry Reasons Often need not be stated; some states require reasons Mid-term equivalent Non-renewal is not a cancellation; no mid-term refund Exceptions Some states bar non-renewal after a claim; others allow

Non-renewal is commonly used to manage accumulation or deteriorating risk without asserting a cancellation ground.

docs.title: Refund Calculations
docs.text:
Scenario Refund Insurer cancellation Pro-rata refund for unearned premium Insured cancellation (P&C) Short-rate — refund less penalty (often 10%) Non-renewal No refund of unearned premium (premium earned to expiry) Audit premium Adjusted at audit regardless of cancellation

Short-rate penalties must comply with filed rules.

docs.title: The Process
docs.text:
1. Identify grounds and verify eligibility
2. Prepare notice (reason if required, effective date, refund computation)
3. Send notice within statutory window
4. Handle appeal/inquiry period
5. Process refund or additional premium
6. Update systems; notify producers and reinsurers
7. Document the file

docs.title: Compliance Considerations
docs.text: Risk Control Late notice Calendar controls; statutory deadline tracking Wrong grounds Legal review before cancellation Unfair discrimination Treat similar risks consistently Notice not received Proof of mailing; mail-return procedures Retaliation No non-renewal for a single claim where barred Refund error Validate pro-rata/short-rate calculations

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Cancellation terminates early; non-renewal lets it lapse.
  • Insurer grounds are statutory and limited.
  • Notice timing and content are strictly regulated.
  • Refunds differ by canceling party (pro-rata vs. short-rate).
  • Documentation and compliance controls prevent disputes.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 6.1 Policy Lifecycle
  • 6.4 Renewals
  • 6.6 Premium Handling & Audits
  • 1.5 The Legal Environment

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Premium handling covers the billing, collection, allocation, adjustment, and audit of premium. For many commercial lines, the final premium is not known until the end of the term because it is based on actual exposures (payroll, receipts, values) — hence the premium audit.

docs.title: Billing and Payment Plans
docs.text: Plan Description Annual premium Single payment at inception Installments Monthly/quarterly payments; service fees often apply Direct bill Insurer bills the insured Agency bill Producer bills and remits Payroll deduction Employer deducts from wages (life/health) Electronic funds ACH/card automatic payments

docs.title: The Premium Cycle
docs.text:
Quote/Issue → Billing → Collection → Allocation → Reconciliation → Audit (if exposure-based) → Adjustment
Stage Activity Billing Generate invoice with due dates Collection Receive payment; apply to policy Allocation Apply to the right policy/coverage Reconciliation Match receipts to invoices, agents, banks Audit Determine actual exposure at term end Adjustment Additional or return premium

docs.title: Payment and Non-Payment
docs.text:
Event Handling Paid in full Policy effective; no outstanding balance Installment missed Grace period; late notice; cancellation exposure NSF/reversal Recover premium; reinstate or cancel Audit additional premium Bill after audit Return premium Refund or apply to other balances

Non-payment procedures must follow policy terms and statutory requirements.

docs.title: The Premium Audit
docs.text:
Premium audits verify the actual exposure base at the end of the policy period.

Audit Type Description Physical audit On-site review of records Mail/desk audit Correspondence-based review Self-audit Insured completes the audit form; insurer verifies Estimated annual Interim estimate; final at term end

docs.title: Audit Basis by Line
docs.text: Line Audited Exposure Workers comp Payroll by class General liability Gross receipts (premises), sales (products) Commercial auto Mileage, fleet composition Property (reporting forms) Monthly values reported

docs.title: Audit Process
docs.text:
1. Send audit request (at expiry or periodically)
2. Insured provides payroll/receipts/exposure records
3. Auditor verifies classification and amounts
4. Calculate adjusted premium
5. Issue additional premium (AP) bill or return premium (RP)
6. Document and record

docs.title: Classification Errors at Audit
docs.text:
Error Impact Wrong class code Premium change; possible misreporting penalties Misstated payroll Incorrect premium; audit exposure Unreported locations Missing exposure Excluded operations performed Premium evasion

The insured is obligated to report accurately; audits verify compliance.

docs.title: Reconciliation and Control
docs.text: Control Purpose Cash application Payments applied to correct policies Aging reports Track overdue balances Write-off authority Controlled bad debt Reconciliation Bank vs. ledger vs. agency balances Premium trust Producer funds held in trust where required Statutory accounting Premium recognition per accounting basis

docs.title: Return and Additional Premiums
docs.text:
Type Trigger AP (additional premium) Endorsement, audit, rate correction RP (return premium) Cancellation, endorsement, audit reduction Short-rate Insured cancellation penalty Refund Overpayment or rescission

All AP/RP must be documented and promptly processed.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Premium handling covers billing, collection, allocation, reconciliation, and audit.
  • Premium audits verify actual exposures for many commercial lines.
  • Classification and reporting accuracy drive correct premium.
  • Non-payment follows policy and statutory procedures.
  • Controls and reconciliation protect the insurer's cash and records.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 6.1 Policy Lifecycle
  • 6.3 Endorsements
  • 6.5 Cancellations & Non-renewals
  • 5.6 Rating by Line

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Policy administration runs on systems that store policy data, generate documents, manage billing, and integrate with underwriting, claims, and finance. Data quality and system controls determine the reliability of the entire insurance operation.

docs.title: The Policy Administration System (PAS)
docs.text: Function Description Policy master Core record: insured, coverages, limits, premium Rating engine Calculates premium from rate tables/models Document generation Produces dec pages, forms, endorsements Billing module Generates invoices, tracks payments Workflow Routes tasks (referrals, audits, renewals) Claims interface Policy data for claim setup Reporting Portfolio, regulatory, management reports Integration Underwriting, claims, finance, analytics systems

docs.title: Core Policy Data Model
docs.text: Entity Key Fields Policy Number, period, status, insurer, producer Insured Legal entity, addresses, contacts Coverages Code, limits, deductibles, premiums Exposures Locations, vehicles, payroll, values Forms Policy forms and endorsements Transactions Issuance, endorsements, renewals, cancellations Premium Charges, payments, balances, adjustments Documents Generated and filed versions

docs.title: Data Quality
docs.text: Dimension Risk of Poor Data Accuracy Wrong coverage, premium, or address Completeness Missing exposures or forms Consistency Conflicting definitions across systems Timeliness Stale policy, billing, or claims data Uniqueness Duplicate policies or customers

docs.title: Data Quality Controls
docs.text:
• Validation rules at entry (required fields, ranges).
  • Referential integrity across policy/billing/claims.
  • Duplicate detection for customers and policies.
  • Reconciliation between systems (premium, coverage, status).
  • Monitoring dashboards for error rates and aging.

docs.title: Reference Data
docs.text:
Reference Example Rate tables Class, territory, factor values Forms library Approved form editions Class codes WC, GL, NAICS/SIC Area codes Territory definitions Producer codes Agency, license, commission

Reference data must be versioned and governed — a change to a rate table affects all future quotes.

docs.title: System Interfaces
docs.text: Interface Purpose Underwriting workbench Referrals, decisions, documents Claims system Policy lookup, coverage verification Finance/GL Premium and payments postings Reinsurance Ceded premium/loss reporting Regulatory reporting Data calls, statutory returns Producer portal Quotes, binding, servicing

docs.title: Technology Considerations
docs.text: Topic Consideration Legacy systems Older PAS; data migration risk Cloud platforms Scalability, availability, security APIs Real-time integration with external data Automation (RPA) Document handling, data entry Security Access controls, data protection (GLBA/GDPR)

docs.title: Reconciliation and Control
docs.text: Control Purpose Policy count reconciliation System vs. issued documents Premium reconciliation Billing vs. ledger Transaction audit trail Every change logged Cut-off controls Period-end processing integrity Suspense accounts Unmatched payments cleared

docs.title: Common System Issues
docs.text: Issue Impact Duplicate policy Double coverage and premium Stale forms Wrong coverage at claim Untracked endorsements Missing documents Broken integration Claims without policy data Data silos Inconsistent customer view Uncontrolled rate change Pricing errors

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The PAS is the operational heart of policy administration.
  • Data quality and reference data governance protect correctness.
  • Interfaces connect underwriting, claims, finance, and regulation.
  • Controls and reconciliation keep systems in balance.
  • Poor data creates coverage, premium, and compliance risk.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Servicing covers the day-to-day interaction with policyholders, producers, and regulators that keeps the policy accurate and the relationship healthy. Compliance ensures those activities meet legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements.

docs.title: Servicing Activities
docs.text: Activity Description Customer service Answers, document requests, policy questions Certificates & evidence Certificates of insurance, letters of good standing Billing inquiries Payment status, plans, adjustments Endorsement requests Changes, additions, removals Renewal assistance Quotes, terms, explanations Claims coordination Notices, documentation, handoff to claims Producer support Agency questions, quotes, binding authority Record updates Address, contact, payment changes

docs.title: Service Standards
docs.text: Standard Example Response time Phone/email resolution within SLAs Accuracy Correct policy information on first call Empathy Professional and respectful communication Resolution Complete answers, no follow-up needed Documentation Call notes and records retained

docs.title: Certificates of Insurance
docs.text:
• Purpose — evidence that coverage exists; not a contract change.
  • Issuance — certificate holder, insured, limits, period, insurer.
  • Accuracy — verify requested coverage exists before issuing.
  • Additional insured status — only if endorsed on the policy.
  • Control — certificates must not misstate coverage.

docs.title: Regulatory Compliance
docs.text:
Area Key Rules Cancellation notices Statutory timing and content Non-renewal notices Notice period; reasons where required Adverse action FCRA notice for credit-based decisions Privacy GLBA/GDPR — data protection and use Records retention Regulatory minimums Market conduct Fair treatment, no misrepresentation Producer licensing Appointments, commissions, authority

See 1.5 The Legal Environment.

docs.title: Market Conduct
docs.text:
Market conduct reviews assess whether insurers treat consumers fairly:

  • Complaint handling — timely, fair resolution.
  • Sales practices — no misrepresentation, suitability.
  • Advertising — truthful, not misleading.
  • Claims practices — timely, accurate (Volume 7).
  • Underwriting practices — no unfair discrimination.

docs.title: Data Protection and Privacy
docs.text: Requirement Practice Lawful basis Process data only with basis (consent, contract, law) Minimization Collect only what is necessary Security Access controls, encryption, monitoring Breach response Notification where required Consumer rights Access, correction, erasure where applicable

docs.title: Recordkeeping
docs.text:
Record Retention Driver Policy documents Contract period + claims statue + regulation Claims files Long-tail liability only Billing records Premium disputes, audits Correspondence Servicing and complaints Regulatory filings Permanent

Retention schedules should be documented and enforced.

docs.title: Complaint Management
docs.text:
Receive complaint → Log → Investigate → Respond → Remediate → Report
Step Practice Log Central record; category, date, owner Investigate Gather policy, servicing, claims records Respond Clear, timely explanation; resolution offered Remediate Correct the issue; adjust policy/premium Report Internal and regulatory reporting

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Servicing keeps policies accurate and customers supported.
  • Certificates and evidence must not misstate coverage.
  • Compliance spans notices, privacy, market conduct, and records.
  • Market conduct and complaint management protect consumers and the insurer.
  • Documentation and retention support audits and disputes.

docs.title: Volume 7 — Claims
docs.text: Volume 7 covers the claims function — from first notice of loss through investigation, coverage analysis, resolution, and recovery. It explains the claims process, the skills and tools used by adjusters, and the legal and regulatory framework that governs fair, prompt, and accurate claim handling.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Chapter Title Contents 7.1 Claims Overview Role of claims, stakeholders, process, KPIs 7.2 Notification & Investigation FNOL, statement, records, experts, liability 7.3 Coverage Analysis Policy interpretation, duties, reservations of rights 7.4 Claims Resolution Settlement, negotiation, forums, litigation 7.5 Reserving & Settlement Case reserves, payments, authority, releases 7.6 Reinsurance & Subrogation Recoveries, salvage, subrogation, reimbursement 7.7 Claims Systems & Analytics Systems, fraud detection, data, automation 7.8 Claims Compliance & Best Practice Regulations, fair claims, documentation, quality

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this volume you should be able to:

  1. Explain the role of claims in the insurance operation.
  2. Investigate a claim from notification to conclusion.
  3. Analyze coverage and apply policy interpretation.
  4. Resolve claims fairly and efficiently.
  5. Set reserves and manage settlement authority.
  6. Handle recoveries: reinsurance, subrogation, salvage.
  7. Use claims systems, data, and analytics.
  8. Apply compliance and best-practice standards.

docs.title: Suggested Reading
docs.text:
• Start with 7.1 Claims Overview.
  • For the core process see 7.2 Notification & Investigation and 7.3 Coverage Analysis.
  • Cross-reference underwriting (Volume 4), pricing (Volume 5), and policy administration (Volume 6).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The claims function fulfills the insurer's promise to pay. It is where the product is tested, where the customer experience is defined, and where the insurer's financial results are determined. Good claims handling is fair, prompt, and accurate.

docs.title: The Role of Claims
docs.text: Purpose Description Promise fulfillment Pay covered losses per the policy Loss measurement Determine amounts, set reserves Liability determination Establish whether the claim is covered Cost control Prevent overpayment and fraud Recovery Subrogation, salvage, reinsurance Feedback loop Data to underwriting, pricing, and risk management

docs.title: Stakeholders
docs.text: Stakeholder Interest Insured Prompt, fair payment of covered loss Third-party claimant Compensation for injury/damage Producer/broker Claims service for clients Defense counsel Legal representation Adjusters & experts Investigation and valuation Regulators Fair claims practices Reinsurers Their share of loss Shareholders Loss ratio and reserving accuracy

docs.title: The Claims Process
docs.text:
Notification (FNOL)
      ↓
Coverage verification
      ↓
Investigation
      ↓
Coverage determination
      ↓
Reserving
      ↓
Resolution (settlement or denial)
      ↓
Payment / Recovery
      ↓
File closure & audit
Step Description FNOL First notice of loss; capture details Coverage verification Policy in force; applicable coverage Investigation Facts, statements, evidence, experts Coverage determination Covered? Excluded? Reservation of rights Reserving Case reserve estimate Resolution Settlement, litigation, or denial Recovery Subrogation, salvage, reinsurance Closure File complete; potential audit

docs.title: Types of Claims
docs.text: Type Characteristics First-party Insured's own loss (property, auto physical damage) Third-party liability Claim against insured (GL, auto liability, professional) Workers comp Statutory benefits to employees Life/health Benefits on death, disability, illness Large loss High-severity; specialized handling Catastrophe Many claims from one event; surge response Fraud Suspected dishonesty; SIU referral

docs.title: Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)
docs.text: Metric Definition Cycle time Time from FNOL to resolution Claim count & frequency Volume trends Severity Average cost per claim Loss ratio Incurred vs. earned premium Settled vs. reserved Accuracy of case reserves Litigation rate % of claims in suit SIU referrals Fraud investigations Customer satisfaction Survey and complaint measures Aged open claims Claims not closed within target

docs.title: Claims Quality
docs.text: Principle Practice Fair Pay what is owed; deny what is not Prompt Meet regulatory and internal timeliness Accurate Correct coverage, valuation, documentation Empathetic Recognize the insured's situation Transparent Clear communication of decisions

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Claims fulfills the promise and defines the customer experience.
  • The process runs notification → investigation → coverage → resolution → recovery.
  • KPIs (cycle time, severity, loss ratio, reserving accuracy) measure performance.
  • Quality means fair, prompt, accurate, empathetic, and transparent handling.
  • Claims feed underwriting, pricing, and risk with data.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The claim begins with notification and proceeds through investigation — gathering the facts needed to determine coverage, liability, and value. Thorough, timely investigation is the foundation of fair and accurate claims handling.

docs.title: First Notice of Loss (FNOL)
docs.text:
Element Details Captured Insured Policy number, contact, relationship Loss details Date, time, location, description Damage/injury Nature, extent, value indicators Third parties Names, contact, witnesses Police/regulatory Report numbers, citations Prior claims History and context

FNOL must be prompt — regulatory deadlines may apply to acknowledgment and contact.

docs.title: Notification Channels
docs.text:
• Phone, portal, mobile app, email, agent/broker.
  • 24/7 intake for auto and property.
  • Catastrophe surge — mass notification response plans.

docs.title: Verification Steps
docs.text:
1. Policy in force — effective dates, status.
  2. Coverage applicable — the loss event and coverage trigger.
  3. Notice compliance — the insured's duty to give prompt notice.
  4. Premium paid — payment status where relevant.
  5. Potential exclusions — early identifiers.

docs.title: The Investigation Plan
docs.text: Scope Examples Liability Fault, comparative negligence, contracts Coverage Occurrence, exclusions, conditions Damages Property, injury, BI, defense costs Subrogation Third-party fault, contractual indemnity Fraud indicators SIU criteria, red flags

docs.title: Investigation Activities
docs.text: Activity Purpose Take statement Insured, witnesses, claimant Inspect scene/property Damage assessment, photos Review records Police, medical, employment, financial Interview experts Engineers, medical, forensic Obtain documents Contracts, invoices, payroll Check databases Loss history, fraud indicators Verify facts Coverage, limits, condition

docs.title: Recorded statements and Examinations
docs.text:
Tool Use Signed statement Claimant version of facts Recorded statement Consistent record; legal limits apply EUO (Examination Under Oath) Insured's duty to cooperate; permitted per policy IME (Independent Medical Exam) Workers comp / disability verification

Each tool has legal and regulatory boundaries — use within the policy and law.

docs.title: Liability Analysis
docs.text:
• Third-party claims — determine the insured's legal liability.
  • Comparative/contributory negligence — allocation.
  • Contracts — indemnity and additional insured status.
  • Statutory duties — premises liability, product defect, auto fault.

docs.title: Reports and Documentation
docs.text:
Document Content Preliminary report Facts, coverage, initial assessment Investigation file Statements, photos, records, expert reports Coverage memo Analysis of applicability and reservations Reserve recommendation Initial and updated case estimates

Documentation must be objective, complete, and reviewable.

docs.title: Timeliness and Communication
docs.text: Requirement Practice Acknowledge FNOL Within regulatory deadlines Contact insured Promptly; explain next steps Update claimant Periodic status communications Scope authority Advise of investigation or coverage issues Meet deadlines Statutory and internal SLAs

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Notification captures the claim and verifies policy applicability.
  • Investigation gathers facts: statements, records, inspections, experts.
  • Liability and coverage analysis drive the decision.
  • Documentation must be complete and objective.
  • Prompt, transparent communication is both regulatory and good practice.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 7.1 Claims Overview
  • 7.3 Coverage Analysis
  • 7.4 Claims Resolution
  • 7.5 Reserving & Settlement

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Coverage analysis determines whether a claim is covered by the policy. It requires reading the policy as a whole, applying legal principles of interpretation, and documenting the reasoning. Errors in coverage analysis are among the most expensive claims failures.

docs.title: The Coverage Question
docs.text: Question Example Is the policy in force? Effective dates, status, retroactive date Is the event covered? Insuring agreement trigger Is an exclusion applicable? Pollution, intentional act, wear and tear Are conditions met? Notice, cooperation, suit requirement What is the limit? Per occurrence, aggregate, sub-limits Does a coverage trigger apply? Occurrence, claims-made, accident

docs.title: Policy Interpretation Principles
docs.text: Principle Meaning Plain meaning Ordinary meaning of policy language Ambiguity resolves against drafter Against the insurer (typically) Reasonable expectations Insured's reasonable understanding Exclusions strictly construed Narrow reading of exclusions Whole policy reading No clause read in isolation Trade usage Terms have industry meanings

docs.title: Structure of Analysis
docs.text:
1. Identify the applicable coverage parts
2. Apply the insuring agreement (is the loss within it?)
3. Check definitions (occurrence, insured, property damage)
4. Check exclusions (does any apply?)
5. Check conditions (notice, cooperation, suit)
6. Determine limit, deductible, and trigger
7. State the conclusion with reasoning

docs.title: Common Coverage Issues
docs.text: Issue Handling Occurrence vs. claims-made Trigger date and retroactive date Intentional act Excluded; coverage for accidents only Pollution exclusion Absolute vs. sudden-and-accidental Contractual liability Assumed liability; insured contract carve-out Employee injuries WC/employers liability vs. GL Mold/fungus Sub-limits and exclusions Business auto use Hired/non-owned vs. owned auto

docs.title: Reservation of Rights
docs.text:
When coverage is uncertain, the insurer issues a reservation of rights (ROR):

Element Content Notice Advises of potential coverage issues Investigation Insurer continues investigating Defense May still defend the insured Rights preserved Insurer may later deny coverage

A ROR does not deny coverage — it preserves the insurer's rights while investigating.

docs.title: Declaratory Judgment
docs.text:
• The insurer may seek a court determination of coverage.
  • Used where coverage depends on disputed facts or law.
  • May run alongside the underlying claim.

docs.title: Coverage Determination Outcomes
docs.text: Outcome Meaning Accept Claim covered; proceed to valuation and payment Deny Not covered; provide clear explanation to insured Reserve rights Coverage unresolved; continue investigation Partially cover Some elements covered; others not Defense obligation only Indemnity uncertain; defend under ROR

docs.title: Coverage Documentation
docs.text:
The coverage memo should record:

  • Policy references (forms, endorsements, conditions).
  • The facts as known.
  • Application of insuring agreement, exclusions, conditions.
  • Legal authority where relevant.
  • The decision and basis.
  • Communications with the insured.

docs.title: Bad Faith Exposure
docs.text: Risk Consequence Wrong denial Breach of contract; bad faith damages Unreasonable delay Statutory penalties; interest Inadequate investigation before denial Bad faith finding Failure to explain denial Regulatory complaint Failed ROR Waiver or estoppel arguments

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Coverage analysis answers is this claim within the policy?
  • Use insuring agreement, definitions, exclusions, conditions, limits, triggers.
  • Follow interpretation principles — plain meaning, contra proferentem, reasonable expectations.
  • Reservation of rights protects the insurer during investigation.
  • Documented, prompt, and fair decisions avoid bad faith.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 7.1 Claims Overview
  • 7.2 Notification & Investigation
  • 7.4 Claims Resolution
  • 1.5 The Legal Environment

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Resolution is the step where the claim is settled, litigated, or denied. The goal is a fair, prompt, and accurate outcome — paying what is owed, defending when appropriate, and denying only with sound basis.

docs.title: Resolution Options
docs.text: Outcome Description Settlement Agreement on damages; payment and release Negotiated compromise Resolution without full trial value Denial Claim not covered or not valid Litigation Underlying claim goes to court Alternative dispute resolution Mediation, arbitration, mini-trial Structured settlement Payments over time (liability, workers comp)

docs.title: Settlement Authority
docs.text:
Level Authority Adjuster Settle within delegated limit Supervisor/manager Higher limits; approvals Claims committee Large or complex claims Home office Very large, class-exposure, or unusual

Authority is delegated and documented. Settling outside authority is a serious control breach.

docs.title: The Settlement Decision
docs.text:
Factors in valuing and settling:

Factor Consideration Liability Probability of adverse verdict or finding Damages Past/future medical, wage loss, pain and suffering Coverage Limits, exclusions, defense costs Comparative fault Allocation of responsibility Jury exposure Venue, sympathy, inflation of awards Costs of defense Litigation expense to verdict Collectibility Ability to pay judgment Claimant Representation, demands, credibility

docs.title: Negotiation
docs.text: Practice Description Anchor with evidence Open with reasoned, documented value Know authority Clear internal limit before negotiating Document offers All demands and offers recorded Time discipline Deadlines, litigation pressure Fair dealing No bad faith, no unreasonable offers

docs.title: Payment and Release
docs.text:
The settlement is completed with:

Document Purpose Release Claimant releases claims against insured/insurer Settlement agreement Terms, amounts, confidentiality Indemnity clause Protection for related future claims Dismissal (if in suit) Court dismissal with prejudice Check / EFT Payment issued to proper parties

docs.title: Denials
docs.text:
A denial must be:

Requirement Practice Timely Within regulatory timeframes In writing Clear statement of decision Reasoned Explain coverage basis and policy terms Fair Based on complete investigation Documented File supports the decision

Denial is a last resort after full investigation — premature or unfounded denials create bad faith exposure.

docs.title: Litigation and Defense
docs.text: Element Description Duty to defend Broader than duty to indemnify Panel counsel Approved defense attorneys Litigation management Budgets, strategies, settlement authority ROR/declaratory Coverage resolution parallel to defense Appeals Post-verdict appellate risk management

docs.title: ADR
docs.text:
Method Use Mediation Facilitated negotiation; non-binding Arbitration Binding decision by arbitrator Summary jury trial Advisory verdict to guide settlement Early neutral evaluation Expert opinion on value

ADR is often faster, cheaper, and more controllable than trial.

docs.title: Large and Complex Claims
docs.text: Feature Requirement Catastrophe Surge teams, fast triage, well-defined process Class actions Coverage strategy, defense coordination Environmental Multi-party, long-tail exposures, coverage issues Cyber Incident response, notification obligations, specialists

docs.title: Documentation of Resolution
docs.text:
The file must record:

  • The basis of the decision (evidence, liability, damages).
  • Authority and approvals.
  • All offers, demands, and counter-offers.
  • Settlement terms or denial reasons.
  • Payments and releases.
  • Communications with the insured and claimant.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Resolution is settlement, negotiation, ADR, litigation, or denial.
  • Authority limits must be respected and documented.
  • Settlements end claims with release and payment.
  • Denials require full investigation and clear explanation.
  • Documentation protects every decision.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:

  • 7.3 Coverage Analysis

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Reserving estimates the future cost of each claim; settlement converts that estimate into actual payment. Accurate reserves are essential for financial reporting, pricing, and management decisions.

docs.title: Case Reserves
docs.text:
The case reserve is the estimate of what the claim will ultimately cost, including:

Component Description Indemnity Payment to or for the insured/claimant Defense costs Legal fees and expenses Allocated loss expense (ALAE) Expert, investigation, medical costs Interest/penalties Potential statutory charges Salvage/subrogation Expected recoveries (net down if certain)

docs.title: Reserve Setting
docs.text: Principle Practice Best estimate Most likely ultimate cost, not minimum or maximum Timely Set at first evaluation; update as facts emerge Consistent Same methodology across the claim Reviewed Regular reserve adequacy reviews Documented Basis of the estimate recorded

docs.title: Reserve Ranges and Categories
docs.text: Category Meaning Initial reserve Set from FNOL and first investigation Minimum/maximum Range of possible outcomes Most likely Point estimate used for the case reserve Incurred but not reported (IBNR) Actuarial estimate for unreported claims (not the adjuster's case reserve)

docs.title: Reserve Adequacy
docs.text: Signal Meaning Settlements vs. reserves Actual payments above or below case reserves Aging of open claims Claims not closing; reserves may be stale Large loss reviews Periodic reassessment of high-severity claims Actuarial analysis Compare case + IBNR to ultimate estimates

docs.title: Payments
docs.text: Payment Type Example Advance Early payment for medical or emergency needs Interim Partial payment while claim continues Final Full settlement with release Defense payments Panel counsel and expert invoices Structured Periodic payments over time

docs.title: Settlement Mechanics
docs.text:
1. Value the claim (reserve review)
2. Obtain settlement authority
3. Negotiate to agreement
4. Prepare release and settlement documents
5. Issue payment to correct parties
6. Record and close reserve
7. Recover (subrogation/reinsurance) if applicable

docs.title: Payment Controls
docs.text: Control Purpose Payee verification Correct claimant, insured, attorney, provider Authority threshold Payment within delegated authority Two-party checks Where required (insured + lender) Duplicate payment checks No double payment Approval workflow Large payments reviewed Documentation Release, proof, file record

docs.title: Release Types
docs.text: Type Scope General release Claimant releases all claims related to the incident Indemnity agreement Protects insured/insurer from future claims Compromise release Settlement of disputed claim Release of subrogation Waives insurer's right to recover Structured settlement documents Payout terms, annuity

docs.title: Reserve and Settlement Review
docs.text: Review Frequency Initial reserve At claim setup Periodic review With investigation updates Large loss Monthly/weekly for high-severity Pre-settlement Final adequacy check Post-closure audit Compare actual vs. reserved

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Reserves estimate ultimate cost; settlement realizes it.
  • Reserves include indemnity, defense, ALAE, and net recoveries.
  • Authority, documentation, and controls govern payments.
  • Reserve adequacy reviews protect financial accuracy.
  • Settlement finalizes with releases, payments, and closure.

docs.title: Related Chapters
docs.text:
• 7.1 Claims Overview
  • 7.4 Claims Resolution
  • 7.6 Reinsurance & Subrogation
  • 5.2 Data & Loss Reserving

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Recoveries reduce the net cost of a claim. Reinsurance shifts loss to the reinsurer; subrogation recovers from responsible third parties; salvage recovers from damaged property. Effective recovery management materially improves loss ratios.

docs.title: The Recovery Concept
docs.text:
Gross loss
  − Reinsurance recovery (ceded share)
  − Subrogation recovery (third party)
  − Salvage recovery (property)
  = Net cost to the insurer

docs.title: Reinsurance in Claims
docs.text: Concept Description Ceded loss The reinsurer's share per the treaty/agreement Retention The insurer's own net retention Cession to quota share Fixed percentage of every loss Excess of loss Reinsurer pays above the retention per occurrence Per-risk vs. per-occurrence Attachment basis Recoverables Amount due from reinsurer Bordereaux Periodic claim reporting to reinsurers

docs.title: Claim Reporting to Reinsurers
docs.text:
Requirement Practice Notification Advise reinsurers of claims likely to hit the treaty Documentation Claim files, reserves, settlement rationale Bordereaux Periodic listing of ceded claims Settlement Bill recoverables after payment Approval rights Follow the treaty — settlement authority may require reinsurer consent

Treaty and facultative certificates define the claims cooperation and follow-the-fortunes clauses.

docs.title: Subrogation
docs.text:
Subrogation gives the insurer the right to step into the insured's position and recover what it paid from the party responsible for the loss.

Element Description Basis Equitable and contractual doctrine Insured must not prejudice No release of wrongdoer without consent Deductible The insured's deductible may be recoverable first Waiver of subrogation Contractual waiver; common in construction Limitations Preserves rights; prevent waiver

docs.title: Subrogation Process
docs.text:
1. Identify potential recovery (third-party fault, product, negligence)
2. Preserve evidence and legal deadlines
3. Investigate liability and collectibility
4. Demand or pursue claim against wrongdoer
5. Litigate or arbitrate if necessary
6. Recover; reimburse insured deductible and expenses
7. Allocate net recovery (insurer and insured shares)

docs.title: Salvage
docs.text: Type Example Salvage property Damaged total-loss vehicle sold or retained Salvage of goods Cargo, contents recovered Salvage offset Reduce net claim by salvage value Proof of salvage Inspection, salvage title, disposition

docs.title: Allocation of Recoveries
docs.text:
The allocation of a recovery among insurer, reinsurer, and insured depends on:

  • The excess or primary nature of the policy.
  • The reinsurance treaty terms.
  • The insured's deductible and self-insured retention.
  • Costs and expenses of the recovery.
Party Recovery Share (typical) Insured Deductible recovered first Primary insurer Its paid loss Reinsurer Its ceded share

docs.title: Recovery Ratio and Tracking
docs.text: Metric Purpose Subrogation recovery rate % of paid claims with recoveries Salvage recovery rate Salvage vs. paid total losses Reinsurance recovery Ceded recoverable received vs. billed Net loss ratio Loss ratio after recoveries

docs.title: Recovery Controls
docs.text: Control Purpose Recovery pipeline Track open recovery opportunities Deadline management Statutes of limitations Bordereaux accuracy Correct ceded premiums and claims Reconciliations Reinsurer statements vs. records Write-off authority Uncollectible recoveries approved

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Reinsurance, subrogation, and salvage reduce net claim cost.
  • Reinsurers require timely reporting and documentation.
  • Subrogation requires preserving rights and pursuing wrongdoers.
  • Salvage recovers value from damaged property.
  • Allocation and tracking ensure recoveries are credited properly.

  • 7.5 Reserving & Settlement
  • 5.8 Reinsurance
  • 1.3 The Insurance Business

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Claims operations depend on systems that handle notification, workflow, payments, and documents, and on analytics that detect fraud, predict outcomes, and measure performance. Good systems and data make claims faster, fairer, and more accurate.

docs.title: The Claims Management System (CMS)
docs.text: Function Description FNOL intake Capture, triage, and route claims Claim file Parties, coverage, documents, notes Reserving Case reserve setup and updates Workflow Assignments, approvals, task management Payments Checks, EFT, authority, releases Litigation management Counsel, budgets, deadlines Recovery tracking Subrogation, salvage, reinsurance Reporting Regulatory, management, performance

docs.title: Claims Data
docs.text:
Data Type Use Policy data Coverage verification, limits Claim data Facts, parties, damages Payment data Reserves, payouts, expenses Litigation data Counsel, fees, outcomes Fraud data Red flags, SIU cases External data Credit, weather, police, medical

Data quality controls — validation, deduplication, reconciliation — apply as in Volume 6.

docs.title: Analytics in Claims
docs.text: Application Description Fraud detection Rules and models flag suspicious claims Triaging Route claims by complexity and severity Reserve estimation Predictive models for reserve ranges Settlement prediction Likely outcome and value ranges Litigation prediction Verdict and cost forecasts Customer scoring Complexity, service needs Hotspot mapping Catastrophe and weather response

docs.title: Fraud Detection
docs.text:
Indicator Example Late reporting Delay with suspicious timing Inconsistent story Changing details between statements Staged/planned events Common patterns (auto, slip-and-fall) Exaggerated damage/demands Built-up losses False documentation Forged bills, medical reports Relationships Claimant-insured connections MVR/prior claims History of similar losses

Refer suspicious claims to Special Investigation Unit (SIU).

docs.title: The SIU Process
docs.text:
Referral → Review → Investigation → Conclusion → Action
Step Activity Referral Adjuster flags indicators Review SIU confirms or clears Investigation Surveillance, statements, records Conclusion Deny, prosecute, or close Action Referral to law enforcement if criminal

docs.title: Automation
docs.text: Automation Benefits FNOL auto-adjudication Simple claims settled instantly Document OCR Faster intake and indexing Workflow routing Claim to the right adjuster Payment automation Fewer errors, faster payments Chatbots First-line customer service Robotic process automation (RPA) Repetitive tasks (data entry, checks)

docs.title: Claims Analytics Metrics
docs.text: Metric Use Fraud referral rate SIU volume and culling Reserve accuracy Settlements vs. reserves Cycle time Speed of resolution Cost per claim Indemnity + expenses Recovery rate Subrogation/salvage success Customer satisfaction NPS, complaints Litigation rate Claims ending in suit

docs.title: Systems Integration
docs.text: Interface Purpose Policy system Coverage, limits, status Billing Premium and deductible details Finance Payments, GL posting Reinsurance Ceded claim reporting Fraud databases Industry loss and fraud sharing External vendors Repair networks, medical, experts

docs.title: Common System Issues
docs.text: Issue Impact Stale policy data Wrong coverage decisions Manual data entry Errors and delays Siloed systems No single claim view Poor document capture Evidence conflicts Uncontrolled access Privacy and security risk

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The CMS manages notification through closure.
  • Analytics detect fraud, predict outcomes, and guide triage.
  • SIU investigates suspicious claims.
  • Automation improves speed, accuracy, and cost.
  • Integration and data quality are foundational.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Claims are one of the most regulated and scrutinized functions in insurance. Fair, prompt, and accurate claim handling is both a legal requirement and the foundation of trust. Compliance failures produce regulatory action, litigation, and reputational damage.

docs.title: Fair Claims Practices
docs.text:
Principle Application Prompt acknowledgment Respond to claims within deadlines Complete investigation Reasonable inquiry before decision Fair settlement Offer what is owed; no lowballing No unreasonable delay Timely decisions and payments Clear communication Explain decisions and policy basis No misrepresentation Never misstate policy terms or coverage Good faith Act honestly toward the insured

Most jurisdictions have Unfair Claims Settlement Practices Acts (or equivalent) with specific prohibited acts.

docs.title: Regulatory Frameworks
docs.text:
Framework Scope US state regulations Claims practice acts, unfair trade practices, licensing NAIC model acts Model unfair claims settlement practices UK FCA rules Fair treatment of customers, claims outcomes EU/EEA Conduct of business, consumer protection Market conduct exams State reviews of claims practices

See 1.5 The Legal Environment.

docs.title: Compliance Requirements
docs.text: Requirement Practice Acknowledgment of notice Within regulatory timeframe Coverage decision Within statutory deadline Claim payment Promptly after agreement or judgment Denial explanation Written, with policy basis Reservation of rights Issued when coverage uncertain Record retention Claims files kept per schedule Complaint handling Centralized, timely, reported Privacy Protect claimant and medical data

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The US insurance market is the world's largest, characterized by state-based regulation, a wide range of distribution channels, and a deep reinsurance market. It is a property/casualty and life/health market served by thousands of insurers, spanning personal, commercial, and specialty lines.

docs.text: Participant Role Insurers Primary risk bearers (stock, mutual, reciprocal) Reinsurers Capacity and risk transfer above primary limits Producers Independent agents, captive agents, brokers MGAs/MGUs Delegated underwriting and policy issuance TPAs Claims and administration services Advisory organizations ISO, NCCI, AAIS — forms and data Regulators State insurance departments and NAIC

The US is served by global reinsurers (Munich Re, Swiss Re, Hannover Re) and domestic specialists.

docs.text:
• The US market is the world's largest insurance market.
  • State regulation and admitted/non-admitted structure define the market.
  • Distribution spans agents, brokers, direct, and MGAs.
  • Reinsurance provides capacity and stability.
  • The market is cyclical, influenced by capacity, losses, and investments.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The US insurance regulatory system is state-based. Each state regulates the business of insurance within its borders — insurer solvency, market conduct, rates, forms, producer licensing, and consumer protection. The NAIC provides coordination, while a limited federal role has developed through the Federal Insurance Office (FIO) and specialized statutes (e.g., Dodd-Frank, TRIA).

docs.title: The Constitutional Basis
docs.text:
• The McCarran-Ferguson Act (1945) grants states the authority to regulate the "business of insurance" without federal preemption.
  • States define insurance, license insurers and producers, and regulate rates and forms.
  • Federal law applies to insurance only where a specific statute directs (e.g., antitrust, RICO, employment).

docs.title: Key Regulators
docs.text: Regulator Role State insurance department Solvency, market conduct, licensing, consumer protection Nationwide association (NAIC) Model laws, financial standards, accreditation, interstate coordination Federal Insurance Office (FIO) Federal monitoring, international agreements (Treasury) Federal Reserve / FSOC Insurance companies deemed systemically important; thrift holding companies Department of Labor ERISA plans; fiduciary and claims standards SEC Variable life/annuity and securities-linked products

docs.title: State Regulatory Functions
docs.text: Function Description Licensing/admission Certificate of authority to transact business Financial regulation Capital, reserves, RBC, examinations Rate regulation Filing, approval, or use-and-file Form regulation Policy form and endorsement filings Market conduct Marketing, underwriting, claims, complaints Producer licensing Agents, brokers, adjusters, MGAs Consumer protection Complaints, unfair trade practices, market conduct exams

docs.title: NAIC Model Laws and Accreditation
docs.text:
The NAIC develops model laws that states may adopt:

Model Purpose Risk-Based Capital (RBC) Capital requirements scaled to risk Financial examination Uniform examination standards Market conduct annual statement Uniform market conduct reporting Unfair Claims Settlement Practices Fair claim handling standards Privacy (GLBA) Consumer financial privacy protections Insurance Holding Company Group supervision and solvency

States that adopt key models are accredited — accreditation is required for regulatory cooperation.

docs.title: Rate and Form Regulation
docs.text:
System Description States Prior approval Rates/forms in effect only after approval Many personal lines states Use-and-file Rates used; filed after use Some commercial states File-and-use Filed before/with use; effective then Liberal states Open competition No formal filing; market discipline Larger commercial states Flex rating Rate changes within band without filing A few states

See 8.3 Forms, Rates & Rules.

docs.title: Market Conduct Regulation
docs.text:
Area Key Requirements Underwriting No unfair discrimination (protected classes) Rates Not excessive, inadequate, or unfairly discriminatory Claims Fair claims practice acts; prompt, timely handling Advertising Truthful; no misleading statements Privacy GLBA financial privacy rules Complaints Respond to state regulator inquiries

States conduct market conduct examinations — targeted or full-scope reviews of an insurer's business practices.

docs.title: The Federal Role
docs.text: Statute Scope McCarran-Ferguson State authority; limited antitrust exemption Terrorism Risk Insurance Act (TRIA) Federal backstop for certified terrorism losses Dodd-Frank FIO, FSOC, federal oversight of systemic risk Flood Insurance (NFIP) Federally administered flood program Surplus lines (NRRA) Surplus lines licensing reform — single home state ERISA Employee benefit plan regulation

docs.title: Insurance Guaranty Funds
docs.text:
• Each state has a guaranty fund for insolvent insurers.
  • Funds pay covered claims up to statutory limits.
  • Funded by assessments on insurers based on premium.
  • Cover admitted insurers; surplus lines have separate mechanisms.

docs.title: Consumer Protection
docs.text: Protection Practice Free look Life/health cancellation periods Cancellation rules Notice periods and reasons Renewal/non-renewal notice Statutory notice requirements Fraud bureau State fraud investigation units Complaint handling State complaint process and records

docs.title: Regulatory Trends
docs.text: Trend Impact NAIC modernization Data collection, cyber, climate risk Rate transparency Public rate filing data Consumer duty Conduct-of-business standards Climate risk Disclosure and solvency scrutiny Technology Regulatory sandboxes, AI guidance

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The US system is state-based, coordinated by the NAIC.
  • States regulate solvency, rates, forms, market conduct, and licensing.
  • The federal role is limited but growing (FIO, TRIA, systemic risk).
  • Guaranty funds protect policyholders from insolvency.
  • Insurers must navigate state-specific filing and conduct rules.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: States regulate the forms (policy wordings), rates (pricing), and rules (classification and eligibility standards) used by insurers. The filing system and approval standards differ by state and line of business — personal lines are more strictly controlled; commercial and surplus lines allow greater freedom.

docs.title: The Three Components
docs.text: Component Definition Forms Policy language — insuring agreements, exclusions, conditions, endorsements Rates Premium pricing — base rates, rating factors, schedules Rules Eligibility, classification, coverage rules, underwriting restrictions

docs.title: Filing Systems
docs.text: System How It Works Use Prior approval Rates/forms effective only after regulator approval Personal lines in many states File-and-use Filed; use after a waiting period Common hybrid Use-and-file Used; filed after effective date Commercial lines Open competition No filing; compliance with standards Some commercial states Flex rating Pre-approved band; changes outside need filing A few states

docs.title: Standards for Approval
docs.text:
Rates must not be:

  • Excessive — above what is justified by expected losses and costs.
  • Inadequate — below the cost of coverage and expenses.
  • Unfairly discriminatory — differences not related to risk.

Forms are reviewed for:

  • Compliance with state insurance law.
  • Clarity — no misleading or deceptive language.
  • Consistency with filed rates and rules.
  • Public policy — no provisions contrary to law.

docs.title: The Filing Process
docs.text:
1. Prepare filing (forms, rates, rules, actuarial support)
2. File with the state (SERFF or paper)
3. Regulator review (approval, modification, rejection)
4. Implement on approval or after waiting period
5. Maintain and update (revisions, withdrawals)

SERFF (System for Electronic Rate and Form Filing) is the NAIC's e-filing platform.

docs.title: What Must Be Filed
docs.text:
Filing Typical Requirement New forms Policy and endorsement forms Rate changes Base rates, rating factors Rule changes Eligibility, classifications New products Full package filing Program changes Deviations from bureau filings

Large commercial insureds and surplus lines may be exempt from form/rate filings.

docs.title: Advisory Organizations
docs.text:
Organization Role ISO (Insurance Services Office) Commercial and personal forms, advisory rates NCCI Workers compensation forms and class rates AAIS Database and forms services State rating bureaus Some states retain approved bureaus

Insurers may adopt bureau filings or file independently (deviations).

docs.title: Rate Filings — Actuarial Support
docs.text: Element Support Experience data Losses, exposure, premium history Trend Loss cost trend and inflation Development Loss development to ultimate Credibility Volume-weighted blending Expenses Acquisition, overhead, premium taxes Profit/risk load Target return and volatility Loss reserve margin Provision for adverse deviation

docs.title: Implementation Controls
docs.text: Control Purpose Approval tracking Effective dates per state Version control Correct form edition in force Rate tables Approved rates loaded correctly System updates Rating engine aligned with filings Audit trail Filing status and approvals documented

docs.title: Common Filing Issues
docs.text: Issue Impact Late filing Use of unapproved rates/forms Incorrect rate table Over/undercharging Form vs. rule mismatch Underwriting errors Missing state-specific endorsement Non-compliance No actuarial support Rejection or re-filing

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Forms, rates, and rules are filed and regulated per state.
  • Approval standards — not excessive, inadequate, or unfairly discriminatory.
  • SERFF and bureau filings streamline the process.
  • Actuarial support justifies rate changes.
  • Controls align approved filings with actual issuance.
